definition: Not willing or eager to do something, usually because you are uncertain, uncomfortable, or have doubts about it.
usage: Usually followed by “to + verb”: reluctant to admit, reluctant to commit, reluctant to intervene. The adverb “reluctantly” is very common: “She reluctantly agreed.” Compared with “unwilling”, “reluctant” suggests hesitation rather than a flat refusal; a reluctant person may still go ahead in the end.
examples: I was reluctant to go at first, but I'm glad I did.
She was reluctant to accept the offer because of the long commute.
He's usually reluctant to talk about his personal life.
The company was reluctant to invest more money without seeing better results.
Many participants were reluctant to disclose their income, which may have skewed the survey results.

definition: To accept or admit that something exists, is true, or is important, often after resisting it at first. It can also mean to show that you have noticed someone or received something.
usage: Common patterns: acknowledge that…, acknowledge a problem/mistake/limitation, be widely acknowledged as… In academic writing it is a key verb for conceding a point before arguing against it: “While it must be acknowledged that…, …”. “Acknowledge receipt of” is a formal email phrase meaning to confirm that you have received something.
examples: The authors acknowledge that their sample was relatively small.
He finally acknowledged that he had made a mistake.
She didn't even acknowledge me when I walked into the room.
Please acknowledge receipt of this email at your earliest convenience.
It is widely acknowledged that early intervention leads to better outcomes.

definition: A tendency to favour one person, group, or idea over another in a way that is unfair or that distorts your judgement.
usage: Often followed by “against” or “towards/in favour of”: a bias against older applicants. Collocations: confirmation bias, gender bias, unconscious bias, media bias, introduce/reduce bias. The adjective “biased” (biased reporting, a biased sample) is just as common. In research, “bias” also means a systematic error in how data is collected or analysed, not only personal prejudice.
examples: Confirmation bias leads us to notice evidence that supports what we already believe.
The study was criticized for selection bias, since all the volunteers were university students.
I try not to let personal bias affect how I mark the essays.
There is a well-documented bias against candidates with foreign-sounding names.
Every news outlet has some degree of bias, so it helps to read more than one.

definition: Certain to happen and impossible to avoid or prevent.
usage: Often used in “it is inevitable that…” or as a noun phrase: “accept the inevitable”. The adverb “inevitably” frequently opens a sentence to signal a predictable consequence. Collocations: an inevitable consequence/result/conflict; almost/virtually/seemingly inevitable. In casual speech it can sound mildly ironic: “the inevitable question about when I'm getting married”.
examples: Some disagreement is inevitable when people with different backgrounds work together.
With costs rising so quickly, a price increase was almost inevitable.
Job losses are an inevitable consequence of automation in some industries.
At every family dinner, there's the inevitable question about when I'm going to get married.
Inevitably, the meeting ran over time.
Change can feel uncomfortable, but it is often inevitable.

definition: To accept that something is true without having proof of it. In a more formal sense, it can also mean to take on a role, responsibility, or quality.
usage: Most often followed by a “that” clause, with “that” frequently dropped in speech: “I assumed (that) you'd already left.” “Let's assume…” introduces a hypothetical scenario. In academic writing: “This model assumes that…”, “It is commonly assumed that…”. The noun “assumption” collocates with make, challenge, and underlying. The formal sense appears in “assume responsibility/control/office”.
examples: I assumed you'd already heard the news, so I didn't mention it.
The model assumes that consumers always act rationally, which is rarely the case.
Don't assume everyone understands the jargon; explain it the first time you use it.
She will assume the role of department head next month.
Let's assume, for the sake of argument, that the budget doubles next year.

definition: General agreement among the members of a group about something.
usage: Patterns: reach/achieve/build a consensus; a broad/growing/general consensus; a consensus on/about something; a consensus that… “Scientific consensus” refers to the collective position of experts in a field. “General consensus” is sometimes criticized as redundant, but it is widely used. Watch the spelling: it is “consensus”, not “concensus”.
examples: After hours of discussion, the committee finally reached a consensus.
There is a broad scientific consensus that human activity is driving climate change.
We couldn't reach a consensus on where to eat, so we ended up ordering pizza.
The growing consensus among economists is that interest rates will fall next year.
Good leaders try to build consensus rather than simply impose decisions.

definition: Large or important enough to have a noticeable effect or to deserve attention. In statistics, it describes a result that is unlikely to have occurred by chance.
usage: Collocations: a significant increase/difference/impact/role; statistically significant; significantly higher/lower. In research writing, avoid using “significant” loosely if you have not run a statistical test, because readers may take it in its technical sense. “Significant other” is a neutral, slightly informal way to refer to someone's partner.
examples: There has been a significant increase in remote work since 2020.
The difference between the two groups was not statistically significant.
Social media plays a significant role in how young people form opinions.
Moving abroad was the most significant decision I've ever made.
Rents are significantly higher in the city centre.
You're welcome to bring your significant other to the party.

definition: To expect something to happen, and often to prepare for it in advance.
usage: Patterns: anticipate a problem/demand/change; anticipate that…; anticipate doing something. It is more formal than “expect” and often implies acting ahead of time: a good manager anticipates problems before they arise. “Eagerly/highly anticipated” describes something people are excited about, such as a film or a product launch.
examples: We didn't anticipate so many people turning up, so we ran out of chairs.
The authors anticipate that demand for electric vehicles will continue to rise.
A good teacher anticipates where students are likely to struggle.
Her new novel is one of the most eagerly anticipated books of the year.
Try to anticipate the interviewer's questions and prepare your answers in advance.

definition: Something that limits or restricts what you can do.
usage: Often plural: time constraints, budget/financial constraints, practical constraints. Patterns: a constraint on something; work within (the) constraints; impose constraints. The verb “constrain” and the adjective “constrained” (“we're constrained by…”) are also common in academic and professional English. Compared with “limitation”, “constraint” tends to suggest an external pressure rather than a weakness.
examples: Due to time constraints, we'll have to skip the Q&A session.
The project had to be completed within tight budget constraints.
Funding constraints meant that the study could only follow participants for six months.
Living with my parents puts some constraints on my social life.
Good design often comes from working creatively within constraints.

definition: Large in amount, size, or importance; considerable. It can also describe something solidly built, or a meal that is filling.
usage: Collocations: a substantial amount/number/increase/improvement; substantial evidence; substantially reduce/improve. It is more formal than “big” or “large” and is common in academic and business writing. “Substantial” emphasizes real, measurable size, whereas “significant” emphasizes importance or impact.
examples: The new policy led to a substantial reduction in waiting times.
There is substantial evidence that regular exercise improves mental health.
He inherited a substantial sum of money from his grandfather.
Make sure you eat a substantial breakfast before the hike.
The second draft is substantially better than the first.

definition: To say or believe that something is caused by a particular thing, or that a piece of work, a quotation, or a quality belongs to a particular person.
usage: The key pattern is “attribute something to something/someone”: attribute success to hard work; a quotation often attributed to Einstein. It is frequently passive in academic writing: “The decline can be attributed to…”. As a noun (/ˈætrɪbjuːt/, stressed on the first syllable), an attribute is a quality or feature: “Patience is an important attribute in a teacher.”
examples: She attributes her success to a supportive family and a lot of hard work.
The drop in sales can largely be attributed to the economic slowdown.
This quote is often attributed to Einstein, but there's no evidence he ever said it.
Researchers attribute the improvement to smaller class sizes.
He attributed his bad mood to a lack of sleep.

definition: A situation in which you have to make a difficult choice between two or more options, especially when none of them is entirely satisfactory.
usage: Collocations: face a dilemma, be in a dilemma, a moral/ethical dilemma, resolve a dilemma. “The dilemma of whether to…” introduces the choice. Strictly speaking, a dilemma involves a hard choice, so avoid using it as a simple synonym for “problem”. “On the horns of a dilemma” is an idiomatic, slightly literary expression.
examples: I'm facing a real dilemma: take the better-paid job or stay somewhere I'm happy.
Doctors often face ethical dilemmas when resources are limited.
The study highlights a familiar dilemma between protecting privacy and improving public safety.
Many parents face the dilemma of whether to go back to work or stay at home with their children.
She was in a dilemma about whether to tell her friend the truth.

definition: Behaving or happening in the same way over time; also, in agreement with other facts or principles, so that there is no contradiction.
usage: Two main patterns: “consistent in” (consistent in quality/approach) and “consistent with” (the results are consistent with earlier studies). “Consistent with” is a standard academic phrase for saying that findings support or match something. The adverb “consistently” (consistently high, consistently late) and the noun “consistency” are also very common. The opposite is “inconsistent”.
examples: These findings are consistent with previous research on sleep and memory.
If you want to improve, you need to practise consistently, not just before exams.
Her performance has been remarkably consistent throughout the season.
His story wasn't consistent with what the witnesses said.
Use a consistent referencing style throughout your essay.

definition: To make something clearer or easier to understand, usually by explaining it in more detail.
usage: Patterns: clarify a point/issue/position; clarify what/how/whether… “Just to clarify, …” is a polite way to check understanding or correct a misunderstanding. The noun is “clarification”: ask for/seek clarification. In meetings and emails, “Could you clarify…?” is a polite, professional way to ask for more detail.
examples: Could you clarify what you mean by “flexible hours”?
Just to clarify, are we meeting at ten or eleven?
The second section clarifies the key terms used in the study.
I emailed the lecturer to ask for clarification on the essay question.
The company issued a statement to clarify its position on the issue.

definition: A difference between two things that should be the same or that are expected to match.
usage: Patterns: a discrepancy between A and B; a discrepancy in something (figures, accounts, results). Collocations: a significant/slight discrepancy; notice/explain/resolve a discrepancy. It is a formal word typical of academic, financial, and legal contexts. In everyday speech, people might say “a difference” or “something doesn't add up”.
examples: There is a clear discrepancy between what the company says and what it actually does.
The auditors found several discrepancies in the accounts.
Can you explain the discrepancy between these two sets of figures?
The discrepancy in the results may be due to differences in sample size.
I noticed a small discrepancy between the price on the shelf and the price at the till.

definition: Closely connected to the subject or situation being discussed, and therefore useful or important.
usage: Usually followed by “to”: relevant to the topic/question/discussion. Collocations: highly/directly relevant; relevant information/experience/evidence. “Stay relevant” means continuing to matter or to be popular. The opposite is “irrelevant”, and the noun is “relevance”.
examples: Only include information that is directly relevant to the research question.
Do you have any relevant work experience?
That's an interesting point, but I'm not sure it's relevant to what we're discussing.
Traditional media companies are struggling to stay relevant.
Please bring all relevant documents to the appointment.

definition: To reduce or balance out the bad effect of something; also, to pay someone money because they have suffered loss, injury, or inconvenience.
usage: Patterns: compensate for something (compensate for a lack of experience); compensate someone for something (compensate workers for overtime). Note the preposition: you compensate for a weakness, not compensate a weakness. The noun “compensation” is common in legal and HR contexts, where it can also mean pay and benefits as a whole (“a compensation package”).
examples: She works extra hard to compensate for her lack of experience.
The airline compensated passengers for the long delay.
Nothing can compensate for the loss of a loved one.
Higher salaries may partly compensate for the high cost of living in the capital.
Victims of the accident will be fully compensated.

definition: A disadvantage or problem that makes something less attractive or useful.
usage: Patterns: a drawback of/to something; the main/major/only drawback. Typical in balanced discussions: “One drawback of this approach is that…”. It is a little less formal than “disadvantage” and is often used when weighing pros and cons. Near-synonyms: downside (informal), limitation (academic), shortcoming.
examples: The main drawback of living in the city centre is the noise.
One drawback of this method is that it requires a very large sample.
The job pays well, but the long hours are a major drawback.
Every option has its drawbacks, so we need to decide which ones we can live with.
The only drawback is that the hotel is a bit far from the station.

definition: Extremely important, especially because it will decide what happens next.
usage: Patterns: crucial to/for something; it is crucial that…; it is crucial to + verb. Collocations: a crucial role/factor/moment/decision. “Crucial” is stronger than “important” and suggests that success depends on it. In formal writing, “it is crucial that” is often followed by the base form of the verb: “It is crucial that every student attend.”
examples: Sleep plays a crucial role in consolidating memory.
It's crucial to back up your files regularly.
The next few weeks will be crucial for the company's future.
Early diagnosis is crucial to successful treatment.
He missed a crucial penalty in the final minutes of the match.

definition: To show or state that something is not true because it is the opposite of another statement or fact; also, to openly disagree with what someone has just said.
usage: Patterns: contradict a statement/claim/finding; contradict someone; contradict yourself (say two things that cannot both be true). Collocations: directly/flatly contradict. The noun “contradiction” and the adjective “contradictory” (contradictory evidence) are common in academic writing. Contradicting someone in public can sound rude, so people often soften it: “I don't want to contradict you, but…”.
examples: These results directly contradict the findings of earlier studies.
You're contradicting yourself: a minute ago you said you hated the film.
I didn't want to contradict my boss in front of the client.
The witness's statement contradicts the footage from the security cameras.
Recent data appears to contradict the government's claim that unemployment is falling.

definition: Enough in quantity, or good enough in quality, for a particular purpose, though often no more than that.
usage: Patterns: adequate for something; adequate to + verb. Collocations: adequate funding/resources/training/sleep; an adequate supply. Note the nuance: “adequate” often sounds lukewarm, so calling a performance or a hotel “adequate” implies it was acceptable but not impressive. The opposite, “inadequate”, is common when criticizing policies or provision: “inadequate housing”.
examples: Many students don't get adequate sleep during exam season.
The hospital lacks adequate funding to hire more nurses.
The hotel was adequate, but I wouldn't stay there again.
Make sure you allow adequate time for revision before the final exam.
Without adequate training, staff are unlikely to use the new system properly.

definition: To become worse in quality, condition, or value over time.
usage: Intransitive: something deteriorates (you don't “deteriorate something”). Collocations: health/relations/conditions/the situation deteriorate(s); deteriorate rapidly/sharply/steadily; deteriorate into chaos/violence. The noun is “deterioration”. It is more formal than “get worse” and is common in news reports, medical contexts, and academic writing.
examples: His health deteriorated rapidly after the operation.
Relations between the two countries have deteriorated over the past year.
If the weather deteriorates, the match will be postponed.
Without regular maintenance, the old building has steadily deteriorated.
The discussion quickly deteriorated into a shouting match.

definition: A set of ideas, principles, or rules that forms the basis for how something is organized, understood, or decided. Literally, a supporting structure around which something is built.
usage: Collocations: a theoretical/conceptual/legal/regulatory framework; within a framework; provide/develop/establish a framework. In academic writing, a “theoretical framework” is the set of theories a study uses to interpret its data. In software, a framework is a reusable structure for building applications.
examples: The study draws on a theoretical framework developed in the 1980s.
The government needs a clear legal framework for regulating artificial intelligence.
All decisions must be made within the framework of the existing budget.
This checklist provides a simple framework for planning your week.
Most web developers use a framework rather than writing everything from scratch.

definition: Able to be understood in more than one way, so that the intended meaning is unclear.
usage: Collocations: an ambiguous statement/answer/message/result; deliberately/highly ambiguous. The noun is “ambiguity”. Don't confuse “ambiguous” (having more than one possible meaning) with “ambivalent” (having mixed feelings). In academic writing, ambiguous results are ones that could support more than one conclusion.
examples: The wording of the question is ambiguous, so students interpreted it in different ways.
His reply was deliberately ambiguous: he didn't say yes, but he didn't say no either.
The results were ambiguous and require further investigation.
“I saw her duck” is a classic example of an ambiguous sentence.
Try to avoid ambiguous terms when you write instructions.

definition: To become, or to make something, smaller, weaker, or less important.
usage: Can be intransitive (the pain gradually diminished) or transitive (diminish the risk/impact). “Diminishing returns” describes a situation where each additional effort brings less benefit than the last. “Diminish someone's achievements” means to make them seem less impressive than they really are. It is more formal than “reduce” or “decrease”.
examples: The pain should diminish over the next few days.
Regular exercise can diminish the risk of heart disease.
Her enthusiasm for the project diminished as the deadlines piled up.
After about two hours of studying, you start to experience diminishing returns.
I don't want to diminish his achievement, but he did have a lot of help.

definition: An idea or explanation based on limited evidence that has not yet been proved, used as a starting point for further investigation.
usage: Plural: hypotheses /haɪˈpɒθəsiːz/. Collocations: test/support/reject/confirm a hypothesis; formulate/propose a hypothesis; the hypothesis that… In research, a hypothesis is a specific, testable prediction; in everyday speech, people more often say “theory” for the same idea. The adjective “hypothetical” describes an imagined situation: “a hypothetical question”.
examples: The data supports the hypothesis that bilingual children develop stronger attention control.
The researchers designed an experiment to test this hypothesis.
Our initial hypothesis turned out to be wrong.
One hypothesis is that the virus jumped from animals to humans.
My working hypothesis is that the printer stopped working because someone changed the settings.

definition: Seeming reasonable and likely to be true, though not necessarily proven.
usage: Collocations: a plausible explanation/argument/excuse/scenario; perfectly/highly plausible. “It is plausible that…” is common in academic writing. The word can carry a note of caution: a plausible excuse may still be false. The opposite is “implausible”, and the noun is “plausibility”.
examples: There are several plausible explanations for these results.
Her excuse sounded plausible, but I still didn't quite believe her.
It is plausible that the policy had some effect, but the evidence is weak.
The film's plot is entertaining, if not entirely plausible.
A more plausible scenario is that prices will rise gradually rather than suddenly.

definition: To give special importance or attention to something in speech or writing, so that people notice it.
usage: Patterns: emphasize something; emphasize that…; emphasize the importance/need for something. There is no “on” after the verb: you emphasize a point (not “emphasize on” it), but you put or place emphasis on it. British English also accepts the spelling “emphasise”. In speech, you can emphasize a word simply by stressing it.
examples: The report emphasizes the need for further research.
I want to emphasize that this is only a first draft.
The teacher emphasized the importance of citing sources correctly.
She emphasized every word to make sure I understood.
The brochure emphasizes the hotel's location, not its rather small rooms.

definition: A possible effect or result of an action or decision, usually one that is not immediately obvious; also, something that is suggested without being stated directly.
usage: Often plural: the implications of something for something (“the implications of AI for education”). Collocations: have implications; serious/important/far-reaching implications; consider the implications. In the second sense: “The implication is that…”, “by implication”. The related verb is “imply”.
examples: We need to consider the implications of this decision for local businesses.
The findings have important implications for how we teach reading.
The implication of her comment was that I wasn't working hard enough.
Few people understand the long-term financial implications of taking out a student loan.
He criticized the manager and, by implication, the whole department.

definition: Possible to do or achieve in practice, given the time, money, and resources available.
usage: Patterns: it is feasible to + verb; feasible for someone; technically/economically/financially feasible. A “feasibility study” assesses whether a project is practical before it begins. “Feasible” focuses on practicality, whereas “possible” is broader: something can be possible in theory but not feasible in reality.
examples: Is it feasible to finish the project by Friday?
The plan is technically feasible but far too expensive.
Working from home isn't feasible for everyone, especially people in healthcare.
Building a second airport may not be economically feasible.
The most feasible option is to delay the launch by a month.

definition: To improve the quality, value, or effectiveness of something, especially something that is already good or useful.
usage: Collocations: enhance performance/quality/understanding/reputation/the experience. “Enhance” usually suggests adding to something that already has value, while “improve” can also mean fixing something that is bad. It is common in academic, marketing, and technical language: “performance-enhancing drugs”, “enhanced security”.
examples: Good lighting can enhance the atmosphere of a room.
The course is designed to enhance students' critical thinking skills.
Volunteering abroad can enhance your CV.
The new version of the app features enhanced security.
Several athletes were banned for using performance-enhancing drugs.

definition: Something that encourages a person or organization to do something, such as a reward or the prospect of a benefit.
usage: Patterns: an incentive to do something; an incentive for someone; incentives for something. Collocations: a financial/tax incentive; provide/offer an incentive; have little/no incentive to… In economics, people are said to “respond to incentives”, meaning their behaviour changes when rewards or costs change. The opposite is “disincentive”.
examples: The government offers tax incentives to companies that invest in renewable energy.
There's little incentive to save when interest rates are so low.
Bonuses give employees an incentive to work harder.
A free coffee was enough of an incentive to get me to the meeting on time.
Economists argue that people respond to incentives, even when they don't realize it.

definition: Including all, or nearly all, the details or aspects of something; complete and thorough.
usage: Collocations: a comprehensive review/guide/study/list/overview; comprehensive coverage/insurance. It often describes research or documents that aim to cover a topic fully. Don't confuse it with “comprehensible”, which means “able to be understood”. In the UK, a “comprehensive school” is a state secondary school that does not select pupils by ability.
examples: This is the most comprehensive study of the topic to date.
The website offers a comprehensive guide to applying for a student visa.
We need a comprehensive plan, not a series of short-term fixes.
Comprehensive car insurance covers damage to your own vehicle as well as to others.
The report gives a comprehensive overview of the housing market.

definition: To make an action or process easier, or to help it happen more smoothly.
usage: Takes a direct object: facilitate learning/communication/discussion/trade (not “facilitate someone to do something”). It is formal and very common in academic and professional writing. A “facilitator” is someone who guides a discussion or workshop without directing its content.
examples: The new software facilitates communication between departments.
Good lighting and comfortable seating can facilitate learning.
Her role is to facilitate the discussion, not to give her own opinions.
The agreement is designed to facilitate trade between the two countries.
Online banking has facilitated the shift towards a cashless society.

definition: A clear and deep understanding of a complex situation or problem; also, a piece of knowledge that helps you understand something better.
usage: Patterns: insight into something; gain/provide/offer insight(s). Collocations: valuable/useful/fresh/deep insight. The adjective “insightful” means showing deep understanding: an insightful comment. In business, “insights” often refers to useful conclusions drawn from data.
examples: The interviews gave us valuable insight into how students actually use the library.
Travelling abroad gave me new insights into my own culture.
Her memoir offers fascinating insights into the life of a surgeon.
Thanks for your feedback; that was a really insightful comment.
The aim of the survey is to gain insight into customer behaviour.

definition: Causing a lot of public disagreement or heated debate, because people hold very different opinions about it.
usage: Collocations: a controversial issue/decision/figure/topic; highly/deeply controversial. The noun is “controversy”: cause/spark/provoke controversy. In discussion, “This may be controversial, but…” signals that you are about to say something others may disagree with. In British English the noun has two accepted stress patterns: /ˈkɒntrəvɜːsi/ and /kənˈtrɒvəsi/.
examples: Nuclear power remains a controversial topic in many countries.
The referee made a controversial decision in the final minute.
This might be a controversial opinion, but I think the sequel is better than the original.
The policy proved highly controversial and was eventually withdrawn.
Social media platforms are under pressure to deal with controversial content.

definition: To make it difficult for something to happen or progress, or for someone to do something.
usage: Patterns: hinder progress/development/growth; hinder someone from doing something; hinder someone's efforts. It is more formal than “hold back” and weaker than “prevent”: hindering slows something down, while preventing stops it completely. The noun is “hindrance”: “more of a hindrance than a help”.
examples: Poor internet access can hinder students' learning.
Heavy rain hindered rescue efforts throughout the day.
Strict regulations may hinder innovation in the tech sector.
Her shyness hindered her from speaking up in meetings.
Don't let one bad grade hinder your progress.

definition: An idea, belief, or concept, especially one that is vague, questionable, or not fully supported by evidence.
usage: Patterns: the notion that…; the notion of something. Collocations: reject/challenge/support the notion; a vague notion; have no notion of. In academic writing, “the notion of” introduces a concept under examination: “the notion of national identity”. “Notion” often suggests that an idea is doubtful or only partly formed.
examples: Many people still hold the notion that intelligence is fixed at birth.
This study challenges the notion that older adults cannot learn new languages.
I had a vague notion that the deadline was sometime next week.
The essay explores the notion of freedom in modern society.
She rejected the notion that success is purely a matter of luck.

definition: Easily harmed or hurt, whether physically, emotionally, or in some other way; also, open to attack or criticism.
usage: Patterns: vulnerable to something (vulnerable to infection/attack/criticism). Collocations: vulnerable groups/people/children; particularly/highly vulnerable. The noun is “vulnerability”. In personal contexts, “being vulnerable” can be positive, meaning being emotionally open and honest.
examples: Older people are especially vulnerable to the flu.
The policy aims to protect the most vulnerable members of society.
Outdated software leaves your computer vulnerable to attack.
It takes courage to be vulnerable and admit that you're struggling.
Coastal cities are particularly vulnerable to rising sea levels.

definition: To put a plan, decision, policy, or system into action.
usage: Collocations: implement a plan/policy/strategy/change/reform; fully/successfully implement. The noun is “implementation”. It is common in business, government, and computing (“implement a feature”). As a noun, “implement” (/ˈɪmplɪmənt/) means a tool, especially one used in farming or cooking.
examples: The school will implement the new timetable next term.
The government has been slow to implement the recommended reforms.
Coming up with a good idea is easy; implementing it is the hard part.
The developers implemented the new feature in just two weeks.
Successful implementation depends on support from staff at every level.

definition: Able to continue over a long period without causing serious damage or running out; especially, using natural resources in a way that does not harm the environment.
usage: Two senses: environmental (sustainable energy/development/fishing/fashion) and general (a sustainable pace/level of growth/business model). “Sustainable development” means meeting present needs without compromising those of future generations. The noun “sustainability” is very common in policy and corporate language. The opposite is “unsustainable”: “This level of spending is unsustainable.”
examples: The city is investing heavily in sustainable transport, such as cycle lanes and electric buses.
Working twelve hours a day isn't sustainable in the long run.
Consumers are increasingly willing to pay more for sustainable products.
Economic growth must be sustainable if it is to benefit future generations.
The company aims to make all its packaging sustainable by 2030.

definition: To suggest or express something indirectly, without saying it openly; also, to show that something is likely to be true or to follow as a consequence.
usage: Patterns: imply that…; imply something. Collocations: strongly/clearly imply. Don't confuse “imply” with “infer”: the speaker or writer implies, while the listener or reader infers. In academic writing, “These results imply that…” presents a conclusion the results suggest without proving it.
examples: Are you implying that I'm lying?
These results imply that the treatment is more effective in younger patients.
Her tone implied that she wasn't happy with the decision.
The word “estimate” implies that the figure isn't exact.
Rising rents imply growing demand for housing in the area.

definition: A particular way of thinking about or viewing something, often shaped by your experiences or position; also, the ability to judge how important something really is.
usage: Patterns: from a … perspective; from someone's perspective; a perspective on something. “Put something into perspective” means to compare it with other things so that you see its true importance; “keep things in perspective” means not exaggerating a problem. In academic writing, “from a historical/economic perspective” is a common way to frame an argument.
examples: From an economic perspective, the policy makes sense.
Living abroad gave me a completely new perspective on my own country.
Try to see the situation from your parents' perspective.
Failing one exam isn't the end of the world; try to keep things in perspective.
Talking to patients with serious illnesses really puts your own problems into perspective.

definition: Existing very commonly, or happening often, among a particular group or at a particular time.
usage: Patterns: prevalent among/in a group or place. Collocations: increasingly/widely prevalent; prevalent attitudes/views. The noun “prevalence” is used in medicine and social science: “the prevalence of obesity”. “Prevalent” is more formal than “common” and is often used for problems, diseases, or beliefs.
examples: Anxiety is increasingly prevalent among university students.
This attitude is still prevalent in many workplaces.
The disease is more prevalent in tropical regions.
Online scams have become more prevalent in recent years.
Short-term contracts are now prevalent in the creative industries.

definition: To reach a conclusion or opinion based on the evidence or information available, rather than on what is stated directly.
usage: Patterns: infer something from something; infer that… The past forms double the “r”: inferred, inferring. The noun is “inference”: draw/make an inference. Strictly, the listener or reader infers and the speaker implies; using “infer” to mean “imply” is common in speech but is considered incorrect in careful writing.
examples: From her silence, I inferred that she didn't agree.
What can we infer from these results?
Readers are expected to infer the character's feelings from her actions.
It is difficult to infer cause and effect from a single survey.
We can reasonably infer that the letter was written before 1900.

definition: A fact, event, or situation that can be observed, especially one that is unusual or difficult to explain. Informally, a person or thing that is remarkably successful or popular.
usage: Plural: phenomena /fəˈnɒmɪnə/. Common mistakes are “phenomenons” and using “phenomena” as a singular. Collocations: a natural/social/cultural/global phenomenon; a relatively recent phenomenon. In academic writing, it is a neutral term for anything being studied; calling something “a phenomenon” in everyday speech suggests extraordinary popularity.
examples: The northern lights are a natural phenomenon caused by particles from the sun.
Working from home is not a new phenomenon, but it has become far more widespread.
The study examines the phenomenon of “quiet quitting” among young employees.
The singer became a global phenomenon almost overnight.
Scientists still can't fully explain this phenomenon.

definition: Not obvious or easy to notice, because it is small, delicate, or indirect; also, clever in an understated way.
usage: Note the silent “b”. Collocations: a subtle difference/change/hint/flavour; subtle humour. The adverb is “subtly” and the noun “subtlety” (plural: the subtleties of a language). “Subtle” can be a compliment (subtle elegance) or describe something hard to detect (a subtle bias).
examples: There's a subtle difference between “assume” and “presume”.
She dropped a few subtle hints about what she wanted for her birthday.
The changes to the logo are subtle, but they make it look much more modern.
It takes years to appreciate the subtleties of a foreign language.
Subtle forms of discrimination can be harder to challenge than obvious ones.

definition: To explain or decide on the meaning of something, such as data, a text, or someone's behaviour; also, to translate spoken words from one language into another as they are spoken.
usage: Patterns: interpret something as something (“She interpreted his silence as agreement.”); interpret data/results/a poem. The noun is “interpretation”: open to interpretation, a different interpretation. An “interpreter” translates speech, while a “translator” usually works with written text. The past form is “interpreted”, with no doubled “t”.
examples: How should we interpret these results?
He interpreted her silence as agreement.
The poem can be interpreted in several different ways.
Her aunt had to interpret for her at the doctor's appointment.
The rules are vague and open to interpretation.

definition: The reasons or logical basis behind a decision, belief, or course of action.
usage: Patterns: the rationale for/behind something; the rationale for doing something. Collocations: a clear/strong rationale; explain/provide the rationale. It is a formal noun used in academic and professional contexts; in a research proposal, the “rationale” section explains why the study is needed. Don't confuse it with the adjective “rational” (based on reason).
examples: Can you explain the rationale behind this decision?
The rationale for the study is that little research has been done in this area.
I understand the rationale, but I still think the policy is unfair.
There was no clear rationale for closing the library at weekends.
Every proposal must include a brief rationale and a timeline.

definition: Stated clearly and in detail, leaving no room for confusion or doubt; also, showing or describing sex or violence very openly.
usage: Patterns: be explicit about something; make something explicit. Collocations: explicit instructions/permission/reference; sexually explicit content. The opposite is “implicit” (suggested but not stated directly). The adverb “explicitly” is common: “The contract explicitly states that…”.
examples: The instructions were explicit: no phones in the exam room.
Please be explicit about what you expect from the team.
The contract explicitly states that payment is due within thirty days.
The film contains explicit scenes and is not suitable for children.
The author never makes her political views explicit, but they're clear from the text.

definition: To show or prove that a decision, action, or idea is reasonable or right; also, to be a good reason for something.
usage: Patterns: justify something; justify doing something; justify something to someone. Collocations: hard/difficult to justify; fully justified. The noun “justification” (there is no justification for…) and the adjective “justified” (feel justified in…) are both common. In academic writing, you are often expected to justify your choice of method or sources.
examples: How can you justify spending so much money on a phone?
The results justify further research in this area.
You need to justify your choice of method in the methodology section.
Nothing can justify violence against civilians.
I don't feel I have to justify my decisions to anyone.

definition: The range of things that a subject, activity, or piece of work deals with; also, the opportunity or possibility to do something.
usage: Patterns: the scope of something; within/beyond/outside the scope of; scope for something (scope for improvement). Collocations: broaden/widen/narrow/limit the scope. “Beyond the scope of this study/essay” is a standard academic way to set boundaries. In project management, “scope creep” means a project gradually growing beyond its original aims.
examples: A detailed analysis of costs is beyond the scope of this essay.
There is plenty of scope for improvement in our customer service.
We decided to narrow the scope of the project to just one city.
The job offers a lot of scope for creativity.
Keep an eye on scope creep, or the project will never be finished.

definition: Based on chance or personal whim rather than on reason, a system, or a fair principle.
usage: Collocations: an arbitrary decision/rule/choice/number; seemingly/completely arbitrary. In legal and political contexts, it suggests the unfair use of power: “arbitrary arrest”. The adverb is “arbitrarily”. In mathematics and science, “arbitrary” can be neutral, meaning any value at all: “choose an arbitrary point”.
examples: The decision to cut the budget by 20 per cent seems completely arbitrary.
Why do we have to finish at five? It feels like an arbitrary rule.
Human rights groups have condemned the arbitrary arrest of journalists.
The cut-off age of 65 is somewhat arbitrary.
Choose an arbitrary number between one and ten.

definition: To fail to give enough care or attention to someone or something; also, to fail to do something, often through carelessness.
usage: Patterns: neglect someone/something; neglect to do something. Also a noun: years of neglect, child neglect. Collocations: neglect your health/studies/duties; badly/largely neglected. In academic writing, “a neglected area of research” is a topic that has received too little attention.
examples: He worked so hard that he started to neglect his health.
The house had been neglected for years and was in terrible condition.
She neglected to mention that she'd already accepted another offer.
This is a relatively neglected area of research.
The charity supports children who have suffered abuse or neglect.

definition: A problem or event that delays progress or makes a situation worse than it was.
usage: Collocations: suffer/experience a setback; a major/serious/temporary/minor setback; a setback for someone/something. It often describes temporary obstacles: “Despite a few setbacks, we finished on time.” The phrasal verb “set back” means to delay progress, and informally, to cost: “That dinner set me back fifty pounds.”
examples: The injury was a major setback for her career.
Despite a few setbacks, the project was completed on time.
Failing the driving test was a setback, but I passed the second time.
The court's decision is a serious setback for the campaign.
Every successful entrepreneur has faced setbacks along the way.

definition: Logical and well organized, so that it is easy to understand; also, of a person, able to speak clearly and sensibly.
usage: Collocations: a coherent argument/strategy/plan/essay/explanation. In academic writing, “coherence” refers to how logically ideas connect across a text, and examiners often assess it explicitly. Applied to people, the word often appears in the negative: “He was barely coherent.” The opposite is “incoherent”.
examples: Your essay needs a more coherent structure.
The government lacks a coherent strategy for dealing with the housing crisis.
She was so tired that she could barely give a coherent answer.
A coherent argument moves logically from one point to the next.
The team needs to present a coherent message to investors.

definition: To notice or become aware of something through the senses; also, to understand or think of someone or something in a particular way.
usage: The second sense is very common: perceive someone/something as something (“He is perceived as arrogant”). The noun “perception” (public perception; change people's perceptions) and the adjective “perceptive” (good at noticing things) are frequent. Spelling tip: “e” before “i” after “c”, as in “receive”.
examples: Many people perceive public speaking as extremely stressful.
The brand is perceived as expensive, even though its prices are average.
Dogs can perceive sounds that humans cannot hear.
How you perceive a situation affects how you react to it.
Women are still often perceived differently from men in leadership roles.

definition: A balance between two desirable things that you cannot have fully at the same time, so that gaining more of one means accepting less of the other.
usage: Patterns: a trade-off between A and B; make a trade-off. It is also spelled “tradeoff”, especially in American English. Common in economics, engineering, and everyday decision-making: “the trade-off between speed and accuracy”. The phrasal verb “trade off” means to give up one thing in exchange for another.
examples: There's always a trade-off between speed and accuracy.
Living further from the city means a longer commute, but that's a trade-off I'm willing to make.
Policymakers face difficult trade-offs between economic growth and environmental protection.
Cheaper flights usually come with trade-offs, such as less legroom and no free luggage.
Every design decision involves trade-offs.

definition: Able to exist, work, or be used together without problems or conflict.
usage: Patterns: compatible with something/someone. Collocations: fully/highly/backward compatible; compatible devices/software. It is used for technology (“This charger is compatible with most phones”), for people (“We just weren't compatible”), and for ideas (“Is economic growth compatible with protecting the environment?”). The opposite is “incompatible”, and the noun “compatibility”.
examples: Is this charger compatible with my laptop?
They're lovely people, but we just weren't compatible as flatmates.
Can economic growth be compatible with protecting the environment?
The new version is fully compatible with older files.
Check that the software is compatible with your operating system before you buy it.

definition: To continue to exist or happen for longer than expected; also, to keep trying to do something despite difficulties or opposition.
usage: Patterns: persist in (doing) something; persist with something; problems/symptoms/myths persist. The adjective “persistent” (a persistent cough, a persistent salesperson) and the noun “persistence” are both common. Persistence is usually admired, but “persist in” can suggest stubbornness: “He persists in ignoring my advice.”
examples: If the symptoms persist, see a doctor.
Despite the evidence, the myth that we only use 10 per cent of our brains persists.
She persisted with her application even after being rejected twice.
He persists in calling me by the wrong name.
Inequality persists in many areas of society.

definition: So great or strong that it is difficult to deal with or resist; also, so large in number or amount that it cannot reasonably be argued against.
usage: Collocations: an overwhelming majority/amount/feeling; an overwhelming sense of something; overwhelming evidence/support. The verb “overwhelm” and the adjective “overwhelmed” describe feeling unable to cope: “I'm feeling a bit overwhelmed at work.” Note that “overwhelming” can be positive (overwhelming support) or negative (an overwhelming workload).
examples: The evidence against him was overwhelming.
An overwhelming majority of students voted in favour of the proposal.
Starting a new job in a new country can be overwhelming.
I'm feeling a bit overwhelmed by everything I have to do this week.
The response to our appeal has been overwhelming; thank you all.

definition: To try to achieve something, or to make progress in an activity, over a period of time; also, to follow or chase someone or something.
usage: Collocations: pursue a career/goal/degree/dream/interest; pursue a policy/strategy; pursue a matter (continue to deal with it). The noun is “pursuit”: the pursuit of happiness, in pursuit of something. It is more formal than “go after” and is common in academic and professional writing, especially about careers and studies.
examples: She left her job to pursue a master's degree in public health.
If you're passionate about music, you should pursue it.
The government is pursuing a policy of lower taxes.
The police pursued the stolen car through the city centre.
I asked about the refund twice but decided not to pursue the matter any further.

definition: The level or point at which something starts to happen or to have an effect; literally, the floor or entrance at the bottom of a doorway.
usage: Collocations: reach/cross/exceed a threshold; the tax/pain/income threshold; a low/high threshold for something. “On the threshold of” means at the beginning of something new: “on the threshold of a new career”. Watch the spelling: only one “h” in the middle (“threshold”, not “threshhold”).
examples: You only pay tax once your income passes a certain threshold.
Everyone has a different pain threshold.
The vaccination programme aims to reach a threshold of 80 per cent coverage.
I have a pretty low threshold for boredom.
She stood nervously on the threshold, wondering whether to knock.

definition: Boring and tiring because it goes on too long, is repetitive, or requires little thought.
usage: Collocations: a tedious task/process/job/journey; tedious paperwork. It is stronger than “boring” in suggesting that something is also tiring or frustrating. It is often used for work that is necessary but unpleasant: “Formatting references is tedious but important.”
examples: Entering all that data by hand was incredibly tedious.
The application process is long and tedious.
Formatting the references is tedious, but it's worth doing properly.
The film was beautifully shot but rather tedious in places.
Software can automate many of the more tedious parts of the job.

definition: To gradually weaken or damage something, such as confidence, authority, or an effort, often in a way that is not immediately obvious.
usage: Collocations: undermine confidence/trust/authority/efforts/credibility/democracy; seriously undermine. “Undermine someone” can mean to make them less effective or less respected, often in an indirect or sneaky way. It is common in academic and journalistic writing when discussing threats to institutions or arguments.
examples: Constant criticism can undermine a child's confidence.
These findings undermine the claim that the policy was a success.
Corruption undermines public trust in government.
I felt my manager was undermining me in front of the team.
One weak example can undermine an otherwise strong argument.

definition: A serious responsibility, duty, or problem that causes difficulty, worry, or hard work; literally, a heavy load that is carried.
usage: Collocations: a heavy/financial/tax burden; ease/reduce/share the burden; be a burden on/to someone. “The burden of proof” is the responsibility for proving something in a legal case or an argument. The adjective “burdensome” describes rules or tasks that are difficult and tiring to deal with.
examples: Student debt is a huge financial burden for many young people.
I don't want to be a burden to my children when I'm older.
The new rules will place an extra administrative burden on small businesses.
Talking to a friend can help ease the burden of stress.
In a criminal trial, the burden of proof lies with the prosecution.

definition: Showing extremely careful and precise attention to every detail.
usage: Patterns: meticulous about/in something. Collocations: meticulous attention to detail; meticulous planning/research/records. It is a compliment in most contexts, and stronger and more formal than “careful”. The adverb “meticulously” is common: “meticulously planned”.
examples: She's meticulous about keeping records of every expense.
The wedding was meticulously planned down to the last detail.
His research is meticulous, and his conclusions are hard to argue with.
The job requires meticulous attention to detail.
Restoring the old painting was slow, meticulous work.

definition: To officially give a particular amount of time, money, or resources to someone or something for a specific purpose.
usage: Patterns: allocate something to/for someone/something; allocate something for doing something. Collocations: allocate funds/resources/time/seats. The noun is “allocation”. It is common in business, government, and project planning, and in study advice: “allocate time for revision”.
examples: The government has allocated £2 billion to improving rail services.
Try to allocate at least an hour a day to revision.
Each team was allocated a small budget for the event.
We were allocated seats right at the back of the plane.
Hospitals must decide how to allocate limited resources fairly.

definition: An agreement in which each side gives up some of what it wants in order to settle a disagreement. As a verb, to reach such an agreement, or to weaken or put at risk something such as safety or your principles.
usage: Patterns: reach/make/agree on a compromise; a compromise between A and B; compromise on something. The verb has two senses: positive, as in “compromise on the price” (meet halfway), and negative, as in “compromise safety/quality/security/your principles” (weaken). “Without compromising” is a common phrase: “improve speed without compromising quality”.
examples: After hours of negotiation, both sides finally reached a compromise.
I wanted the beach and she wanted the mountains, so we compromised on a lake.
Living together means being willing to compromise.
Cutting costs must not compromise passenger safety.
Is it possible to succeed in politics without compromising your principles?

definition: Able to do many different things well, or to be used in many different ways.
usage: Collocations: a versatile player/actor/performer; a versatile tool/material/ingredient. It is a compliment for people and a selling point for products. The noun is “versatility”. The British pronunciation ends in /aɪl/; the American one usually ends in a weak /əl/.
examples: She's a versatile actor who can do comedy and drama equally well.
Eggs are one of the most versatile ingredients in the kitchen.
A good blazer is versatile enough to wear to work or out to dinner.
Employers value versatile graduates who can adapt to different roles.
Bamboo is a remarkably versatile material.

definition: To publicly support or recommend a particular idea, policy, or course of action.
usage: Patterns: advocate something; advocate doing something; advocate for something/someone (especially in American English). The noun “advocate” (/ˈædvəkət/) is a person who supports a cause (an advocate of/for something), and in some legal systems, a lawyer. To “play devil's advocate” is to argue against an idea, often just to test it.
examples: Many experts advocate a shorter working week.
The author advocates teaching financial skills in secondary schools.
She has spent her career advocating for the rights of disabled people.
He's a strong advocate of learning languages through reading.
I'm not against the idea; I'm just playing devil's advocate.

definition: The ability to understand and share the feelings of another person, as if you were in their situation.
usage: Patterns: empathy for/with someone; show/feel/lack empathy. The verb is “empathize (with)” and the adjective “empathetic” or “empathic”. Empathy is not the same as sympathy: sympathy is feeling sorry for someone, while empathy is understanding how they feel from their point of view.
examples: Good doctors show empathy as well as medical expertise.
It's hard to feel empathy for someone you've never met.
Reading fiction may help children develop empathy.
He lacks empathy and rarely considers how others feel.
As a former international student, I can really empathize with what you're going through.

definition: Very great or intense; also, showing deep understanding or serious thought.
usage: Collocations: a profound effect/impact/change/influence; profound respect/sadness; a profound question/insight. The adverb “profoundly” (profoundly deaf, profoundly affected) is a strong intensifier. It is more formal and emotionally weightier than “deep” or “big”.
examples: The internet has had a profound effect on the way we communicate.
Losing her father at a young age had a profound impact on her.
The book raises profound questions about what it means to be human.
I have profound respect for nurses and the work they do.
Some of the most profound changes in education took place during the pandemic.

definition: To express or communicate an idea, feeling, or impression so that others understand it; in formal or technical use, to carry or transport something.
usage: Patterns: convey something to someone; convey that/how… Collocations: convey a message/meaning/idea/feeling; convey a sense of something. It is common in the analysis of texts and images: “The poem conveys a sense of loss.” The transport sense survives mainly in technical words such as “conveyor belt”.
examples: It's hard to convey sarcasm in a text message.
The photograph conveys a powerful sense of isolation.
Please convey my thanks to your team.
Good presenters can convey complex ideas in simple language.
Her tone conveyed more than her words did.

definition: The quality of being honest and having strong moral principles; also, the state of being whole, complete, and undamaged.
usage: Collocations: personal/professional/academic integrity; a person of integrity; maintain/compromise your integrity. “Academic integrity” means honesty in academic work, such as avoiding plagiarism. The second sense appears in technical contexts: “the structural integrity of a building”, “data integrity”.
examples: She's a woman of great integrity who always keeps her word.
Universities take academic integrity very seriously, and plagiarism can lead to expulsion.
Engineers checked the structural integrity of the bridge after the earthquake.
Accepting the bribe would have compromised his integrity.
Journalists must maintain their integrity even under pressure from advertisers.

definition: Having doubts that a claim is true, or that something will happen, until you see clear evidence.
usage: Patterns: sceptical about/of something. Collocations: deeply/highly/a little sceptical; remain sceptical. The American spelling is “skeptical”, and related words follow the same pattern (sceptic/skeptic, scepticism/skepticism). Being sceptical is usually seen as a strength in academic thinking, as long as it is based on evidence rather than cynicism.
examples: I was sceptical at first, but the app has actually improved my sleep.
Many economists are sceptical about the government's growth forecasts.
Scientists should remain sceptical until results have been replicated.
She gave me a sceptical look when I said I'd be ready in five minutes.
Consumers are increasingly sceptical of companies that claim to be “green”.

definition: To deal successfully with a difficult situation or problem.
usage: Patterns: cope with something; cope without something; (be unable to) cope. Collocations: cope with stress/pressure/change/the workload; learn to cope. “Coping strategies” or “coping mechanisms” are the ways people handle stress or difficulty. The word is neutral and very common in both everyday speech and academic fields such as psychology and social work.
examples: How do you cope with stress during exams?
The hospital is struggling to cope with the number of patients.
I don't know how I'd cope without my phone.
Everyone develops their own coping strategies.
She coped remarkably well with the move to a new country.

definition: The ability to decide and act on your own without waiting for someone to tell you what to do; also, a new plan or action intended to solve a problem or achieve a goal.
usage: Patterns: take the initiative (be the first to act); on your own initiative; an initiative to do something. Collocations: show/use initiative; a government/community/new initiative; launch an initiative. Employers often list “initiative” as a key quality in job adverts.
examples: We're looking for someone who can work independently and show initiative.
She took the initiative and organized the whole event herself.
The government has launched a new initiative to reduce youth unemployment.
He fixed the problem on his own initiative, without being asked.
If you want a promotion, you'll need to take more initiative.

definition: Existing as a natural, basic, or permanent part of something, so that it cannot be separated from it.
usage: Patterns: inherent in something; inherent to something. Collocations: inherent risk/danger/weakness/value/bias/limitation. The adverb “inherently” is common: “inherently risky”, “not inherently good or bad”. In academic writing, it helps you argue that a problem is built into a system rather than accidental. Some speakers say /ɪnˈherənt/.
examples: There are risks inherent in any surgical procedure.
Technology is not inherently good or bad; it depends on how we use it.
Self-reported data has inherent limitations.
Some psychologists believe that humans have an inherent need to belong.
Investing in shares always carries some inherent risk.

definition: To give more details or information about something you have already said or written.
usage: Patterns: elaborate on something; “Could you elaborate (on that)?” As an adjective, pronounced /ɪˈlæbərət/, “elaborate” means detailed and complicated: an elaborate plan/design/meal. “Without elaborating” is often used when someone deliberately gives little explanation.
examples: Could you elaborate on that point?
The minister refused to elaborate on the reasons for her resignation.
In your next paragraph, elaborate on the example you introduced.
He said he had “personal reasons” for leaving but didn't elaborate.
They came up with an elaborate plan to surprise her on her birthday.

definition: Allowed by law or by the rules; also, reasonable and justifiable.
usage: Collocations: a legitimate business/government/claim; a legitimate concern/question/reason. The second sense (“a legitimate concern”) is very common when you want to acknowledge that an objection is fair. The informal abbreviation “legit” means genuine or acceptable. The noun is “legitimacy”, and the opposite is “illegitimate”.
examples: That's a legitimate concern, and we'll address it at the next meeting.
Is this a legitimate website, or is it a scam?
Parents have a legitimate interest in what their children are taught.
The restaurant was a legitimate business used as a front for money laundering.
Feeling exhausted after a long week is a perfectly legitimate reason to cancel plans.

definition: To describe something as larger, better, worse, or more important than it really is.
usage: Patterns: exaggerate something; exaggerate the importance/extent/risk of something. Collocations: grossly/wildly/greatly exaggerated. “It's no exaggeration to say that…” is a common way of adding emphasis. Spelling: double “g”, single “r”.
examples: Don't exaggerate; it was only a small scratch.
The media tend to exaggerate the risks of rare diseases.
It's no exaggeration to say that this book changed my life.
Reports of the company's collapse have been greatly exaggerated.
Many applicants exaggerate their language skills on their CVs.

definition: A very small difference in meaning, feeling, tone, or colour that is not immediately obvious but is nonetheless important.
usage: Patterns: the nuances of something; nuance in something. The adjective “nuanced” (a nuanced argument/view/understanding) is very common in academic and journalistic writing and is a compliment: it means taking complexity into account rather than oversimplifying. To “lack nuance” is a common criticism.
examples: It takes years to master the nuances of a foreign language.
Machine translation often misses nuances of tone and humour.
She has a more nuanced view of the issue than most commentators.
Debates on social media tend to lack nuance.
A good actor can convey subtle nuances of emotion with a single look.

definition: Not yet certain or confirmed, and likely to change; also, done without confidence, in a hesitant way.
usage: Collocations: a tentative plan/agreement/date/conclusion; a tentative smile/step. The adverb “tentatively” is common: “tentatively scheduled for Friday”. In academic writing, describing conclusions as “tentative” signals that the evidence is limited, which is a form of hedging.
examples: We've made tentative plans to visit Japan next spring.
The meeting is tentatively scheduled for Friday afternoon.
Given the small sample, these conclusions are only tentative.
She gave me a tentative smile, unsure whether I'd recognized her.
The two sides have reached a tentative agreement, but nothing has been signed yet.

definition: To keep delaying something that you should do, often because it is unpleasant or boring.
usage: Usually intransitive: “I always procrastinate.” The noun “procrastination” is very common. Unlike “postpone”, which is a neutral, deliberate decision to delay, “procrastinate” implies an unnecessary and often irrational delay. Informal equivalents: put things off, leave things until the last minute.
examples: I tend to procrastinate when I have a big assignment due.
Stop procrastinating and just send the email.
Procrastination is often linked to anxiety rather than laziness.
If you procrastinate until the night before, the quality of your work will suffer.
Breaking a task into smaller steps makes it harder to procrastinate.

definition: The understanding of a situation or event that you only have after it has happened.
usage: Mostly used in the phrases “in hindsight” and “with (the benefit of) hindsight”. “Hindsight is a wonderful thing” (or, in American English, “hindsight is 20/20”) means that it is easy to judge a decision once you know the outcome. Compare “foresight”, the ability to predict what will happen and plan for it.
examples: In hindsight, I should have studied harder for that exam.
With the benefit of hindsight, the decision looks like a mistake.
It's easy to criticize with hindsight, but no one could have predicted the crisis.
In hindsight, moving abroad was the best thing I've ever done.
Hindsight is a wonderful thing; at the time, it seemed like a good idea.

definition: No longer used or useful because something newer or better has replaced it.
usage: Collocations: become/render/make something obsolete; largely/virtually obsolete; obsolete technology/equipment. “Render something obsolete” is a formal phrase common in writing about technology and the economy. Compare “outdated” (old-fashioned but possibly still in use) with “obsolete” (no longer in use, or no longer fit for use).
examples: Many of the skills I learned at university are now obsolete.
Smartphones have made devices such as alarm clocks and MP3 players almost obsolete.
Will artificial intelligence render some jobs obsolete?
The factory's equipment was obsolete and had to be replaced.
Cheques are becoming obsolete in many countries.

definition: To fail to notice or consider something; also, to deliberately ignore a fault or mistake. Literally, to have a view of a place from above.
usage: Patterns: overlook something; be easily overlooked; overlook the fact that… Collocations: an important/often overlooked factor. In the forgiving sense: “I'll overlook it this time.” In the physical sense: “a hotel room overlooking the sea”. Don't confuse it with “oversee”, which means to supervise.
examples: It's easy to overlook small errors when you're tired.
The study overlooks the role of family income.
I'm willing to overlook the mistake this time, but please be more careful.
Mental health is an often overlooked aspect of student life.
We stayed in a small hotel overlooking the harbour.

definition: Real and exactly what it appears to be, not fake; also, of a person or feeling, sincere and honest.
usage: Collocations: genuine leather; a genuine concern/interest/mistake/effort; a genuine person. “Genuine” emphasizes sincerity: “a genuine apology” is one that is truly meant. The adverb “genuinely” is very common in speech: “I'm genuinely surprised.” Pronunciation tip: the last syllable is /ɪn/, not /aɪn/.
examples: Is this bag made of genuine leather?
She showed a genuine interest in my research.
It was a genuine mistake; I wasn't trying to cheat.
He's one of the most genuine people I know.
I'm genuinely surprised that so few people applied.

definition: To provide enough space for someone or something; also, to adapt to or provide for someone's needs or wishes.
usage: Patterns: accommodate someone/something; accommodate someone's needs/request. Collocations: accommodate guests/students/passengers; accommodate different learning needs. The noun “accommodation” is very common and is uncountable in British English: “We need to find accommodation.” Spelling: double “c” and double “m”.
examples: The new hall can accommodate up to 500 people.
We'll do our best to accommodate your request.
Teachers need to accommodate students with different learning needs.
Finding affordable accommodation in London is a real challenge.
The schedule was changed to accommodate everyone's availability.

definition: To recognize or show the difference between two or more things or people; also, to make someone or something different or special.
usage: Patterns: distinguish between A and B; distinguish A from B; distinguish yourself (do something that earns respect). The related adjectives are “distinguished” (respected and admired) and “distinctive” (easy to recognize). In academic writing, “It is important to distinguish between…” introduces a key distinction.
examples: Young children often find it hard to distinguish between fantasy and reality.
It's important to distinguish correlation from causation.
What distinguishes this phone from its competitors?
I can't distinguish one twin from the other.
She distinguished herself as one of the brightest students in her year.

definition: To change frequently in level or amount, going up and down in an irregular way.
usage: Patterns: fluctuate between X and Y; fluctuate wildly/considerably. Typical subjects: prices, temperatures, exchange rates, moods, numbers. The noun is “fluctuation”. It is a key verb for describing trends in charts and graphs, for example in IELTS Writing Task 1.
examples: Petrol prices have fluctuated wildly over the past year.
Temperatures can fluctuate between 10 and 30 degrees in a single day.
The number of visitors fluctuates depending on the season.
Her mood seemed to fluctuate from hour to hour.
The graph shows that sales fluctuated throughout the year before rising sharply in December.

definition: To make something harmful, bad, or unpleasant less severe or serious.
usage: Collocations: mitigate the effects/impact/risk(s)/damage of something. The noun is “mitigation”: climate change mitigation. “Mitigating circumstances” are factors that make a failure or wrong action seem less serious, such as illness affecting exam performance. Don't confuse “mitigate” with “militate against”, which means to make something less likely to happen.
examples: Planting trees can help mitigate the effects of climate change.
We need a plan to mitigate the risks before launching the product.
The university will take mitigating circumstances into account.
Nothing could mitigate the damage done to the company's reputation.
Wearing a mask can mitigate, though not eliminate, the risk of infection.

definition: To make an idea, belief, or feeling stronger; also, to make a structure or object physically stronger.
usage: Collocations: reinforce a message/stereotype/belief; reinforce learning; reinforce the idea that…; reinforced concrete. In education, it means helping learning stick: “Homework reinforces what was taught in class.” In psychology, “positive reinforcement” means rewarding good behaviour so that it is repeated.
examples: Regular review helps reinforce what you've learned.
These adverts reinforce harmful gender stereotypes.
The latest data reinforces the case for early intervention.
The bridge was reinforced with steel after the earthquake.
Praising effort, not just results, reinforces good habits.

definition: To form ideas or guesses about something without having enough information to be certain; also, to buy property or shares in the hope of making a quick profit.
usage: Patterns: speculate about/on something; speculate that… Collocations: widely speculated; it is too early to speculate. The noun “speculation” (pure/media/wild speculation) and the adjective “speculative” are common. In academic writing, it signals that a claim is a guess: “We can only speculate about the cause.”
examples: It's too early to speculate about the cause of the accident.
The media have been speculating that the CEO will resign.
We can only speculate about why the ancient city was abandoned.
Rather than speculating, let's wait for the official results.
Many people lost money speculating on cryptocurrencies.

definition: To make a determined effort to deal with a difficult problem or task; in sport, to try to take the ball from an opponent.
usage: Collocations: tackle a problem/issue/challenge/task; tackle climate change/inequality/crime. It is more energetic than “deal with” and suggests direct action. It is very common in news, policy documents, and essays: “Governments must do more to tackle…”.
examples: The government must do more to tackle youth unemployment.
Let's tackle the hardest task first, while we still have energy.
This essay tackles the question of whether exams are a fair measure of ability.
I finally tackled the pile of laundry that had been sitting there all week.
He was injured after being tackled from behind.

definition: To grow, develop, or succeed strongly and healthily.
usage: Patterns: thrive on something (enjoy it or do well because of it: “She thrives on pressure”); thrive in a particular environment. The past tense is usually “thrived” (“throve” is old-fashioned). The adjective “thriving” describes a successful business, community, or city.
examples: Some people thrive under pressure, while others struggle.
These plants thrive in warm, humid conditions.
Children thrive when they feel safe and supported.
The town has a thriving tech industry.
She thrives on challenges and gets bored easily.

definition: To be greater or more important than something else.
usage: Pattern: A outweighs B, as in “the benefits/advantages outweigh the risks/costs/disadvantages”. This is a classic structure in academic and IELTS writing: “Do the advantages outweigh the disadvantages?” It can be intensified with “far” or “clearly”.
examples: In my view, the benefits of studying abroad far outweigh the costs.
For most people, the advantages of vaccination clearly outweigh the risks.
The positives of the job outweighed the long commute.
Do the advantages of social media outweigh the disadvantages?
Her experience outweighed her lack of formal qualifications.

definition: To decide which tasks or issues are most important so that you can deal with them first; also, to treat something as more important than other things.
usage: Patterns: prioritize something (over something else); prioritize tasks/needs/safety. The spelling “prioritise” is also common in British English. The noun “priority” (a top/high/low priority; get your priorities right) is closely related.
examples: When you have too much to do, you need to prioritize.
The government says it will prioritize healthcare and education.
Learn to prioritize your tasks according to urgency and importance.
Many young people now prioritize work-life balance over salary.
The hospital prioritizes patients with the most serious conditions.

definition: To carefully judge the quality, value, importance, or effectiveness of something.
usage: Collocations: evaluate the evidence/results/effectiveness/impact/performance; critically evaluate. The noun “evaluation” is common in academic and professional contexts. “Critically evaluate” is a frequent essay instruction asking you to weigh strengths and weaknesses rather than simply describe. “Assess” is very similar but is often preferred for measuring ability or risk.
examples: Critically evaluate the strengths and weaknesses of this argument.
We need to evaluate the effectiveness of the new teaching method.
All patients are evaluated by a specialist before surgery.
It's difficult to evaluate a job offer when you know very little about the company.
Employees are evaluated on their performance every six months.

definition: To officially end a law, system, practice, or institution.
usage: Typical objects: abolish slavery/the death penalty/a tax/tuition fees/a post. It is formal and usually describes action by a government or organization. The noun is “abolition”, and someone who campaigns to abolish something is an “abolitionist”.
examples: Many countries have abolished the death penalty.
The government plans to abolish tuition fees for students from low-income families.
Slavery was abolished in the British Empire in 1833.
Some staff want to abolish the dress code altogether.
Rather than abolishing the exam, the board decided to reform it.

definition: Sudden and unexpected, often in an unpleasant way; also, of a person's manner, short and unfriendly.
usage: Collocations: an abrupt change/halt/end/departure; come to an abrupt end. Applied to people, it suggests rudeness through brevity: “She was rather abrupt on the phone.” The adverb “abruptly” is very common: “He left abruptly.”
examples: The meeting came to an abrupt end when the fire alarm went off.
There was an abrupt change in the weather around noon.
I didn't mean to sound abrupt; I was just in a hurry.
He abruptly stood up and walked out of the room.
The policy's abrupt reversal confused voters.

definition: Completely unreasonable, illogical, or ridiculous.
