usage: Common patterns: it is absurd to + verb; it is absurd that… ; an absurd idea/situation/claim. It is stronger than “silly” and often expresses impatience or disbelief. “The absurd” can also refer to the philosophical idea that life lacks inherent meaning.
examples: It's absurd to expect anyone to read a 200-page report overnight.
The idea that the moon landing was faked is absurd.
Prices in the airport shop were absurdly high.
The situation became so absurd that we couldn't stop laughing.
Critics described the new parking rules as absurd and unworkable.

definition: Existing in large quantities; more than enough.
usage: Collocations: abundant resources/evidence/wildlife/rainfall. The noun is “abundance” (in abundance), and the adverb “abundantly” appears in “make it abundantly clear”. It is more formal than “plenty of”.
examples: The region has abundant natural resources, including oil and timber.
There is abundant evidence that sleep affects learning.
Fresh fruit is abundant in the summer markets.
She made it abundantly clear that she disagreed.
Wildlife is abundant along the river.

definition: To happen, or to make something happen, faster or earlier than before; of a vehicle, to increase speed.
usage: Can be transitive (accelerate growth/change/the process) or intransitive (growth accelerated). The noun is “acceleration”. In academic and business writing, it often describes trends: “The pandemic accelerated the shift to online shopping.”
examples: The pandemic accelerated the shift to remote work.
The government wants to accelerate the move to renewable energy.
Inflation accelerated sharply in the second quarter.
The car accelerated as it pulled onto the motorway.
Regular practice can accelerate your progress in a new language.

definition: Responsible for your decisions or actions and expected to explain or justify them when asked.
usage: Patterns: be accountable to someone (for something); hold someone accountable. It is common in discussions of politics, management, and ethics. The noun “accountability” is very frequent: “There needs to be more accountability.”
examples: Politicians must be held accountable for the promises they make.
Each team leader is accountable to the project director.
If something goes wrong, who will be accountable?
The new system makes managers more accountable for their budgets.
Having a study partner keeps me accountable.

definition: To gradually gather or build up a large amount of something over time.
usage: Can be transitive (accumulate wealth/data/experience/debt) or intransitive (dust accumulates). The noun is “accumulation”, and the adjective “cumulative” describes an effect that grows as things add up.
examples: Over the years, she accumulated a huge collection of vinyl records.
Dust had accumulated on every surface of the abandoned house.
Researchers have accumulated a large body of data on sleep patterns.
It's easy to accumulate debt if you rely on credit cards.
Small savings accumulate faster than you might expect.

definition: The act of gaining or obtaining something, such as knowledge, a skill, or property; in business, a company bought by another company.
usage: Collocations: language acquisition, the acquisition of skills/knowledge; a major/recent acquisition; mergers and acquisitions (M&A). The verb is “acquire”. “Second language acquisition” is the academic field studying how people learn additional languages.
examples: Children's language acquisition happens remarkably quickly.
The company's latest acquisition is a small software start-up.
The museum's newest acquisition is a painting by Monet.
The course focuses on the acquisition of practical skills.
The acquisition was completed for an undisclosed sum.

definition: Very serious, severe, or intense; also, of the senses or mind, sharp and highly perceptive. In medicine, describing an illness that starts suddenly.
usage: Collocations: an acute shortage/problem/crisis; acute pain; acutely aware. In medicine, “acute” (sudden and severe) contrasts with “chronic” (long-lasting). “Acutely aware” means very conscious of something.
examples: There is an acute shortage of nurses in rural areas.
He was admitted to hospital with acute chest pain.
Dogs have an acute sense of smell.
I was acutely aware that everyone was watching me.
The housing problem is particularly acute in big cities.

definition: To follow a rule, plan, or belief closely; literally, to stick firmly to a surface.
usage: Always followed by “to”: adhere to the rules/guidelines/a schedule/a diet. It is formal and common in official and academic writing. The noun “adherence” is used for following rules or treatment (“adherence to medication”); an “adherent” is a supporter of a belief.
examples: All staff must adhere to the safety guidelines.
It's hard to adhere to a strict diet when you eat out a lot.
The study adhered to strict ethical standards.
We need to adhere to the original timeline.
The label won't adhere properly to a wet surface.

definition: Next to or very near something else.
usage: Often followed by “to”: adjacent to the station. Common in formal descriptions of places, property, and diagrams (adjacent rooms/buildings/angles). In everyday speech, people usually say “next to”.
examples: The hotel is adjacent to the main train station.
We booked adjacent rooms so the kids could be near us.
The fire spread quickly to the adjacent buildings.
Parking is available in the adjacent car park.
In the diagram, the two adjacent angles add up to 180 degrees.

definition: Negative and harmful, or unfavourable to success.
usage: Collocations: adverse effects/conditions/weather/reaction/publicity. It is formal and common in medical, legal, and news contexts. Don't confuse it with “averse” (unwilling): you are “averse to risk”, but a drug has “adverse effects”. The noun is “adversity”.
examples: The drug has few adverse side effects.
Flights were cancelled due to adverse weather conditions.
The scandal attracted a lot of adverse publicity.
Rising interest rates could have an adverse impact on small businesses.
Some patients had an adverse reaction to the vaccine.

definition: The arrival or beginning of an important new development, invention, or period.
usage: Almost always in “the advent of”: the advent of the internet/smartphones/AI. It is formal and frequent in academic and journalistic writing about historical change. “Advent” with a capital A is the Christian period before Christmas.
examples: The advent of the internet transformed how we access information.
Since the advent of smartphones, people rarely print maps.
The advent of cheap air travel made tourism accessible to millions.
Many jobs disappeared with the advent of automation.
The advent of AI tools raises new questions about academic honesty.

definition: Relating to beauty and to the appreciation of beauty; as a noun, a particular style or set of principles about what looks good.
usage: As an adjective: aesthetic value/appeal/choices; for aesthetic reasons. As a noun: a minimalist/vintage aesthetic. On social media, “aesthetic” is also used informally to mean visually pleasing. The adverb is “aesthetically” (aesthetically pleasing). American spelling: “esthetic” (less common).
examples: The building was designed for both practical and aesthetic reasons.
I like the clean, minimalist aesthetic of Scandinavian furniture.
The new logo is more aesthetically pleasing than the old one.
Some people choose plants purely for their aesthetic appeal.
The film has a distinctive retro aesthetic.

definition: Having a lot of money and a comfortable standard of living.
usage: Collocations: affluent areas/neighbourhoods/families/societies/consumers. It is more formal and neutral than “rich”. The noun “affluence” is used in social and economic discussion: “growing affluence”.
examples: The school is located in an affluent suburb.
Affluent consumers are willing to pay more for organic food.
Affluent families tend to spend more on education and travel.
Life expectancy is higher in more affluent areas.
The charity raises money from affluent donors.

definition: To make a bad situation, problem, or injury worse; informally, to annoy someone.
usage: Typical objects: aggravate a problem/an injury/a condition/tensions. The informal meaning “annoy” is very common in speech (“It really aggravates me”) but some careful writers avoid it. Compare “exacerbate”, a more formal synonym for the first meaning.
examples: Running on the injured knee will only aggravate it.
Heavy rain aggravated the flooding in low-lying areas.
His comments aggravated tensions between the two groups.
Stress can aggravate skin conditions such as eczema.
It really aggravates me when people talk during films.

definition: To arrange things so that they form a line or are in the right position; also, to make plans, ideas, or goals agree with each other.
usage: Patterns: align A with B; be aligned with something; align yourself with a group (support it). In business, “align” is very common: align goals/strategy/teams. The noun is “alignment”: in alignment with.
examples: Make sure the text is aligned to the left margin.
Our marketing strategy needs to align with the company's overall goals.
The party has aligned itself with environmental groups.
Her values didn't align with the company's culture, so she left.
The mechanic aligned the wheels after replacing the tyres.

definition: To claim that someone has done something wrong or illegal, without giving proof.
usage: Patterns: allege that…; it is alleged that…; be alleged to have done something. The adjective “alleged” and adverb “allegedly” are used in news reports to avoid stating guilt as fact: “the alleged attacker”. The noun is “allegation”.
examples: The report alleges that the company ignored safety warnings.
He is alleged to have stolen thousands of pounds from his employer.
Police arrested the alleged attacker on Tuesday.
The minister allegedly accepted gifts from a property developer.
She denies all the allegations made against her.

definition: To make pain, suffering, or a problem less severe.
usage: Collocations: alleviate pain/symptoms/poverty/stress/congestion/the burden. It is formal; everyday alternatives are “ease” or “relieve”. Note that alleviating a problem reduces it but doesn't necessarily solve it.
examples: The medication helped alleviate her symptoms.
The new bypass should alleviate traffic congestion in the town centre.
Policies aimed at alleviating poverty have had mixed results.
Exercise can alleviate stress and improve your mood.
Hiring two more nurses would alleviate the pressure on the team.

definition: Having mixed or contradictory feelings about something or someone.
usage: Patterns: ambivalent about/towards something. The noun is “ambivalence”. Don't confuse it with “ambiguous” (having more than one possible meaning): a person feels ambivalent, while a statement is ambiguous.
examples: I'm ambivalent about moving to the city: it's exciting but expensive.
Many voters remain ambivalent towards both candidates.
She felt ambivalent about leaving her job after so many years.
The public's attitude to nuclear power is deeply ambivalent.
Researchers found that many young people are ambivalent about social media.

definition: To make changes to a text, law, or agreement, usually to improve or correct it.
usage: Collocations: amend a law/the constitution/a contract/a document. The noun “amendment” is common in legal and political contexts. The separate phrase “make amends” means to do something to show you are sorry.
examples: Parliament voted to amend the law.
Please amend the date on the invoice before sending it.
The contract was amended to include a cancellation clause.
The Constitution has been amended several times.
He tried to make amends by buying her flowers.

definition: A feature or service that makes a place pleasant, comfortable, or convenient to live in or visit.
usage: Usually plural: local amenities, basic amenities, hotel amenities (pool, gym, Wi-Fi). It is common in property listings, travel writing, and urban planning.
examples: The flat is close to shops, schools, and other local amenities.
Many villages lack basic amenities such as a doctor or a bank.
The hotel's amenities include a spa and a rooftop pool.
Parks are an important amenity in densely populated cities.
The rent is higher, but the amenities are excellent.

definition: More than enough; plenty.
usage: Collocations: ample time/space/opportunity/evidence/parking. It usually comes before the noun. It sounds slightly formal and reassuring: “There is ample time to finish.”
examples: Don't worry, there's ample time to finish before the deadline.
The house has ample storage space.
Students will have ample opportunity to ask questions.
There is ample evidence that the policy works.
The venue offers ample free parking.

definition: A comparison between two things that share certain features, used to explain an idea or make it easier to understand.
usage: Patterns: draw/make an analogy between A and B; by analogy with. A good analogy clarifies; a “false analogy” compares things that are not really alike. The adjective is “analogous” (similar in some way).
examples: The teacher drew an analogy between the heart and a pump.
To use an analogy, learning a language is like learning a musical instrument.
The analogy breaks down when you look at the details.
Critics called it a false analogy, since the two situations were very different.
By analogy with other cities, we can expect prices to rise.

definition: A short, interesting, or amusing story about a real person or event.
usage: Collocations: tell/share an anecdote; a funny/personal anecdote. The adjective “anecdotal” describes evidence based on personal stories rather than systematic research, so “anecdotal evidence” is considered weak in academic contexts.
examples: She opened her speech with a funny anecdote about her first job.
My grandfather loves telling anecdotes about his time in the navy.
The book is full of personal anecdotes.
His claims are based on anecdotal evidence rather than data.
A short anecdote can make a presentation much more engaging.

definition: Something that is different from what is normal, usual, or expected.
usage: Collocations: a statistical anomaly; detect/explain an anomaly. In research, an anomaly is a result that doesn't fit the pattern and may need investigating or excluding. The adjective is “anomalous”.
examples: The unusually warm January was seen as an anomaly rather than a trend.
Researchers excluded one anomaly from the data set.
The software is designed to detect anomalies in bank transactions.
His poor result was an anomaly; he usually performs very well.
Scientists are still trying to explain the anomaly.

definition: A lack of interest, enthusiasm, or concern, especially about things that people are expected to care about.
usage: Collocations: voter/political/public apathy; widespread apathy. The adjective is “apathetic”. It often appears in discussions of low election turnout or disengaged students.
examples: Low turnout was blamed on widespread voter apathy.
The campaign aims to tackle apathy among young people.
There's a general apathy towards the issue in the office.
Apathy can be a symptom of depression.
The teacher was frustrated by the students' apathy.

definition: Worried or nervous that something bad or unpleasant may happen.
usage: Patterns: apprehensive about/of something; apprehensive that… It is a slightly more formal, milder alternative to “anxious”. The noun is “apprehension”.
examples: I was a bit apprehensive about starting a new job.
Many investors remain apprehensive about the market.
She felt apprehensive as she opened the letter.
Patients are often apprehensive before surgery.
He was apprehensive that the plan might fail.

definition: Involving a lot of effort, energy, and difficulty over a long period.
usage: Collocations: an arduous journey/task/process/climb. It is more formal than “hard” and suggests that something is both difficult and tiring.
examples: Applying for a visa can be an arduous process.
After an arduous climb, they finally reached the summit.
Rebuilding the town was an arduous task.
The journey was long and arduous, but worth it.
Writing a thesis is an arduous but rewarding experience.

definition: Able to express ideas and feelings clearly and effectively in speech or writing.
usage: As an adjective: an articulate speaker/student. As a verb (/ɑːˈtɪkjuleɪt/): to express something clearly: articulate a vision/your feelings/concerns. Both are compliments in academic and professional contexts.
examples: She's an articulate speaker who can explain complex ideas simply.
He struggled to articulate his feelings.
The report clearly articulates the risks involved.
Employers look for confident, articulate graduates.
Can you articulate exactly what the problem is?

definition: To have a strong desire to achieve something or to become a particular kind of person.
usage: Patterns: aspire to something; aspire to be/become… The adjective “aspiring” (an aspiring writer) describes someone hoping to enter a profession. The noun “aspiration” means a hope or ambition.
examples: She aspires to become a doctor.
Many young people aspire to own their own home.
He's an aspiring actor who works in a café while he auditions.
We should all aspire to treat others with respect.
The company aspires to be the market leader within five years.

definition: To state something firmly and confidently as true; also, to behave in a way that shows your authority or rights.
usage: Patterns: assert that…; assert your rights/authority/independence; assert yourself (behave confidently so others respect you). The noun “assertion” is common in academic writing for a claim that may need evidence.
examples: The author asserts that social media harms concentration.
He asserted his innocence throughout the trial.
You need to assert yourself more in meetings.
The new manager quickly asserted her authority.
Teenagers often assert their independence by challenging rules.

definition: Confident and direct in expressing your opinions and needs, without being aggressive.
usage: It is usually positive and is often contrasted with “passive” and “aggressive”. Collocations: assertive communication/behaviour; be more assertive. The noun is “assertiveness”.
examples: You need to be more assertive if you want a pay rise.
Assertive communication means stating your needs respectfully.
She's assertive without being rude.
The course teaches nurses to be assertive with difficult patients.
He became more assertive as he gained experience.

definition: To fully understand and absorb new information or ideas; also, to become part of a group or culture, or to make someone do so.
usage: Patterns: assimilate information/knowledge; assimilate into a society/culture. The cultural sense can be sensitive, as it may imply losing one's original identity. The noun is “assimilation”.
examples: It takes time to assimilate so much new information.
Immigrant children often assimilate into the new culture faster than their parents.
Students need time to assimilate what they've learned.
Some communities resisted pressure to assimilate.
The new employees were quickly assimilated into the team.

definition: To succeed in achieving or reaching something, usually after a lot of effort.
usage: Collocations: attain a goal/level/standard/qualification/position. It is more formal than “achieve” or “reach”. The noun “attainment” is used in education: “academic attainment”.
examples: Few athletes ever attain this level of fitness.
She attained a first-class degree in economics.
The company attained its sales target two months early.
Peace is difficult to attain without compromise.
Children from poorer families are less likely to attain top grades.

definition: To increase the size, amount, or value of something by adding to it.
usage: Collocations: augment your income/a team/existing resources. It is formal; everyday alternatives are “add to” or “boost”. “Augmented reality” is technology that adds digital images to a view of the real world.
examples: She augments her salary by tutoring in the evenings.
The team was augmented by two specialists from head office.
The new data augments earlier findings.
Augmented reality apps let you see furniture in your room before buying it.
The hospital augmented its staff during the flu season.

definition: Real and genuine, not a copy; also, true to the original style or tradition, or sincere in character.
usage: Collocations: authentic food/documents/materials/experience; an authentic signature. In language teaching, “authentic materials” are texts made for native speakers rather than learners. The noun is “authenticity”.
examples: This restaurant serves authentic Vietnamese street food.
Experts confirmed that the painting is authentic.
Teachers often use authentic materials such as news articles.
Travellers increasingly want authentic local experiences.
She comes across as warm and authentic in interviews.

definition: The freedom to make your own decisions and act independently; for a region or organization, the right to govern itself.
usage: Collocations: personal/financial/regional autonomy; give/grant someone autonomy. The adjective is “autonomous” (autonomous vehicles = self-driving cars). In workplaces, autonomy is linked to motivation and job satisfaction.
examples: Employees value autonomy over how they organize their work.
The region has been granted greater autonomy.
Teenagers want more autonomy from their parents.
Learner autonomy is a key goal of modern language teaching.
Financial autonomy was the main reason she started her own business.

definition: Extremely enthusiastic about an activity or interest.
usage: Almost always before a noun describing a person: an avid reader/fan/collector/follower. It suggests long-term, eager involvement.
examples: She's an avid reader who gets through two books a week.
As an avid football fan, he never misses a match.
My uncle is an avid collector of old coins.
The magazine has an avid following among young designers.
He was an avid traveller long before it became fashionable.

definition: A strong, negative reaction by many people against a recent event, decision, or trend.
usage: Patterns: a backlash against something; provoke/spark/face a backlash; a public/political backlash. It is common in news and social media contexts.
examples: The decision to raise ticket prices provoked a backlash from fans.
The company faced a social media backlash over its advert.
There has been a backlash against fast fashion in recent years.
Politicians fear a voter backlash if taxes rise.
The backlash forced the minister to apologize.

definition: To confuse someone completely, so that they cannot understand or explain something.
usage: Often passive: be baffled by something. The adjective “baffling” describes something very puzzling. Typical subjects: a question, behaviour, a mystery, symptoms.
examples: The sudden drop in sales baffled the managers.
Doctors were baffled by her symptoms.
I'm baffled as to why he quit his job.
The instructions were baffling, so I watched a video instead.
The case has baffled detectives for years.

definition: A standard or point of reference against which other things can be measured or judged.
usage: Patterns: a benchmark for something; set a benchmark; use something as a benchmark. As a verb: benchmark something against something. Common in business, education, and technology.
examples: The new phone sets a benchmark for battery life.
We use last year's results as a benchmark.
The company benchmarks its salaries against competitors.
IELTS 7.0 is often treated as a benchmark for university entry.
Her performance became the benchmark for the rest of the team.

definition: Kind and gentle, or not harmful; in medicine, describing a growth that is not cancerous.
usage: Collocations: a benign tumour; a benign smile; environmentally benign. The medical opposite is “malignant”. In general use, it suggests something harmless or mild.
examples: Fortunately, the tumour was benign.
The chemical is relatively benign compared with older pesticides.
He gave us a benign smile and waved us in.
Most of these bacteria are benign.
The climate here is fairly benign all year round.

definition: Very strange and unusual, sometimes in a way that is hard to believe.
usage: Collocations: a bizarre situation/story/twist/coincidence. It is stronger than “strange” and common in speech. The adverb “bizarrely” often comments on a surprising fact. Don't confuse it with “bazaar” (a market).
examples: It was a bizarre coincidence that we booked the same hotel.
The film has a bizarre plot that's hard to follow.
His behaviour at the party was frankly bizarre.
Bizarrely, the shop was open on Christmas Day but closed on Monday.
Some of the questions in the survey were quite bizarre.

definition: Very obvious and done openly, without any attempt to hide it, especially when it is wrong.
usage: Collocations: a blatant lie/disregard/example/attempt; blatant discrimination. It is always negative. The adverb “blatantly” is common: “blatantly obvious”, “blatantly unfair”.
examples: That's a blatant lie, and you know it.
The referee missed a blatant foul.
The company showed a blatant disregard for safety rules.
It was a blatant attempt to avoid paying tax.
The answer was blatantly copied from a website.

definition: Without hope or encouragement; also, of a place or weather, cold, empty, and unwelcoming.
usage: Collocations: a bleak future/outlook/picture/landscape. “Paint a bleak picture” means to describe a situation very negatively. It is common in news about the economy and the environment.
examples: The economic outlook for next year looks bleak.
The report paints a bleak picture of the state of the oceans.
Without a degree, his job prospects seemed bleak.
We walked across the bleak, windswept moor.
It was a bleak winter afternoon, and the streets were empty.

definition: To support or strengthen something, such as confidence, an argument, or the economy.
usage: Collocations: bolster confidence/morale/support/an argument/the economy. It is common in journalistic and academic writing. Everyday alternatives are “boost” or “strengthen”.
examples: The good news bolstered investor confidence.
She used statistics to bolster her argument.
Winning the first match bolstered the team's morale.
The government cut interest rates to bolster the economy.
New evidence has bolstered the case for early screening.

definition: An act of breaking a law, rule, agreement, or relationship of trust; also, a gap or break in a wall or barrier.
usage: Collocations: a breach of contract/trust/confidentiality/the rules; a data breach; a security breach. As a verb: breach a contract/regulations. Very common in legal, business, and IT contexts.
examples: Sharing patient records without consent is a serious breach of confidentiality.
The company was sued for breach of contract.
A data breach exposed millions of customers' details.
His lie was a breach of trust that she couldn't forgive.
The firm was fined for breaching environmental regulations.

definition: The quality of using few words to express something; also, the fact of lasting only a short time.
usage: Common in “for the sake of brevity” and “for brevity”. It is valued in writing and presentations. The proverb “Brevity is the soul of wit” (from Shakespeare) praises concise expression.
examples: For the sake of brevity, I'll only mention the main points.
The editor praised the brevity and clarity of her writing.
The brevity of his visit surprised everyone.
In emails, brevity is usually appreciated.
The report's brevity makes it easy to read.

definition: A system of government or management with many complicated rules and procedures, often seen as slow and inefficient.
usage: Often negative: cut/reduce bureaucracy; layers of bureaucracy; government bureaucracy. A “bureaucrat” is an official; “bureaucratic” describes slow, rule-bound procedures. Watch the spelling: bu-reau-cra-cy.
examples: Starting a business here involves a lot of bureaucracy.
The new government promised to cut bureaucracy.
Doctors complain that bureaucracy takes time away from patients.
Getting a work permit meant dealing with layers of bureaucracy.
Large companies can become slow because of internal bureaucracy.

definition: Full of busy, energetic activity and people.
usage: Collocations: a bustling city/market/street/port. It is usually positive, suggesting liveliness rather than chaos. The related phrase “bustling with” means full of: “bustling with tourists”.
examples: Hanoi's Old Quarter is a bustling area full of street vendors.
We wandered through the bustling night market.
The station was bustling with commuters.
She swapped her quiet village for a bustling capital city.
The once bustling port is now almost deserted.

definition: Honest and direct, even when the truth is uncomfortable; of a photograph, taken informally without the subject posing.
usage: Collocations: a candid conversation/interview/admission/assessment; to be candid (= to be honest). It suggests refreshing frankness rather than rudeness. The noun is “candour” (US: candor).
examples: To be candid, I don't think the plan will work.
In a candid interview, the actor talked about his struggle with anxiety.
I appreciate your candid feedback.
The best wedding photos are often the candid shots.
She was surprisingly candid about her mistakes.

definition: A person or event that causes an important change to happen quickly; in chemistry, a substance that speeds up a reaction without being changed itself.
usage: Patterns: a catalyst for change/growth/reform; act as a catalyst. The verb “catalyse” (US: catalyze) means to cause or accelerate something.
examples: The protest became a catalyst for political reform.
Losing his job was the catalyst for starting his own business.
Investment in transport can act as a catalyst for regional growth.
The enzyme acts as a catalyst in the reaction.
Her speech was the catalyst that changed public opinion.

definition: A warning or condition that should be considered before something is accepted or done.
usage: Patterns: with the caveat that…; add/include a caveat; one caveat is that… Common in academic and professional writing to signal limitations. Note the pronunciation: three syllables, /ˈkæviæt/.
examples: The results are encouraging, with the caveat that the sample was small.
I'll agree to the plan, with one caveat: we review it in three months.
The report includes several caveats about the reliability of the data.
One important caveat is that the drug hasn't been tested on children.
He offered the advice with the caveat that he wasn't an expert.

definition: To stop happening or existing, or to stop doing something.
usage: Patterns: cease to exist; cease + -ing; cease operations/trading. It is formal; “stop” is the everyday word. “Never cease to amaze” is a common emphatic phrase. A “ceasefire” is an agreement to stop fighting.
examples: The company ceased trading last year.
Her kindness never ceases to amaze me.
Without funding, the programme will cease to exist.
Fighting ceased after the two sides signed an agreement.
Production will cease at the end of the month.

definition: Lasting for a long time or happening repeatedly, especially of an illness or a problem that is hard to solve.
usage: Collocations: chronic illness/pain/fatigue; a chronic shortage; chronic unemployment. In medicine, it contrasts with “acute” (sudden and short). Informally, it can mean very bad: “The service was chronic.”
examples: She suffers from chronic back pain.
There is a chronic shortage of affordable housing.
Chronic stress can damage your health.
Diabetes is a chronic condition that needs careful management.
The city has a chronic traffic problem.

definition: To find a way of avoiding a rule, restriction, or difficulty, often in a clever or dishonest way.
usage: Collocations: circumvent the rules/the law/restrictions/censorship. It is formal and often implies something not entirely legitimate. Everyday alternatives: “get around”, “bypass”.
examples: Some users use VPNs to circumvent online censorship.
The company found a way to circumvent the new regulations.
We need a solution that doesn't circumvent the approval process.
Smugglers circumvented border controls by using small boats.
The loophole allowed firms to circumvent tax rules.

definition: A fight, argument, or serious disagreement; also, an occasion when two events happen at the same time, or colours look bad together.
usage: As a noun or verb: clash with someone/something; a clash of personalities/cultures/interests. Events can clash (“My exam clashes with the wedding”), and so can colours.
examples: Police clashed with protesters outside the parliament.
There's a clash of personalities between the two managers.
Unfortunately, the concert clashes with my sister's birthday.
That orange shirt clashes with your purple trousers.
The film explores the clash between tradition and modernity.

definition: To make someone do something by using force or threats.
usage: Pattern: coerce someone into (doing) something. The noun is “coercion” and the adjective “coercive” (coercive control). It is formal and strongly negative.
examples: The suspect claimed he had been coerced into confessing.
No one should be coerced into signing a contract.
Employees felt coerced into working unpaid overtime.
The government denied coercing journalists.
Manipulative partners may coerce their victims through financial control.

definition: Relating to mental processes such as thinking, learning, remembering, and understanding.
usage: Collocations: cognitive development/ability/skills/decline/load/bias. It is very common in psychology, education, and health. “Cognitive behavioural therapy” (CBT) is a widely used form of talking therapy.
examples: Reading to children supports their cognitive development.
Lack of sleep can impair cognitive performance.
Regular exercise may slow cognitive decline in older adults.
Too many slides increase the cognitive load on the audience.
Confirmation bias is a common cognitive bias.

definition: Forming a united whole, with parts that fit together well; of a group, working together closely.
usage: Collocations: a cohesive team/group/society/unit; a cohesive argument/essay. The noun “cohesion” is used in writing assessment (“coherence and cohesion”) and social science (“social cohesion”).
examples: The manager's main goal is to build a cohesive team.
Linking words help make your essay more cohesive.
A cohesive community is better able to recover from disasters.
The album feels cohesive, with every song sharing a similar mood.
The party struggled to present a cohesive message.

definition: To work together with another person or group to produce or achieve something.
usage: Patterns: collaborate with someone on/in something. The noun “collaboration” and adjective “collaborative” are very common in academic and business English. Historically, “collaborate” can also mean to help an enemy occupying your country.
examples: The two universities collaborated on the research project.
She has collaborated with several famous musicians.
Students are encouraged to collaborate rather than compete.
The app makes it easy for teams to collaborate remotely.
Scientists from twelve countries collaborated to develop the vaccine.

definition: Used in informal, everyday conversation rather than in formal speech or writing.
usage: Collocations: colloquial language/expressions/English. The noun “colloquialism” is an informal word or phrase. Academic writing usually avoids colloquial language such as “a lot of”, “kids”, or “get”.
examples: Avoid colloquial expressions in your academic essays.
The novel captures the colloquial speech of working-class London.
“Gonna” is a colloquial form of “going to”.
The textbook doesn't teach much colloquial English.
His writing style is relaxed and colloquial.

definition: To begin or start.
usage: Patterns: commence something; commence -ing; something commences. It is formal and used in official contexts (ceremonies, contracts, legal proceedings). The noun is “commencement”, which in the US also means a graduation ceremony.
examples: The ceremony will commence at 10 a.m.
Construction is expected to commence next spring.
Please do not commence writing until instructed.
Legal proceedings commenced against the company in May.
Her contract commences on the first of the month.

definition: To praise someone or something formally or publicly; also, to recommend something.
usage: Patterns: commend someone for (doing) something; highly commended. The adjective “commendable” means deserving praise. It is formal and often appears in official statements or reports.
examples: The firefighters were commended for their bravery.
The judge commended the jury for its careful work.
Her essay was highly commended by the panel.
Your patience is commendable.
I commend this book to anyone interested in history.

definition: A product or raw material that can be bought and sold, such as oil, coffee, or metals; also, something useful or valuable.
usage: Collocations: commodity prices/markets; a valuable/precious commodity. Figuratively: “Time is a precious commodity.” In economics, commodities are typically interchangeable goods traded in bulk.
examples: Coffee is one of the world's most traded commodities.
Rising commodity prices have pushed up inflation.
In a busy job, time is a precious commodity.
The country's economy depends heavily on commodity exports.
Water may become a scarce commodity in some regions.

definition: So convincing, interesting, or powerful that it holds your attention or persuades you.
usage: Collocations: compelling evidence/argument/reason/case/story. It is a strong positive word in academic and business contexts. “Compelling” describes things; the verb “compel” means to force.
examples: There is compelling evidence that smoking causes cancer.
She made a compelling case for increasing the budget.
The documentary tells a compelling story.
I can't see any compelling reason to change our plans.
The novel's characters are complex and compelling.

definition: Having enough skill, knowledge, or ability to do something well or to an acceptable standard.
usage: Patterns: competent at/in something; competent to do something. Note that “competent” often means “good enough” rather than outstanding. The noun “competence” and plural “competencies” (skills) are common in HR language.
examples: She's a highly competent lawyer.
You need to be competent in at least one programming language.
He was a competent but not exceptional player.
Only a competent electrician should do this work.
Are you competent to make this decision on your own?

definition: Too satisfied with yourself or a situation, so that you stop trying or fail to notice possible dangers.
usage: Patterns: complacent about something; become/grow complacent. It is always critical. The noun is “complacency”: “There is no room for complacency.”
examples: We can't afford to become complacent just because sales are good.
After winning three games, the team grew complacent.
People have become complacent about the risks of the virus.
Success can make companies complacent.
Don't get complacent; the final exam is still difficult.

definition: To act according to a rule, law, request, or order.
usage: Pattern: comply with something (comply with regulations/the law/a request/standards). The noun “compliance” is very common in business, and the adjective “compliant” means meeting the required rules.
examples: All products must comply with EU safety standards.
Companies that fail to comply with the law face heavy fines.
He refused to comply with the officer's instructions.
We are happy to comply with your request.
The building doesn't comply with fire regulations.

definition: To consist of or be made up of particular parts; also, to form the parts of something.
usage: Traditional use: the whole comprises the parts (“The course comprises six modules”). It is also used the other way: the parts comprise the whole (“Women comprise 60% of staff”). “Is comprised of” is very common but criticized by some careful writers; “consists of” avoids the issue.
examples: The course comprises six modules and a final project.
The committee comprises experts from five countries.
Women comprise over half of the workforce.
The flat comprises two bedrooms, a kitchen, and a bathroom.
The exam comprises three sections: reading, writing, and listening.

definition: To admit, often unwillingly, that something is true; also, to accept defeat or give something up.
usage: Patterns: concede that…; concede a point/defeat/a goal. In argumentative writing, conceding a point before rebutting it is a strong technique. The noun is “concession”.
examples: I concede that the plan has some weaknesses.
The candidate conceded defeat late on election night.
The team conceded two goals in the first half.
She reluctantly conceded that he had a point.
Neither side was willing to concede any ground.

definition: To form an idea or plan in your mind; to imagine something; also, to become pregnant.
usage: Patterns: conceive of something (imagine it); conceive a plan/an idea. The adjective “inconceivable” means impossible to imagine. The noun “concept” and “conception” are related.
examples: The idea for the app was conceived during a long train journey.
I can't conceive of a world without the internet.
The project was badly conceived from the start.
It's hard to conceive how much work went into this book.
They had been trying to conceive for several years.

definition: Giving all the necessary information clearly in few words.
usage: Collocations: a concise summary/explanation/answer; clear and concise. It is a compliment for writing and speech. The adverb is “concisely”.
examples: Keep your answers clear and concise.
The report ends with a concise summary of the findings.
Her explanation was concise and easy to follow.
Try to express your argument more concisely.
A good CV is concise, usually no more than two pages.

definition: To tell someone private or secret information because you trust them.
usage: Patterns: confide in someone; confide something to someone; confide that… The noun “confidant(e)” is a person you confide in. Related: “confidential” (secret) and “confidence” (trust).
examples: She confided in her sister about her financial problems.
He confided that he was thinking of leaving his job.
Teenagers often find it hard to confide in their parents.
I've never confided this to anyone before.
It helps to have a friend you can confide in.

definition: To behave according to the accepted rules or expectations of a group or society; also, to meet a required standard or law.
usage: Patterns: conform to/with rules, standards, expectations; pressure to conform. The noun “conformity” and the person “conformist” (opposite: nonconformist) are related. In social contexts it can imply giving up individuality.
examples: Teenagers often feel pressure to conform to their friends' style.
All electrical products must conform to safety standards.
She refused to conform to traditional expectations of women.
The building doesn't conform with local planning rules.
Schools sometimes punish students who don't conform.

definition: To face a difficult situation or problem and deal with it; also, to challenge someone face to face about something they have done.
usage: Patterns: confront a problem/fear/issue; confront someone about something; be confronted with/by something. The noun “confrontation” and adjective “confrontational” describe aggressive conflict.
examples: We need to confront the problem rather than ignore it.
She finally confronted her colleague about the missing money.
Therapy helped him confront his fear of flying.
Doctors are confronted with difficult decisions every day.
He tends to avoid conflict instead of confronting it.

definition: Careful to do your work well and thoroughly, because you feel a sense of duty.
usage: Collocations: a conscientious student/worker/employee. It is a strong compliment in references and reports. A “conscientious objector” refuses military service for moral reasons. Watch the spelling: con-sci-en-tious.
examples: She's a conscientious student who always submits work on time.
He was a conscientious employee who rarely missed a day.
Conscientious drivers check their tyres regularly.
The report was written by a very conscientious researcher.
Being conscientious is one of the best predictors of job performance.

definition: Following one after another without a break.
usage: Collocations: for the third consecutive year/day/time; consecutive wins/months. It usually appears with an ordinal number. The adverb is “consecutively”.
examples: The team has won five consecutive matches.
Prices have risen for the third consecutive month.
It rained for ten consecutive days.
She was voted best teacher for the second consecutive year.
Make sure the pages are numbered consecutively.

definition: To make something stronger, more secure, or more effective; also, to combine several things into one.
usage: Collocations: consolidate a position/power/knowledge/learning; consolidate debts/accounts. In education, it refers to reviewing material so it sticks. The noun is “consolidation”.
examples: Review sessions help students consolidate what they have learned.
The company consolidated its position as the market leader.
He consolidated his debts into a single loan.
The president moved quickly to consolidate power.
The three offices will be consolidated into one building.

definition: Very easy to see or notice, often because it is unusual or out of place.
usage: Collocations: feel conspicuous; a conspicuous absence; conspicuous consumption (spending to show off wealth). “Conspicuous by its/your absence” means noticeable because it is missing. The opposite is “inconspicuous”.
examples: I felt conspicuous in my bright red coat.
Put the notice in a conspicuous place where everyone will see it.
The minister was conspicuous by his absence at the meeting.
Luxury cars are a form of conspicuous consumption.
There was a conspicuous lack of enthusiasm in the room.

definition: To think carefully about something over a period of time, especially a possible future action; also, to look at something thoughtfully.
usage: Patterns: contemplate (doing) something; contemplate the possibility/future. It suggests serious, deep consideration. The noun “contemplation” and adjective “contemplative” suggest quiet reflection.
examples: She's contemplating a career change.
I can't even contemplate moving abroad right now.
He sat on the beach, contemplating the sunset.
The government is contemplating raising the retirement age.
It's frightening to contemplate what might have happened.

definition: Belonging to the present time; modern. Also, existing or happening at the same time as someone or something else.
usage: Collocations: contemporary art/music/society/issues; contemporary accounts (written at the time). As a noun, someone's contemporaries are people living or working at the same time.
examples: The gallery specializes in contemporary art.
The course examines contemporary issues in British politics.
Contemporary accounts describe the battle as chaotic.
Shakespeare was more successful than most of his contemporaries.
The hotel combines traditional architecture with contemporary design.

definition: To argue or claim that something is true; also, to have to deal with a difficult problem, or to compete for something.
usage: Patterns: contend that… (argue); contend with problems/difficulties (deal with); contend for a title/power (compete). A “contender” is a competitor with a chance of winning.
examples: The author contends that inequality harms economic growth.
Nurses have to contend with long hours and low pay.
Three teams are contending for the title.
Critics contend that the policy will increase poverty.
As if the rain wasn't enough, we also had to contend with a flat tyre.

definition: Likely to cause disagreement or argument.
usage: Collocations: a contentious issue/topic/decision/debate. It is similar to “controversial” but often used for issues within a group or field. It is common in academic and journalistic writing.
examples: Immigration remains a contentious issue in many countries.
The new parking rules proved highly contentious.
Inheritance can be a contentious topic within families.
The most contentious part of the plan is the tax increase.
The meeting became contentious as soon as the budget was discussed.

definition: Following traditional or accepted ways of doing things; ordinary and not original.
usage: Collocations: conventional wisdom/methods/medicine/weapons. “Conventional wisdom” is the generally accepted view, often challenged in essays. It can be neutral or slightly negative (lacking originality). Opposite: “unconventional”.
examples: Conventional wisdom says you should buy a house as soon as possible.
The treatment combines conventional medicine with acupuncture.
She took a less conventional route into journalism.
Electric cars are cheaper to run than conventional petrol cars.
The interview followed a fairly conventional format.

definition: Used to introduce a statement that is the opposite of, or reverses, the one just made.
usage: A linking adverb, usually at the start of a sentence followed by a comma. It signals a reversed relationship, not just a contrast: “A causes B; conversely, B prevents A.” Use “however” or “by contrast” for simple contrasts.
examples: Higher interest rates reduce borrowing; conversely, lower rates encourage it.
Some students learn best alone. Conversely, others need a group.
If prices rise, demand falls. Conversely, when prices fall, demand tends to rise.
Conversely, a lack of sleep can make you feel hungrier.
Exercise improves mood; conversely, inactivity is linked to depression.

definition: Friendly and polite, often in a formal way.
usage: Collocations: cordial relations; a cordial welcome/invitation/meeting. It suggests warmth within formality, e.g. between colleagues or countries. In British English, “cordial” is also a sweet fruit drink concentrate.
examples: The two leaders had a cordial meeting.
Relations between the neighbours remained cordial.
We received a cordial welcome from our hosts.
You are cordially invited to the opening ceremony.
Their relationship was cordial but never close.

definition: To provide evidence or information that supports a statement, theory, or finding.
usage: Collocations: corroborate a story/claim/finding/account; corroborating evidence. It is formal and common in legal and research contexts. The noun is “corroboration”.
examples: Two witnesses corroborated his account of the accident.
The new study corroborates earlier findings.
Police found no evidence to corroborate her claim.
CCTV footage corroborated the driver's version of events.
These results need to be corroborated by further research.

definition: Able to be believed or trusted; convincing.
usage: Collocations: a credible source/witness/explanation/threat/alternative. In academic writing, “credible sources” are reliable ones. The noun “credibility” is common: lose/gain/damage credibility.
examples: Make sure you use credible sources in your research.
The police found her story credible.
The opposition has failed to offer a credible alternative.
The minister's explanation was not credible.
There is no credible evidence that the vaccine causes autism.

definition: A standard or principle by which something is judged or decided.
usage: Plural: criteria. A very common mistake is using “criteria” as a singular. Patterns: meet/satisfy/fulfil the criteria; criteria for something; the main/key criterion.
examples: Price is not the only criterion when choosing a laptop.
Applicants must meet all the selection criteria.
The main criterion for success is customer satisfaction.
What criteria do examiners use to assess essays?
Each criterion is scored from one to nine.

definition: Large, heavy, and difficult to carry or use; also, of a process, slow and complicated.
usage: Collocations: cumbersome equipment/luggage; a cumbersome process/procedure/system. It is often used to criticize bureaucracy or outdated technology.
examples: Early mobile phones were cumbersome devices.
The application process is slow and cumbersome.
Carrying all that camera equipment was cumbersome.
The new software replaced a cumbersome paper-based system.
The sentence is grammatically correct but rather cumbersome.

definition: To control or limit something, especially something harmful.
usage: As a verb or noun: curb inflation/spending/emissions/your appetite; a curb on immigration/spending. In American English, “curb” is also the edge of the pavement (British: “kerb”).
examples: The government introduced new measures to curb inflation.
Try to curb your spending before the holidays.
New laws aim to curb air pollution in cities.
There are calls for tighter curbs on gambling adverts.
Drinking water before meals can help curb your appetite.

definition: Believing that people are mainly motivated by self-interest; also, doubting that something is sincere or will succeed.
usage: Patterns: cynical about something; a cynical attempt/ploy (done for selfish reasons). The noun is “cynicism” and the person a “cynic”. Compare “sceptical”, which is more neutral and evidence-based.
examples: Many voters have become cynical about politicians' promises.
It was a cynical attempt to win votes.
Don't be so cynical; some people genuinely want to help.
Years of failed reforms made her cynical.
The advert was seen as a cynical marketing ploy.

definition: Seeming difficult or frightening, and therefore making you feel less confident.
usage: Collocations: a daunting task/prospect/challenge; find something daunting. The verb “daunt” is mostly used in the negative: “undaunted” means not discouraged.
examples: Moving to a new country can be a daunting prospect.
Writing a 10,000-word dissertation seemed daunting at first.
The size of the task was daunting.
Many people find public speaking daunting.
Learning Chinese characters is less daunting if you learn a few each day.

definition: Broken pieces of something that has been destroyed or damaged; scattered rubbish.
usage: Uncountable: debris (not “debrises”). Collocations: clear (away) debris; flying/falling debris; space debris. Note the silent “s” in pronunciation.
examples: Workers cleared the debris after the storm.
Several people were hurt by flying debris.
Space debris poses a risk to satellites.
The beach was covered in plastic debris.
Investigators examined the debris from the crash.

definition: To succeed in reading or understanding something that is difficult to read or understand, such as bad handwriting or a code.
usage: Collocations: decipher handwriting/a code/a message/the meaning. It is often used humorously for messy writing or confusing instructions.
examples: I can barely decipher the doctor's handwriting.
It took experts years to decipher the ancient script.
Can you decipher what this message means?
The instructions were almost impossible to decipher.
She tried to decipher the expression on his face.

definition: Able to make decisions quickly and confidently; also, having a very important influence on the final result.
usage: Collocations: decisive action/leadership/victory/factor/moment. Applied to people, it is a compliment. The opposite is “indecisive”. The adverb is “decisively”.
examples: We need decisive action to deal with the crisis.
A good leader must be decisive.
Her goal proved decisive in the final.
Price was the decisive factor in our choice.
The election produced no decisive winner.

definition: To consider or judge something in a particular way.
usage: Patterns: deem something (to be) + adjective/noun; be deemed + adjective. It is formal and common in official, legal, and academic texts: “deemed necessary/appropriate/unsafe”.
examples: The building was deemed unsafe and closed.
Take whatever action you deem necessary.
The film was deemed unsuitable for children.
Her application was deemed incomplete.
Any student absent without reason will be deemed to have withdrawn.

definition: To delay something until a later time; also, to accept someone else's opinion or decision because of their knowledge or authority.
usage: Patterns: defer a decision/payment/a place at university; defer to someone/their judgement. Past forms double the r: deferred, deferring. The noun “deference” means polite respect.
examples: She deferred her university place for a year to travel.
The decision has been deferred until next month.
You can defer payment until the end of the year.
On medical matters, I defer to the doctors.
He always defers to his older brother.

definition: The amount by which something, especially money, is less than what is needed or expected; a lack of something.
usage: Collocations: a budget/trade deficit; reduce/cut the deficit; run a deficit. Outside economics: a sleep deficit, an attention deficit, a deficit in skills. The opposite in finance is “surplus”.
examples: The government has promised to reduce the budget deficit.
The country runs a large trade deficit with China.
After a week of late nights, I had a serious sleep deficit.
The team overcame a two-goal deficit to win the match.
Training programmes aim to address the skills deficit in the industry.

definition: Final and not able to be changed or questioned; also, considered the most complete and reliable of its kind.
usage: Collocations: a definitive answer/decision/guide/study/version. Don't confuse it with “definite” (certain, clear): a definitive guide is the authoritative one.
examples: We still don't have a definitive answer to the question.
This is widely regarded as the definitive biography of Mandela.
No definitive decision has been made yet.
There is no definitive evidence that the drug works.
The website offers a definitive guide to applying for a visa.

definition: To make something worse in quality or condition; also, to treat someone without respect so that they feel worthless.
usage: Collocations: degrade the environment/soil/performance/quality. The adjective “degrading” describes humiliating treatment. “Biodegradable” materials break down naturally. The noun is “degradation”.
examples: Intensive farming can degrade the soil over time.
Old batteries degrade and hold less charge.
Prisoners were subjected to degrading treatment.
Air pollution has degraded the quality of life in the city.
Plastic takes centuries to degrade.

definition: To give part of your work, power, or responsibility to someone else, usually at a lower level.
usage: Patterns: delegate tasks/responsibility/authority to someone. As a noun (/ˈdelɪgət/), a delegate is a person sent to represent others at a conference. The noun “delegation” means both the act and a group of representatives.
examples: Good managers know how to delegate.
She delegated the research to two junior colleagues.
If you don't delegate, you'll burn out.
Some decisions can't be delegated.
Delegates from 50 countries attended the conference.

definition: Done on purpose, intentionally; also, slow and careful in movement or thought.
usage: Collocations: a deliberate attempt/act/choice/decision; deliberate practice (focused, structured practice). As a verb (/dɪˈlɪbəreɪt/), it means to think or discuss carefully: “The jury deliberated for hours.” The adverb “deliberately” is very common.
examples: It wasn't an accident; it was a deliberate attempt to mislead.
She spoke in a slow, deliberate way.
Deliberate practice is more effective than simply repeating tasks.
He deliberately ignored my message.
The jury deliberated for two days before reaching a verdict.

definition: The end or failure of something that was once successful; formally, a person's death.
usage: Collocations: the demise of a company/industry/tradition; lead to/contribute to the demise of. It is formal and common in writing about business and culture.
examples: Online shopping has contributed to the demise of many high-street shops.
The scandal led to the demise of the company.
Many mourned the demise of the local newspaper.
Reports of the novel's demise have been greatly exaggerated.
The film tells the story of the king's rise and eventual demise.

definition: To criticize something or someone strongly and publicly.
usage: Patterns: denounce something as…; publicly/strongly denounce. It is formal and common in political and news language. The noun is “denunciation”.
examples: World leaders denounced the attack.
The plan was denounced as unfair by opposition parties.
She publicly denounced the use of violence.
Human rights groups denounced the arrests.
The newspaper denounced the minister as a hypocrite.

definition: To reduce the amount of something, especially a resource, so that little remains.
usage: Collocations: deplete resources/stocks/reserves/savings; the ozone layer is depleted. The noun is “depletion”. Often passive: “Fish stocks have been severely depleted.”
examples: Overfishing has severely depleted fish stocks.
The long illness depleted her savings.
Intense exercise depletes the body's energy reserves.
We must stop depleting the planet's natural resources.
By Friday, our team was depleted by illness.

definition: To move soldiers or equipment into position for use; more generally, to use something or someone effectively for a purpose.
usage: Collocations: deploy troops/resources/technology/staff; deploy software (release it). The noun is “deployment”. In IT, “deploy” means to release new code or software to users.
examples: Thousands of troops were deployed to the border.
The company plans to deploy AI in its customer service.
Extra police were deployed for the football match.
We'll deploy the update to all users on Monday.
Teachers need to deploy a range of strategies to engage students.

definition: To take something important or necessary away from someone, or prevent them from having it.
usage: Pattern: deprive someone of something (deprive of sleep/food/rights/freedom). The adjective “deprived” describes poor areas or people lacking basic needs: “a deprived neighbourhood”. The noun is “deprivation” (sleep deprivation).
examples: Long working hours deprive people of time with their families.
Many children in the region are deprived of basic education.
The study looked at the effects of being deprived of sleep.
The school serves one of the most deprived areas of the city.
Prisoners should not be deprived of their basic rights.

definition: To discourage someone from doing something, usually by making them afraid of the consequences or by making it difficult.
usage: Patterns: deter someone from (doing) something; deter crime/attacks. Past forms double the r: deterred. The noun “deterrent” is something that deters (“a deterrent to crime”).
examples: High prices deter many young people from buying a home.
Security cameras are meant to deter thieves.
Nothing could deter her from her goal.
Will tougher sentences deter crime?
The bad weather didn't deter thousands of fans from attending.

definition: Causing harm or damage.
usage: Pattern: detrimental to someone/something (detrimental to health/learning/the environment). It is formal and common in academic writing. The noun “detriment” appears in “to the detriment of”.
examples: Too much screen time can be detrimental to children's sleep.
The new policy could be detrimental to small businesses.
Stress has a detrimental effect on memory.
Skipping breakfast is not necessarily detrimental to health.
Cutting the arts budget would be detrimental to education.

definition: To move away from what is normal, planned, or expected.
usage: Pattern: deviate from something (the plan/the norm/the route/the script). The noun is “deviation”, used in statistics in “standard deviation”.
examples: We shouldn't deviate from the original plan.
The pilot had to deviate from the usual route because of the storm.
His answer deviated slightly from the official position.
Results that deviate significantly from the mean should be checked.
She never deviates from her morning routine.

definition: To invent or plan a new method, system, or solution, especially by careful thought.
usage: Collocations: devise a plan/strategy/method/system/scheme. Don't confuse the verb “devise” (/z/) with the noun “device” (/s/), a piece of equipment.
examples: We need to devise a strategy to attract younger customers.
The teacher devised a game to help students learn vocabulary.
Researchers devised a new method for measuring air quality.
They devised a plan to surprise her on her birthday.
The system was devised to reduce waiting times.

definition: Showing steady, careful effort in your work or duties.
usage: Collocations: a diligent student/worker/search; diligent research. The noun “diligence” appears in “due diligence”, the careful checks done before a business deal.
examples: She's a diligent student who reviews her notes every evening.
After a diligent search, they found the missing file.
Success in languages comes from diligent daily practice.
Diligent record-keeping saved the company during the audit.
He was praised for his diligent work on the project.

definition: To make a liquid weaker by adding water or another liquid; also, to make something weaker or less effective.
usage: Patterns: dilute something with water; dilute a message/policy/brand/someone's influence. As an adjective: a dilute solution. The noun is “dilution”.
examples: Dilute the juice with water before giving it to children.
Critics say the changes dilute the original policy.
Adding too many features may dilute the brand.
Issuing new shares will dilute existing shareholders' stakes.
The paint should be diluted before use.

definition: To notice, recognize, or understand something, especially when it is not obvious.
usage: Patterns: discern a pattern/difference/trend; discern whether/what… It is formal. The adjective “discerning” describes someone with good judgement and taste: “discerning customers”.
examples: It's difficult to discern any clear pattern in the data.
I could just discern a figure in the fog.
Children need to learn to discern fact from opinion online.
The hotel attracts discerning travellers.
It was hard to discern what he really meant.

definition: To make information known publicly, especially information that was previously secret or private.
usage: Collocations: disclose information/details/a conflict of interest; refuse to disclose. The noun is “disclosure”. Common in legal, financial, and medical contexts.
examples: The company refused to disclose the terms of the deal.
Patients' details must not be disclosed without consent.
You must disclose any conflict of interest.
He disclosed that he had been offered another job.
The price of the house was not disclosed.

definition: Serious discussion or communication about a subject, especially in speech or writing; in linguistics, language in use beyond the sentence level.
usage: Collocations: public/political/academic discourse; discourse analysis; discourse markers (however, moreover, anyway). It is a key academic term.
examples: Social media has changed the nature of political discourse.
Discourse markers like “however” help readers follow your argument.
The book examines discourse about immigration in the press.
Civil discourse becomes difficult when people stop listening.
She studies the discourse of advertising.

definition: Careful not to cause embarrassment or reveal private information; also, not attracting attention.
usage: Collocations: a discreet inquiry/word/distance; be discreet about something. Don't confuse it with “discrete” (separate and distinct), pronounced the same. The noun is “discretion”.
examples: Please be discreet; I don't want the whole office to know.
She made a few discreet inquiries about the job.
The hotel staff were polite and discreet.
He wore a small, discreet earring.
The bodyguards kept a discreet distance.

definition: A large difference between two or more things, especially an unfair one.
usage: Patterns: a disparity between A and B; disparities in pay/income/health. It is formal and frequent in social science and policy writing.
examples: There is a growing disparity between rich and poor.
The report highlights disparities in pay between men and women.
Health disparities between regions remain significant.
The disparity in their ages didn't seem to matter.
The government aims to reduce regional disparities.

definition: To spread over a wide area, or to make a group of people or things separate and go in different directions.
usage: Collocations: the crowd dispersed; disperse protesters/seeds/heat. Often used in news reports about crowds and in science (light, pollutants). The noun is “dispersal” or “dispersion”.
examples: Police used water cannons to disperse the protesters.
The crowd slowly dispersed after the concert.
Wind helps disperse the seeds of many plants.
The fog dispersed by mid-morning.
The company's employees are dispersed across five countries.

definition: To interrupt or disturb an activity, system, or process so that it cannot continue normally; in business, to change an industry radically.
usage: Collocations: disrupt services/traffic/sleep/supply chains/a class. The adjective “disruptive” describes behaviour or innovations that cause disruption. The noun is “disruption”.
examples: The strike disrupted train services across the country.
Using your phone late at night can disrupt your sleep.
Streaming services have disrupted the music industry.
Protesters tried to disrupt the meeting.
The storm disrupted supply chains for weeks.

definition: Strong disagreement with an official or widely held opinion; as a verb, to express such disagreement.
usage: Collocations: political dissent; voice/express dissent; crush/suppress dissent; dissent from a view. A “dissenter” or “dissident” is someone who disagrees publicly, especially with a government.
examples: The regime does not tolerate political dissent.
There was little dissent when the proposal was put to a vote.
Two judges dissented from the majority opinion.
Healthy organizations encourage dissent rather than silence it.
Several members voiced their dissent at the meeting.

definition: To change the shape, sound, or meaning of something so that it is no longer accurate or natural.
usage: Collocations: distort the facts/truth/results/an image/the market. The noun is “distortion”. In academic writing, “distort” often describes misleading use of data or quotes.
examples: The newspaper distorted the facts to make the story more dramatic.
Outliers can distort the average.
The mirror distorted his reflection.
Subsidies can distort competition in the market.
Her words were distorted and taken out of context.

definition: To separate and go in different directions; also, of opinions or results, to become different from each other.
usage: Patterns: diverge from something; views/paths/results diverge. The opposite is “converge”. The adjective “divergent” is used for differing opinions or for “divergent thinking” (creative, generating many ideas).
examples: Our opinions diverge on this issue.
The path diverges just after the bridge.
The results diverge significantly from earlier predictions.
After university, their careers diverged.
Where the two theories diverge is on the question of cause.

definition: To change the direction or purpose of something; also, to take someone's attention away from something.
usage: Patterns: divert traffic/a flight/funds/resources (to/from); divert attention from something. The noun “diversion” means a change of route or something that distracts.
examples: The flight was diverted to Manchester because of fog.
Traffic is being diverted while the road is repaired.
Funds were diverted from education to defence.
The scandal diverted attention from the economy.
He told a joke to divert attention from his mistake.

definition: Extreme and sudden, with a strong or far-reaching effect.
usage: Collocations: drastic measures/action/changes/cuts. It often implies that the action is severe or risky. The adverb “drastically” is common: “drastically reduce”.
examples: The company took drastic measures to cut costs.
Doctors warned that drastic action was needed.
There's been a drastic change in his behaviour.
Prices have fallen drastically.
Don't do anything drastic until we've talked.

definition: Probably not honest, true, or reliable; also, feeling doubtful about something.
usage: Patterns: dubious claims/methods/sources/honour; be dubious about something (doubtful). “The dubious distinction/honour of” is used ironically for an achievement nobody wants.
examples: The website makes some dubious claims about weight loss.
He made his money through dubious business deals.
I was dubious about the plan at first.
The city has the dubious honour of having the worst traffic in Europe.
Avoid using dubious sources in your essay.

definition: Able to last a long time without breaking or getting weaker.
usage: Collocations: durable materials/goods/products; a durable peace/solution. “Consumer durables” are long-lasting goods like fridges and cars. The noun is “durability”.
examples: These boots are made from durable leather.
Plastic is cheap and durable, which is why it's everywhere.
The two countries are trying to reach a durable peace.
We need a more durable solution to the housing crisis.
Sales of consumer durables fell during the recession.

definition: To gradually become smaller in size, number, or strength.
usage: Intransitive: numbers/supplies/hopes/savings dwindle. Often “dwindle to” a small amount, or “dwindling” as an adjective: “dwindling resources”.
examples: The village's population has dwindled to fewer than 200 people.
Our savings dwindled while we were unemployed.
Hopes of finding survivors are dwindling.
Bee populations have dwindled in recent decades.
The company is struggling with dwindling sales.

definition: Unusual and slightly strange in behaviour, ideas, or appearance, often in a harmless or amusing way.
usage: As an adjective (an eccentric uncle/habit) or noun (a lovable eccentric). It is usually affectionate rather than insulting. The noun “eccentricity” means strange behaviour.
examples: My eccentric aunt keeps twelve cats and talks to all of them.
He was known for his eccentric fashion sense.
The professor was a brilliant but eccentric man.
Wearing sunglasses indoors is one of her eccentric habits.
The town is full of artists and harmless eccentrics.

definition: To get information, a reaction, or a response from someone, often with effort.
usage: Collocations: elicit a response/reaction/information/answers. Teachers “elicit” language from students instead of simply telling them. Don't confuse it with “illicit” (illegal), which sounds similar.
examples: The survey elicited over 2,000 responses.
His joke failed to elicit a single laugh.
Good teachers elicit answers from students rather than giving them.
Police tried to elicit information from the witness.
The proposal elicited a strong reaction from local residents.

definition: Able to express ideas clearly, fluently, and persuasively; also, expressing something clearly without words.
usage: Collocations: an eloquent speaker/speech/plea/defence. “An eloquent silence” or “eloquent testimony” expresses meaning without speech. The noun is “eloquence”.
examples: She gave an eloquent speech about climate justice.
He's an eloquent writer with a gift for metaphor.
The lawyer made an eloquent plea for mercy.
Her silence was more eloquent than any words.
The empty shelves are eloquent evidence of the shortage.

definition: Difficult to find, catch, achieve, or remember.
usage: Collocations: an elusive goal/target/concept/animal; prove elusive. “Success has proved elusive” is a common way of saying something hasn't been achieved.
examples: A cure for the disease remains elusive.
The snow leopard is one of the most elusive animals in the world.
Happiness can be an elusive goal.
Victory has proved elusive for the team this season.
The exact meaning of the poem is elusive.

definition: To start something new, important, or difficult; literally, to get on a ship or plane.
usage: Pattern: embark on/upon something (a career/journey/project/reform). The opposite of the literal sense is “disembark” (get off).
examples: She embarked on a career in medicine.
The government has embarked on an ambitious reform programme.
We're about to embark on a three-month trip around Asia.
Before embarking on a PhD, think carefully about funding.
Passengers began to embark shortly after noon.

definition: To fix something firmly into a surrounding mass or system; also, to make an idea or practice a fixed part of something.
usage: Usually passive: be embedded in something. Collocations: deeply embedded, embed a video/link. Past forms double the d: embedded, embedding.
examples: A splinter of glass was embedded in his foot.
These attitudes are deeply embedded in our culture.
You can embed the video in your website.
Sustainability should be embedded in every business decision.
The chip is embedded in the passport.

definition: To represent or express an idea or quality in a clear, visible form.
usage: Typical objects: values, spirit, ideals, qualities. The noun “embodiment” appears in “the embodiment of”: “She is the embodiment of patience.”
examples: The building embodies the city's modern spirit.
For many fans, he embodies everything good about the sport.
These principles are embodied in the constitution.
Her work embodies a deep respect for nature.
The new logo is meant to embody the company's values.

definition: To accept and support an idea, change, or opportunity enthusiastically; literally, to hug someone.
usage: Collocations: embrace change/technology/new ideas/diversity/an opportunity. It suggests willing, positive acceptance. As a noun: a warm embrace.
examples: Older employees have embraced the new technology.
We should embrace change rather than fear it.
She embraced the opportunity to study abroad.
They embraced each other at the airport.
The company has embraced flexible working.

definition: To appear or come out from somewhere; also, to become known or to develop.
usage: Patterns: emerge from somewhere; it emerged that… (became known); emerge as a leader/winner. The adjective “emerging” describes new and growing things: emerging markets/technologies.
examples: The sun emerged from behind the clouds.
It later emerged that the minister had known about the problem.
She emerged as the clear favourite.
New evidence has emerged in the case.
Several clear themes emerged from the interviews.

definition: Famous and highly respected, especially within a profession.
usage: Collocations: an eminent scientist/scholar/surgeon/lawyer. Don't confuse it with “imminent” (about to happen) or “immanent”. The adverb “eminently” means extremely: “eminently sensible”.
examples: The report was written by an eminent economist.
She is one of the most eminent historians of her generation.
Several eminent scientists signed the letter.
The plan seems eminently sensible.
He was trained by an eminent surgeon in London.

definition: Based on observation, experiment, or experience rather than on theory alone.
usage: Collocations: empirical evidence/research/data/study. It is a key academic word, often contrasted with “theoretical”. The adverb is “empirically”.
examples: There is little empirical evidence to support the claim.
The theory has not yet been tested empirically.
The paper combines theoretical analysis with empirical research.
