We need empirical data, not opinions.
Empirical studies show that sleep improves memory.

definition: To give someone the confidence, power, or authority to do something or control their own life.
usage: Patterns: empower someone to do something; empower women/communities/employees. The noun is “empowerment” and the adjective “empowering”. Common in education, development, and management.
examples: Education empowers women to make their own choices.
Managers should empower staff to make decisions.
The programme empowers local communities to manage their own resources.
Learning to drive was an empowering experience.
The law empowers the police to search vehicles.

definition: To try to be like someone or something you admire, often by copying them.
usage: Typical objects: a role model, a success, a company's model. It is more positive than “copy” or “imitate”. In computing, an emulator imitates another system.
examples: Young players try to emulate their heroes.
Other cities are hoping to emulate Singapore's success.
She wanted to emulate her mother's career.
Few companies have been able to emulate the model.
The software emulates an old games console.

definition: To include a wide range of things; also, to surround or cover an area completely.
usage: Typical subjects: a course, term, definition, area, role. It is formal; everyday alternatives are “include” or “cover”.
examples: The course encompasses history, politics, and economics.
Her role encompasses both marketing and sales.
The term “health” encompasses mental as well as physical well-being.
The national park encompasses mountains, lakes, and forests.
The study encompasses data from over thirty countries.

definition: As a noun, a serious attempt to do something, or an activity requiring effort; as a verb, to try very hard.
usage: Patterns: endeavour to do something; a human/scientific/creative endeavour. It is formal. American spelling: “endeavor”.
examples: We will endeavour to reply within 48 hours.
Space exploration is one of humanity's greatest endeavours.
Despite our best endeavours, the project failed.
She endeavoured to keep the meeting short.
Scientific endeavour depends on international cooperation.

definition: To publicly express support or approval for someone or something; also, to advertise a product by saying you use or like it.
usage: Collocations: endorse a candidate/plan/proposal/product. The noun “endorsement” covers both meanings, including celebrity endorsements.
examples: The newspaper endorsed the opposition candidate.
The committee endorsed the proposal unanimously.
Many athletes earn more from endorsing products than from competing.
I don't endorse his views, but I respect his right to express them.
The guidelines have been endorsed by medical experts.

definition: To suffer something difficult or unpleasant patiently over a long period; also, to continue to exist.
usage: Collocations: endure pain/hardship/suffering; a friendship that endured. The adjective “enduring” means long-lasting (an enduring legacy), and “endurance” is the ability to keep going.
examples: The refugees endured terrible hardship during their journey.
She endured years of pain before getting a diagnosis.
I can't endure another meeting like that.
Their friendship endured for over sixty years.
The novel's enduring popularity surprised its publishers.

definition: To improve the quality of something by adding to it; also, to make someone richer.
usage: Collocations: enrich your life/experience/vocabulary/the soil; enriched with vitamins. “Enriching” describes a rewarding experience.
examples: Reading widely will enrich your vocabulary.
Travel has enriched my understanding of other cultures.
The cereal is enriched with iron and vitamins.
Volunteering abroad was a truly enriching experience.
Critics say the policy enriched a small elite.

definition: To involve something as a necessary part or consequence.
usage: Patterns: entail something; entail doing something; what does X entail? It is common in job and project descriptions: “The role entails a lot of travel.”
examples: What exactly does the job entail?
The project will entail a lot of hard work.
Moving abroad entails more paperwork than you might expect.
The role entails managing a team of ten people.
Any change in policy would entail significant costs.

definition: A person who starts and runs their own business, often taking financial risks to do so.
usage: Collocations: a successful/young/serial/social entrepreneur. The adjective “entrepreneurial” describes the spirit or skills involved (entrepreneurial spirit/mindset). The word comes from French, which explains the spelling.
examples: She became an entrepreneur after leaving her corporate job.
The city offers grants to young entrepreneurs.
A serial entrepreneur, he has founded five companies.
Social entrepreneurs use business methods to solve social problems.
Many entrepreneurs fail several times before they succeed.

definition: Fair and reasonable, treating everyone in a way that is just.
usage: Collocations: an equitable distribution/system/solution/access. “Equitable” stresses fairness that may require treating people differently according to need, while “equal” means the same for everyone. The noun is “equity”.
examples: We need a more equitable distribution of wealth.
The goal is equitable access to healthcare for all.
Both sides agreed that the settlement was equitable.
Is the current tax system really equitable?
Schools are working towards more equitable outcomes for disadvantaged students.

definition: To destroy or get rid of something completely, especially something harmful.
usage: Collocations: eradicate poverty/disease/corruption/a pest. It implies total removal; “reduce” is more realistic for many problems. The noun is “eradication”.
examples: Smallpox was eradicated in 1980.
The charity's mission is to eradicate child poverty.
It's almost impossible to eradicate corruption completely.
Scientists hope to eradicate malaria within a generation.
The new law aims to eradicate discrimination in hiring.

definition: To gradually wear away rock or soil through wind or water; also, to slowly weaken or destroy something such as trust or confidence.
usage: Collocations: erode trust/confidence/support/rights/savings. The figurative sense is very common in news and academic writing. The noun is “erosion”.
examples: The sea has eroded the cliffs over thousands of years.
Repeated scandals have eroded public trust in politicians.
Inflation is eroding the value of people's savings.
Her confidence was gradually eroded by constant criticism.
Critics fear the law will erode civil liberties.

definition: Not regular or predictable; changing suddenly and often.
usage: Collocations: erratic behaviour/driving/performance/heartbeat/sleep patterns. It is usually negative, suggesting a lack of control or consistency.
examples: His behaviour has become increasingly erratic.
Police stopped the driver because of his erratic driving.
The team's performance this season has been erratic.
Shift work can lead to erratic sleep patterns.
The Wi-Fi in this building is erratic.

definition: To become, or to make something, more serious, intense, or larger.
usage: Collocations: the conflict/violence/crisis/costs escalate(s); escalate a complaint (pass it to a higher level). The noun is “escalation”. In customer service, “escalate” means to refer an issue to a manager.
examples: The argument quickly escalated into a fight.
There are fears that the conflict could escalate.
Costs escalated far beyond the original budget.
If the problem isn't solved, I'll escalate it to a manager.
Tensions escalated after the election.

definition: The most important quality or basic nature of something, which makes it what it is.
usage: Common phrases: the essence of something; in essence (basically); time is of the essence (speed is very important). An essence is also a concentrated flavouring (vanilla essence).
examples: The essence of good teaching is clear communication.
In essence, the two proposals are the same.
Time is of the essence, so we need to act quickly.
The photograph captures the essence of city life.
Add a few drops of vanilla essence to the mixture.

definition: Relating to principles of right and wrong; also, morally correct and acceptable.
usage: Collocations: ethical issues/questions/standards/concerns/investment/consumers. In research, “ethical approval” is permission confirming a study meets moral standards. The opposite is “unethical”; the noun “ethics” (plural) means moral principles.
examples: Genetic engineering raises difficult ethical questions.
All studies involving people require ethical approval.
Is it ethical to test cosmetics on animals?
More consumers want to buy from ethical brands.
Journalists face an ethical dilemma when sources ask to stay anonymous.

definition: To bring a memory, feeling, or image into someone's mind.
usage: Collocations: evoke memories/emotions/a sense of something/a response. The adjective “evocative” describes something that strongly brings images or feelings to mind.
examples: The smell of baking evokes memories of my grandmother's kitchen.
The film evokes the atmosphere of 1960s London.
His speech evoked a strong emotional response.
The music evokes a sense of peace.
Her photographs evoke the loneliness of big cities.

definition: To make a problem, bad situation, or negative feeling worse.
usage: Collocations: exacerbate a problem/the situation/tensions/symptoms/inequality. It is formal and very common in academic writing; “make worse” is the everyday alternative.
examples: The drought has exacerbated food shortages.
Stress can exacerbate the symptoms of asthma.
Cutting services would only exacerbate inequality.
His comments exacerbated tensions between the two groups.
Poor planning exacerbated the effects of the flood.

definition: To be a typical example of something; also, to give an example in order to make something clearer.
usage: Patterns: exemplify a trend/quality/approach; be exemplified by something. The adjective “exemplary” means excellent and worth copying (exemplary behaviour).
examples: The building exemplifies the modernist style.
Her career exemplifies the benefits of lifelong learning.
This problem is exemplified by the rise in youth unemployment.
The essay uses case studies to exemplify each point.
His work exemplifies what good journalism should be.

definition: Free from a duty, rule, payment, or obligation that applies to others.
usage: As an adjective: exempt from tax/fees/military service; tax-exempt. As a verb: exempt someone from something. The noun is “exemption”.
examples: Children under five are exempt from the entry fee.
Food is exempt from VAT in the UK.
Students with high IELTS scores may be exempted from the English course.
Charities are often tax-exempt.
No one is exempt from the new security checks.

definition: To use power, influence, or force to make something happen; also, to make a great physical or mental effort.
usage: Collocations: exert influence/pressure/control/force (on someone); exert yourself (try hard physically). The noun “exertion” means physical effort.
examples: Parents exert a strong influence on their children's choices.
The union is exerting pressure on the government.
Don't exert yourself too much after the operation.
Social media exerts a powerful influence on teenagers.
Large companies can exert significant control over prices.

definition: Very thorough and complete, covering every detail or possibility.
usage: Collocations: an exhaustive list/search/study/investigation. “This list is not exhaustive” is a common academic phrase meaning there are more examples. Don't confuse it with “exhausting” (very tiring).
examples: The police carried out an exhaustive search of the area.
This list of examples is not exhaustive.
After exhaustive tests, the drug was approved.
The book provides an exhaustive account of the war.
An exhaustive review of the literature took six months.

definition: To make a process or action happen more quickly.
usage: Collocations: expedite the process/delivery/application/payment. It is formal and common in business and official communication: “Could you expedite this order?”
examples: Is there any way to expedite the visa application?
The new software will expedite the payment process.
We paid extra to expedite delivery.
The government promised to expedite the approval of new housing.
Providing all documents upfront will expedite your claim.

definition: To use something fully and effectively; also, to treat someone unfairly for your own advantage.
usage: Collocations: exploit resources/an opportunity/a weakness/workers. The negative sense (exploit workers/children) is very common. The noun “exploitation” is mostly negative. As a noun (/ˈeksplɔɪt/), “exploits” are brave or exciting deeds.
examples: The company was accused of exploiting cheap labour.
We should exploit renewable energy sources more effectively.
Hackers exploited a weakness in the software.
She exploited every opportunity to improve her English.
The book describes his exploits as a young sailor.

definition: Spending much more money than is necessary or reasonable; also, too extreme or elaborate.
usage: Collocations: an extravagant lifestyle/gift/wedding/claim. It is usually critical. The noun is “extravagance”.
examples: They had an extravagant wedding with 500 guests.
Buying a new car every year seems a bit extravagant.
He lived an extravagant lifestyle until the money ran out.
The advert makes extravagant claims about the product.
It was an extravagant gift for a first date.

definition: One part, side, or aspect of something complex; literally, one of the flat surfaces of a cut jewel.
usage: Collocations: every facet of life/the problem/someone's personality; many facets. The adjective “multifaceted” means having many different aspects.
examples: Technology now affects every facet of our lives.
The course covers all facets of event management.
Humour is an important facet of his personality.
The problem has many facets and no simple solution.
The diamond sparkled as light hit its facets.

definition: A false belief that many people hold; also, an error in reasoning that makes an argument invalid.
usage: Patterns: it is a fallacy that…; a common/popular fallacy; a logical fallacy. In critical thinking, named fallacies include the “straw man” and “slippery slope”. The adjective is “fallacious”.
examples: It's a fallacy that you need to be born with a talent for languages.
The argument is based on a logical fallacy.
A common fallacy is that more expensive always means better.
Students learn to identify fallacies in political speeches.
The idea that the economy will fix itself is a dangerous fallacy.

definition: Weak, especially physically; also, not good enough or not convincing.
usage: Collocations: a feeble excuse/attempt/joke/argument; feeble with age. In the second sense, it expresses scorn: “That's a feeble excuse.”
examples: That's a pretty feeble excuse for missing the meeting.
The old man's voice was feeble.
He made a feeble attempt to apologize.
The government's response to the crisis was feeble.
She laughed at my feeble joke out of politeness.

definition: Having a limit or an end; not infinite.
usage: Collocations: finite resources/time/supply/number. It is common in environmental and economic discussions. In grammar, a “finite verb” shows tense and agrees with its subject.
examples: The planet's resources are finite.
We have a finite amount of time to finish the project.
Oil is a finite resource that will eventually run out.
Hospitals must decide how to use finite budgets.
There are only a finite number of tickets available.

definition: A mistake, weakness, or fault that makes something less effective or perfect.
usage: Collocations: a fatal/fundamental/serious flaw; a flaw in the argument/design/plan; character flaws. The adjective “flawed” means having faults, and “flawless” means perfect.
examples: There's a serious flaw in your argument.
The design had a fatal flaw.
Everyone has character flaws.
The study is fundamentally flawed because the sample was too small.
Her performance was almost flawless.

definition: To grow, develop, or be successful; also, of plants, to grow healthily.
usage: Typical subjects: businesses, arts, plants, children, trade. It is very positive. As a noun, a flourish is a dramatic gesture or decorative detail: “with a flourish”.
examples: Small businesses flourish when taxes are low.
The arts flourished during this period.
These plants flourish in sunny conditions.
Children flourish in a supportive environment.
He signed the document with a flourish.

definition: To encourage the development of something, such as a feeling, skill, or relationship; also, to take care of a child who is not your own for a period of time.
usage: Collocations: foster creativity/cooperation/growth/a sense of belonging/relationships. As an adjective: foster parents/family/care.
examples: Teachers should foster creativity in the classroom.
The programme aims to foster cooperation between schools.
Team activities can foster a sense of belonging.
They have fostered over twenty children.
Open communication helps foster trust.

definition: Easily broken or damaged; also, weak and easily harmed or changed.
usage: Collocations: a fragile economy/peace/ecosystem/state of mind; fragile glass. American pronunciation: /ˈfrædʒl/. The noun is “fragility”.
examples: Be careful with that box; it's fragile.
The peace agreement is still fragile.
Coral reefs are fragile ecosystems.
The economy remains fragile after the recession.
She was in a fragile emotional state after the divorce.

definition: Done quickly and in a disorganized way because of fear, worry, or lack of time; also, extremely worried.
usage: Collocations: a frantic search/rush/pace; frantic with worry. The adverb “frantically” is common: “searching frantically for her keys”.
examples: There was a frantic rush to finish before the deadline.
After a frantic search, we found the passports in the car.
Her parents were frantic with worry when she didn't come home.
Life in the city moves at a frantic pace.
He was frantically trying to call the bank.

definition: Not serious or sensible; also, of spending or activities, unnecessary and wasteful.
usage: Collocations: frivolous spending/purchases/lawsuits/questions. A “frivolous lawsuit” has no serious legal basis. It can be mildly negative or light-hearted.
examples: We can't afford any frivolous spending this month.
The judge dismissed the case as frivolous.
She thought fashion magazines were frivolous.
Don't waste the meeting on frivolous questions.
Buying a third pair of trainers felt a bit frivolous.

definition: Careful to spend as little money as possible and avoid waste; also, of a meal, simple and cheap.
usage: Collocations: a frugal lifestyle; frugal living; a frugal meal. It is generally positive (sensible) compared with “stingy” or “mean” (unwilling to spend). Synonym: thrifty.
examples: They live a frugal lifestyle so they can retire early.
As a student, I had to be very frugal.
We ate a frugal meal of rice and vegetables.
Frugal habits like cooking at home add up over time.
He's frugal, not mean; he's very generous with his time.

definition: Having no chance of success; pointless.
usage: Collocations: a futile attempt/effort/exercise; it is futile to + verb. American pronunciation: /ˈfjuːtl/. The noun “futility” means pointlessness.
examples: It's futile to argue with him once he's made up his mind.
Rescuers made a futile attempt to save the building.
Trying to finish the whole book in one night was futile.
Resistance seemed futile against such a large army.
She felt her efforts were futile, but she kept trying.

definition: To judge, measure, or estimate something, especially people's feelings or reactions; as a noun, an instrument for measuring or a way of judging.
usage: Collocations: gauge public opinion/reaction/interest/someone's mood; a fuel/pressure gauge; a good gauge of something. Watch the spelling: g-a-u-g-e, pronounced like “gage”.
examples: It's difficult to gauge how voters will react.
The survey was designed to gauge customer satisfaction.
She glanced at his face to gauge his mood.
The fuel gauge showed the tank was nearly empty.
Sales are a good gauge of the economy's health.

definition: The main or general meaning of something, without the details.
usage: Common phrases: get the gist (of something); the gist of the argument/conversation. In language learning, “reading for gist” means reading quickly for the main idea.
examples: I didn't understand every word, but I got the gist.
Can you give me the gist of what she said?
The gist of his argument is that taxes are too high.
Read the text quickly for gist, then answer the questions.
That's the gist of it; the rest is just detail.

definition: A real or imagined reason for complaint, especially about unfair treatment; also, a formal complaint.
usage: Collocations: air/voice/address a grievance; a long-standing grievance; a grievance procedure (formal workplace complaints process). It is common in employment and political contexts.
examples: Workers aired their grievances at the meeting.
The union filed a formal grievance against the company.
Many of the protesters' grievances date back decades.
The government promised to address the community's grievances.
She still nurses a grievance about being passed over for promotion.

definition: Easily tricked or persuaded to believe something, because of being too trusting.
usage: Typically describes people (gullible consumers/tourists/investors). Scams often target gullible people. It is critical but often used humorously.
examples: Scammers often target gullible online users.
I was gullible enough to believe his story.
Don't be so gullible; not everything on the internet is true.
The advert was aimed at gullible consumers.
He's not stupid, just a bit gullible.

definition: To slow down or prevent progress or movement; to make something more difficult.
usage: Often passive: be hampered by something (bad weather/lack of funding/injury). It is similar to “hinder”. As a noun, a hamper is a large basket for food (a picnic/Christmas hamper).
examples: Rescue efforts were hampered by heavy snow.
A lack of funding has hampered research.
Injuries hampered the team throughout the season.
Poor internet access hampers students in rural areas.
We received a Christmas hamper full of chocolates.

definition: Done without any planning, order, or organization.
usage: Collocations: a haphazard approach/manner/way; haphazard development. The adverb is “haphazardly”: “books piled haphazardly”.
examples: The city grew in a haphazard way with no clear plan.
Her approach to revision is rather haphazard.
Files were stored haphazardly in boxes.
We need a systematic approach, not a haphazard one.
The furniture was arranged haphazardly around the room.

definition: To control and use something, especially a natural force or resource, for a useful purpose; as a noun, a set of straps for safety or for controlling an animal.
usage: Collocations: harness the power of/energy/technology/talent/potential. Very common in writing about renewable energy and innovation.
examples: Solar panels harness the power of the sun.
Companies are trying to harness AI to improve productivity.
Good teachers know how to harness students' curiosity.
The project harnesses the energy of the tides.
Climbers must wear a safety harness.

definition: Dangerous, especially to people's health or safety.
usage: Collocations: hazardous waste/chemicals/materials/conditions. It is more formal than “dangerous” and common in official and safety contexts. The noun “hazard” means a danger (a fire/health hazard).
examples: Hazardous waste must be disposed of safely.
Driving conditions are hazardous because of ice.
Workers handling hazardous chemicals must wear protective clothing.
Smoking is hazardous to your health.
The old factory site is still considered hazardous.

definition: To pay attention to advice or a warning and act on it.
usage: Collocations: heed advice/a warning/a call; take heed (of something); pay no heed to. It is formal or literary. The adjective “heedless” means not paying attention.
examples: If only I had heeded my parents' advice.
Hikers failed to heed warnings about the storm.
The government must heed the call for reform.
Take heed of what the doctor says.
He paid no heed to the criticism.

definition: To increase or make something stronger, especially a feeling or effect.
usage: Collocations: heighten awareness/tension/fears/anxiety/the effect. The adjective “heightened” is common: “heightened security”, “a heightened sense of”.
examples: The campaign aims to heighten awareness of mental health.
The music heightens the tension in the final scene.
Security has been heightened at airports.
Recent events have heightened fears of a recession.
Caffeine can heighten feelings of anxiety.

definition: Uncertain or slow to do or say something, usually because you are nervous or unsure.
usage: Patterns: hesitant to do something; hesitant about something. The verb is “hesitate” and the noun “hesitation” (without hesitation = immediately).
examples: Many patients are hesitant to ask doctors questions.
She gave a hesitant smile.
I was hesitant about lending him money.
Investors remain hesitant after the recent fall in prices.
His answer was slow and hesitant.

definition: A system in which people or things are arranged in levels according to their importance or power.
usage: Collocations: a strict/rigid/flat hierarchy; the company/social hierarchy; in the hierarchy. The adjective “hierarchical” describes such systems. “Maslow's hierarchy of needs” is a famous psychological model.
examples: Start-ups often have a flat hierarchy.
She quickly rose through the company hierarchy.
Traditional armies have a strict hierarchy.
Maslow's hierarchy of needs places food and safety at the base.
There's a clear hierarchy among the students in the class.

definition: Treating something as a whole system rather than focusing only on separate parts.
usage: Collocations: a holistic approach/view/assessment/education. In medicine, “holistic” care considers mind, body, and lifestyle. Popular in education and business writing.
examples: The school takes a holistic approach to education.
Universities increasingly use a holistic review of applications.
Holistic medicine treats the whole person, not just the symptoms.
We need a holistic view of the problem.
The report recommends a more holistic assessment of student progress.

definition: Unfriendly and showing opposition or aggression; also, of conditions, very difficult to live or work in.
usage: Patterns: hostile to/towards someone; a hostile environment/reception/takeover. A “hostile takeover” is when a company is bought against the wishes of its managers. The noun is “hostility”.
examples: The audience was openly hostile to the speaker.
Plants have adapted to survive in hostile environments.
Many residents are hostile towards the new development.
The company fought off a hostile takeover bid.
I didn't expect such a hostile reaction.

definition: Not proud and not believing you are more important than others; also, simple and not grand.
usage: Collocations: a humble person/attitude/beginnings/home. “Humble beginnings/origins” means a modest background. The verb “humble” means to make someone feel less proud, and the adjective “humbling” describes such an experience.
examples: Despite his success, he remained humble.
She came from humble beginnings in a small village.
In my humble opinion, the film was too long.
Losing in the first round was a humbling experience.
They lived in a humble two-room house.

definition: Behaviour in which someone claims to have moral standards or beliefs that their own actions contradict.
usage: Collocations: sheer/blatant hypocrisy; accuse someone of hypocrisy. A “hypocrite” is a person who does this; “hypocritical” is the adjective.
examples: It's hypocrisy to preach about the environment and fly private jets.
Voters are tired of politicians' hypocrisy.
She accused her critics of hypocrisy.
The film exposes the hypocrisy of the upper classes.
There's a certain hypocrisy in criticizing others for what you do yourself.

definition: Based on an imagined situation or possibility rather than on fact.
usage: Collocations: a hypothetical question/situation/scenario/example. In grammar, conditionals (“If I won the lottery…”) express hypothetical situations. Politicians often refuse to answer “hypothetical questions”.
examples: Let me ask you a hypothetical question.
The minister refused to discuss hypothetical scenarios.
This is purely hypothetical, but what would you do with a million pounds?
The textbook uses a hypothetical company to explain the concepts.
We use the second conditional for hypothetical situations.

definition: To light something up; also, to make something clearer and easier to understand.
usage: Collocations: illuminate a room/building; illuminate an issue/a problem/the past. The adjective “illuminating” means very helpful in explaining something (an illuminating discussion).
examples: The castle is illuminated at night.
The study illuminates the causes of youth unemployment.
Her lecture was genuinely illuminating.
A single lamp illuminated the room.
These letters illuminate the writer's private life.

definition: A false idea or belief; also, something that seems real but is not, such as a visual trick.
usage: Common patterns: have no illusions about something; under the illusion that…; create the illusion of space/depth; an optical illusion. Don't confuse it with “allusion” (an indirect reference).
examples: I have no illusions about how difficult the job will be.
He's under the illusion that he can pass without studying.
Mirrors create the illusion of a bigger room.
The picture is a famous optical illusion.
Social media gives the illusion of connection.

definition: About to happen very soon, especially something unpleasant.
usage: Collocations: imminent danger/threat/collapse/arrival/announcement. Don't confuse it with “eminent” (famous and respected). Often: “be in imminent danger of”.
examples: The building is in imminent danger of collapse.
An announcement is imminent.
Forecasters warned of an imminent storm.
There's no imminent threat to public safety.
Residents were evacuated as the flood seemed imminent.

definition: Not supporting any side; fair and unbiased.
usage: Collocations: impartial advice/judge/observer/inquiry. Judges, referees, and journalists are expected to be impartial. The noun is “impartiality”. Synonyms: neutral, unbiased.
examples: Judges must remain impartial.
The website offers free, impartial advice on pensions.
We need an impartial inquiry into what happened.
As a referee, you have to be completely impartial.
Public broadcasters are required to be politically impartial.

definition: To delay or block the progress or movement of something.
usage: Collocations: impede progress/growth/development/traffic/an investigation. It is formal and similar to “hinder” and “hamper”. The noun “impediment” means an obstacle (a speech impediment is a difficulty in speaking).
examples: Lack of investment has impeded economic growth.
Fallen trees impeded the rescue teams.
Bureaucracy can impede innovation.
He was charged with impeding a police investigation.
Language barriers may impede access to healthcare.

definition: Extremely important and urgent; as a noun, something that must be done.
usage: Patterns: it is imperative that someone (should) do something; it is imperative to + verb; a moral/economic imperative. In grammar, the imperative is the verb form for commands (“Sit down”).
examples: It is imperative that we act now.
It's imperative to back up your data regularly.
Reducing emissions is a moral imperative.
Speed is imperative in an emergency.
For the company, growth has become an economic imperative.

definition: Something that encourages a process or activity to happen or develop faster; a driving force.
usage: Patterns: give/provide (an) impetus to/for something; the impetus behind something; gain/lose impetus. It is formal and uncountable or singular.
examples: The new funding gave fresh impetus to the research.
The disaster provided the impetus for stricter safety laws.
The campaign has lost some of its impetus.
What was the impetus behind your decision to move?
Trade agreements can give an impetus to economic growth.

definition: Suggested or understood without being stated directly; also, complete and without doubt.
usage: Collocations: an implicit assumption/message/criticism/bias; implicit in something; implicit trust/faith (complete). The opposite is “explicit”. “Implicit bias” refers to unconscious attitudes.
examples: There was an implicit criticism in her comment.
The idea that women should care for children is implicit in the advert.
She has implicit trust in her doctor.
Many implicit assumptions underlie the model.
Training aims to reduce implicit bias in hiring.

definition: To officially introduce a rule, tax, or punishment that people must accept; also, to force your ideas or presence on others.
usage: Patterns: impose a tax/ban/fine/sanctions/restrictions on someone or something; impose on someone (cause them inconvenience). The noun is “imposition”.
examples: The government imposed a ban on smoking in public places.
New tariffs were imposed on imported steel.
Parents shouldn't impose their own dreams on their children.
I don't want to impose on you, but could I stay tonight?
Strict limits were imposed on the number of visitors.

definition: Acting suddenly without thinking carefully about the consequences.
usage: Collocations: an impulsive decision/purchase/person. It can be negative (reckless) or positive (spontaneous). An “impulse buy” is something bought without planning.
examples: Buying the car was an impulsive decision that he soon regretted.
Teenagers tend to be more impulsive than adults.
She's impulsive and fun to be around.
Supermarkets place sweets near the tills to encourage impulsive purchases.
Try not to make impulsive choices when you're angry.

definition: Without intending to; by accident.
usage: It is often used to soften responsibility: “I inadvertently deleted the file.” The adjective “inadvertent” (an inadvertent error) is less common.
examples: I inadvertently deleted the whole folder.
The policy may inadvertently harm the people it was meant to help.
He inadvertently revealed the surprise.
The email was inadvertently sent to all staff.
Researchers may inadvertently influence participants' answers.

definition: Continuing without stopping, especially in an annoying way.
usage: Collocations: incessant noise/rain/chatter/demands/complaints. It is always negative. The adverb is “incessantly”.
examples: The incessant noise from the building site kept me awake.
After days of incessant rain, the river flooded.
I'm tired of his incessant complaining.
The phone rang incessantly all morning.
Celebrities face incessant attention from the media.

definition: A feeling that makes you want to do something; a natural tendency.
usage: Patterns: an inclination to do something; have little/no inclination to…; by inclination (naturally). The adjective “inclined” is common: “I'm inclined to agree.”
examples: I have no inclination to go out tonight.
My first inclination was to say no.
She's a teacher by training but a writer by inclination.
He showed little inclination to help.
There's a natural inclination to trust people who seem similar to us.

definition: To include something as part of a larger whole.
usage: Patterns: incorporate something into something; incorporate feedback/ideas/features. In business, an “incorporated” company (Inc.) is legally registered. The noun is “incorporation”.
examples: We've incorporated your suggestions into the final report.
The new design incorporates several safety features.
Try to incorporate more vegetables into your diet.
The course incorporates both theory and practice.
The company was incorporated in 2015.

definition: To experience something unpleasant, such as a cost or penalty, as a result of your actions.
usage: Collocations: incur costs/expenses/debts/losses/a fine/a penalty/someone's anger. Past forms double the r: incurred. Common in finance and contracts.
examples: You may incur a fee if you cancel your booking late.
The company incurred heavy losses last year.
All expenses incurred during the trip will be reimbursed.
Students often incur large debts to pay for university.
He incurred the anger of his colleagues by missing the deadline.

definition: Having no interest in or sympathy for something or someone; also, not very good.
usage: Pattern: indifferent to something/someone. The second sense (mediocre) appears in “good, bad, or indifferent”. The noun is “indifference”.
examples: He seemed completely indifferent to the suffering around him.
Many young people are indifferent to politics.
The food was indifferent and overpriced.
She was indifferent about where we ate.
Don't be indifferent to climate change; it affects everyone.

definition: Naturally existing or originating in a place; especially of people, being the original inhabitants of a region.
usage: Collocations: indigenous people(s)/communities/languages/plants/species. Pattern: indigenous to a place. It is the respectful, preferred term in academic and official contexts.
examples: The rights of indigenous peoples are protected under international law.
Kangaroos are indigenous to Australia.
Many indigenous languages are in danger of disappearing.
The project works closely with indigenous communities.
Farmers are encouraged to grow indigenous crops.

definition: So important or useful that you cannot manage without it.
usage: Patterns: indispensable to/for something/someone; an indispensable tool/part/member. It is stronger than “essential”. “Nobody is indispensable” means anyone can be replaced.
examples: Smartphones have become indispensable for most people.
She quickly made herself indispensable to the team.
A good dictionary is an indispensable tool for language learners.
Volunteers are indispensable to the charity's work.
No employee is completely indispensable.

definition: To cause something to happen; also, to persuade someone to do something.
usage: Patterns: induce sleep/vomiting/labour/a state of…; induce someone to do something. Compounds with “-induced” are common: stress-induced, drug-induced.
examples: Some medicines can induce drowsiness.
Nothing would induce me to go back there.
Doctors decided to induce labour.
Stress-induced illness is increasing among office workers.
Lower prices may induce more people to buy electric cars.

definition: To allow yourself or someone else to have something enjoyable, especially more than is good; also, to let someone do what they want.
usage: Patterns: indulge in something; indulge yourself; indulge someone's wishes. The adjective “indulgent” can mean too generous; “self-indulgent” is critical. The noun is “indulgence”.
examples: I indulged in a huge slice of chocolate cake.
Go on, indulge yourself; it's your birthday.
His grandparents indulge him far too much.
On holiday, we indulged our love of seafood.
She rarely indulges in gossip.

definition: To fill something with air or gas; also, to make something seem larger, more important, or more expensive than it really is.
usage: Collocations: inflate a tyre/balloon; inflate prices/figures/someone's ego; inflated expectations. The noun “inflation” usually refers to rising prices.
examples: Make sure the tyres are properly inflated.
The company was accused of inflating its profits.
Praise from fans inflated his ego.
Hotel prices are inflated during the festival.
Social media can create inflated expectations.

definition: The arrival of a large number of people or things at the same time.
usage: Pattern: an influx of something (tourists/migrants/money/applications); a sudden/huge influx. It is common in news and economics.
examples: The town sees a huge influx of tourists every summer.
An influx of foreign investment has boosted the economy.
The hospital was overwhelmed by an influx of patients.
The university received an influx of applications this year.
The influx of new residents has pushed up rents.

definition: To break a law or rule; also, to limit or interfere with someone's rights or freedom.
usage: Patterns: infringe a law/copyright/patent; infringe on/upon someone's rights/privacy. The noun “infringement” is common in “copyright infringement”.
examples: The company was sued for infringing copyright.
Critics say the law infringes on freedom of speech.
Using the logo without permission infringes their trademark.
Cameras in the workplace may infringe on employees' privacy.
The judge ruled that no rules had been infringed.

definition: Very clever, original, and inventive.
usage: Collocations: an ingenious idea/solution/device/plan/way. Don't confuse it with “ingenuous” (innocent and trusting). The noun is “ingenuity”.
examples: That's an ingenious solution to the problem.
The device uses an ingenious system of pulleys.
She came up with an ingenious way to save money.
The plot of the film is ingenious.
Engineers showed ingenious creativity in designing the bridge.

definition: To prevent something or slow it down; also, to make someone feel too nervous or embarrassed to act naturally.
usage: Collocations: inhibit growth/development/learning. The adjective “inhibited” means shy or restrained; “uninhibited” means free and relaxed. The noun “inhibition” is common in the plural: “lose your inhibitions”.
examples: High taxes can inhibit economic growth.
Fear of making mistakes inhibits many language learners.
This drug inhibits the growth of bacteria.
She felt inhibited speaking in front of her boss.
The cold weather inhibited plant growth.

definition: To start a process or action; also, to introduce someone into a group or an area of knowledge.
usage: Collocations: initiate talks/a conversation/proceedings/change; initiate someone into something. The noun “initiative” (B2) is related; “initiation” is the act of starting or of being admitted to a group.
examples: The government has initiated talks with the unions.
She rarely initiates conversations with strangers.
Legal proceedings were initiated against the company.
Who initiated the project?
New members are initiated into the club in a special ceremony.

definition: Existing from birth; natural rather than learned.
usage: Collocations: an innate ability/talent/sense/curiosity. The “nature vs. nurture” debate asks which abilities are innate and which are learned.
examples: Children have an innate curiosity about the world.
Is language ability innate or learned?
She has an innate sense of rhythm.
Some researchers believe humans have an innate sense of fairness.
His talent for music seemed innate.

definition: Using new methods or ideas; original and creative.
usage: Collocations: an innovative approach/product/design/company/solution. The noun “innovation” and verb “innovate” are very frequent in business and academic English.
examples: The company is known for its innovative products.
We need innovative solutions to the housing crisis.
The school uses innovative teaching methods.
Her design was praised as bold and innovative.
Small start-ups are often more innovative than large firms.

definition: Necessary and important as part of a whole.
usage: Patterns: an integral part of something; integral to something. In mathematics, an integral is a concept in calculus.
examples: Music is an integral part of the school curriculum.
Customer feedback is integral to our design process.
Tourism is integral to the local economy.
She played an integral role in the project's success.
Exercise should be an integral part of daily life.

definition: To combine two or more things so that they work together effectively; also, to become, or help someone become, an accepted part of a group or society.
usage: Patterns: integrate A with/into B; integrate into society/a community. The noun is “integration”, used for social integration and for technology systems.
examples: The app integrates with your calendar.
Immigrants often take years to fully integrate into a new society.
We need to integrate theory and practice in the course.
The school works hard to integrate students with disabilities.
The two systems have been integrated into one platform.

definition: To become involved in a situation in order to change it, improve it, or stop it getting worse.
usage: Patterns: intervene in something; intervene to do something; intervene on someone's behalf. The noun “intervention” is common in politics, medicine, and education (early intervention).
examples: The teacher intervened before the argument turned into a fight.
The central bank intervened to support the currency.
Should governments intervene in the housing market?
Doctors had to intervene surgically.
She intervened on her colleague's behalf.

definition: To frighten or threaten someone, often to make them do what you want; also, to make someone feel nervous and less confident.
usage: Patterns: intimidate someone into (doing) something; feel intimidated by someone/something. The adjective “intimidating” describes something that makes you nervous (an intimidating interview panel).
examples: Witnesses were intimidated into staying silent.
Don't let his loud voice intimidate you.
I felt intimidated by how fluent everyone else was.
The interview panel looked rather intimidating.
Bullies try to intimidate others to feel powerful.

definition: Having many small parts or details arranged in a complicated way.
usage: Collocations: intricate designs/patterns/details/carvings; an intricate plot/system. It is often admiring, suggesting skill and complexity. The noun “intricacies” means complicated details.
examples: The temple walls are covered in intricate carvings.
The novel has an intricate plot with many characters.
She wore a dress with intricate embroidery.
The watch's intricate mechanism contains over 200 parts.
Negotiating the intricate rules of the tax system takes patience.

definition: Belonging naturally to something as a basic part of its nature.
usage: Collocations: intrinsic value/motivation/quality/part. “Intrinsic motivation” (doing something because you enjoy it) contrasts with “extrinsic motivation” (doing it for rewards). The adverb is “intrinsically”.
examples: Learners with intrinsic motivation tend to persist longer.
Gold has little intrinsic value; its price depends on demand.
Risk is intrinsic to any new business.
Music is an intrinsic part of their culture.
There's nothing intrinsically wrong with the idea.

definition: Based on feelings rather than conscious reasoning; also, of a design or system, easy to use without instructions.
usage: Collocations: an intuitive interface/design; an intuitive understanding/sense; intuitive decisions. The noun “intuition” means the ability to know something instinctively.
examples: The app has an intuitive interface.
She has an intuitive understanding of what customers want.
Experienced doctors often make intuitive judgements.
The software is so intuitive that you don't need a manual.
My intuitive reaction was to say no.

definition: Extremely useful; so valuable that its worth cannot be measured.
usage: Patterns: invaluable to/for someone; invaluable help/advice/experience. Despite the prefix “in-”, it does not mean “not valuable”; the opposite of “valuable” is “worthless” or “valueless”.
examples: Your advice has been invaluable.
The internship gave me invaluable experience.
Volunteers provide invaluable support to the hospital.
This dictionary is invaluable for translators.
Her knowledge of the local area proved invaluable.

definition: To mention or use a law, principle, or idea to support an argument or action; also, to call up a feeling or image.
usage: Collocations: invoke a law/rule/right/clause/principle; invoke someone's name/memory. In formal writing, “invoke” suggests appealing to authority.
examples: The company invoked a clause in the contract to cancel the deal.
He invoked his right to remain silent.
Politicians often invoke national pride in their speeches.
She invoked the memory of her grandmother in her speech.
The government invoked emergency powers.

definition: A situation in which the result is the opposite of what was expected; also, the use of words that say the opposite of what you really mean, often for humour.
usage: Patterns: the irony is that…; with/without irony; a touch of irony. The adjective is “ironic” and the adverb “ironically”. Many people use “ironic” loosely to mean “unlucky”, which some careful writers avoid.
examples: The irony is that the fire station burned down.
She said “great weather” with heavy irony as the rain poured.
Ironically, the healthiest person in the office was the first to get ill.
The film is full of dark irony.
There's a certain irony in a dentist with bad teeth.

definition: Not based on reason or logic.
usage: Collocations: an irrational fear/belief/behaviour/decision. Psychology and economics often discuss “irrational” human behaviour. The opposite is “rational”.
examples: I have an irrational fear of spiders.
Panic buying is irrational but understandable.
Investors sometimes make irrational decisions.
It's irrational to expect perfection from yourself.
His anger seemed completely irrational.

definition: Impossible to change back to a previous condition.
usage: Collocations: irreversible damage/change/decline/decision. It is common in medical and environmental contexts. The opposite is “reversible”.
examples: Climate change could cause irreversible damage to ecosystems.
The disease causes irreversible damage to the nerves.
Think carefully; this decision is irreversible.
Some species face irreversible decline.
Deleting the account is irreversible.

definition: Special words and expressions used by a particular profession or group, which are difficult for others to understand.
usage: Collocations: technical/legal/medical/business jargon; full of jargon; avoid jargon. It is usually negative when used to criticize unclear communication.
examples: The report was full of technical jargon.
Try to avoid jargon when you write for a general audience.
Doctors should explain things without using medical jargon.
“Synergy” is a classic piece of business jargon.
I couldn't follow the lawyer's legal jargon.

definition: To put something at risk of being harmed, lost, or destroyed.
usage: Collocations: jeopardize your chances/career/health/safety/a relationship. British spelling also “jeopardise”. The noun phrase “in jeopardy” means at risk.
examples: One mistake could jeopardize your whole career.
Don't jeopardize your health by skipping meals.
The scandal jeopardized the company's reputation.
Missing the deadline could jeopardize our chances of getting the contract.
Cutting the research budget would jeopardize future growth.

definition: To express sadness, regret, or disappointment about something.
usage: Patterns: lament something; lament that…; lament the loss/decline of something. As a noun, a lament is a song or poem expressing grief. The adjective “lamentable” means very bad or regrettable.
examples: Older residents lament the loss of local shops.
Many teachers lament the decline in reading for pleasure.
He lamented that he had never learned to play an instrument.
Critics lamented the lack of originality in the film.
The song is a lament for a lost love.

definition: Present or existing but not yet active, visible, or developed.
usage: Collocations: latent talent/potential/infection/demand/hostility. In medicine, a “latent” infection shows no symptoms yet.
examples: The course helped her discover a latent talent for drawing.
The virus can remain latent for years.
There is latent demand for affordable housing in the city.
The crisis revealed latent tensions within the team.
Good teachers bring out students' latent potential.

definition: Something that is left behind by a person, event, or period and continues to affect the future; also, money or property left to someone in a will.
usage: Collocations: leave a legacy; a lasting/enduring legacy; the legacy of colonialism/the war. In technology, “legacy systems” are old systems still in use.
examples: The Olympics left a lasting legacy of new sports facilities.
Poverty is part of the legacy of colonialism.
Her greatest legacy is the school she founded.
Many banks still rely on legacy computer systems.
He received a small legacy from his aunt.

definition: A law or a set of laws made by a parliament or government.
usage: Uncountable: a piece of legislation (not “a legislation”). Collocations: introduce/pass/propose legislation; new/environmental/anti-discrimination legislation. The verb is “legislate”.
examples: The government plans to introduce new legislation on data privacy.
Parliament passed the legislation by a narrow majority.
Environmental legislation has become much stricter.
This is an important piece of legislation.
Campaigners are calling for legislation to protect gig workers.

definition: The power to influence people or situations to get what you want; as a verb, to use something you have to gain an advantage.
usage: Noun: have/gain/use leverage (over someone). Verb (business): leverage your skills/network/data/technology. The verb is popular in business jargon; in plain English, “use” often works. In finance, leverage means borrowing to invest.
examples: Having another job offer gives you leverage in salary negotiations.
The company aims to leverage its strong brand to enter new markets.
Small countries have little leverage over global trade rules.
She leveraged her language skills to get a job abroad.
We can leverage data to understand customers better.

definition: Legal responsibility for something, especially for paying for damage or loss; also, a person or thing that causes problems.
usage: Collocations: accept/deny liability; legal/financial liability; limited liability company. In accounting, liabilities are debts (opposite: assets). Informally: “He's become a liability to the team.”
examples: The company denied liability for the accident.
Under the new rules, landlords have liability for major repairs.
Our assets are greater than our liabilities.
His temper has made him a liability to the team.
Most small businesses are set up as limited liability companies.

definition: To stay somewhere or continue to exist for longer than usual or expected.
usage: Patterns: linger over coffee/a meal; doubts/smells/memories linger. The adjective “lingering” is common: lingering doubts/effects/smell.
examples: We lingered over coffee after dinner.
The smell of smoke lingered in the house for days.
Some doubts still linger about his story.
She lingered at the door, not wanting to leave.
The lingering effects of the illness lasted months.

definition: The way a person earns the money they need to live.
usage: Collocations: earn/make a livelihood; lose your livelihood; threaten/protect livelihoods. It is common in discussions of economics, development, and disasters.
examples: Fishing is the main livelihood in the village.
Thousands lost their livelihoods when the factory closed.
The drought threatens the livelihoods of farmers.
Tourism provides a livelihood for many local families.
The scheme helps women build sustainable livelihoods.

definition: Producing a lot of money; profitable.
usage: Collocations: a lucrative business/market/contract/career/deal. It is common in business contexts and sometimes suggests easy profits.
examples: She left a lucrative job in finance to become a teacher.
The company won a lucrative government contract.
Online tutoring can be surprisingly lucrative.
The Chinese market is highly lucrative for luxury brands.
Drug trafficking is a lucrative but dangerous trade.

definition: The great size or importance of something; in science, the size of a quantity, such as the strength of an earthquake.
usage: Patterns: the magnitude of the problem/task/crisis; of this magnitude; a magnitude 7 earthquake. “Order of magnitude” means a factor of ten in scale.
examples: Nobody realized the magnitude of the problem at first.
A disaster of this magnitude requires international help.
A magnitude 6.5 earthquake struck the region.
The magnitude of the task was overwhelming.
The new chip is an order of magnitude faster.

definition: Intending to harm or upset other people.
usage: Collocations: malicious gossip/rumours/intent/software (malware)/damage. In law, “malicious intent” is an important concept. The noun is “malice”.
examples: She was upset by malicious rumours about her private life.
The email contained a malicious link.
There was no malicious intent; it was a genuine mistake.
He was charged with causing malicious damage to property.
Malicious software can steal your passwords.

definition: The authority given to a government or organization to act, especially after winning an election; also, an official order. As a verb, to require something officially.
usage: Noun: a clear/strong mandate; a mandate to do something. Verb: mandate something (mask-wearing/testing). The adjective “mandatory” means compulsory.
examples: The new government has a clear mandate for reform.
The law mandates regular safety inspections.
The UN mission's mandate was extended for another year.
Some companies have mandated a return to the office.
Voters gave the party a strong mandate to cut taxes.

definition: Required by law or rules; compulsory.
usage: Collocations: mandatory training/testing/retirement/sentence; it is mandatory for someone to do something. Synonyms: compulsory, obligatory. Opposite: optional, voluntary.
examples: Wearing a helmet is mandatory on construction sites.
All new staff must complete mandatory safety training.
Attendance at the first lecture is mandatory.
Some countries have mandatory voting.
The crime carries a mandatory prison sentence.

definition: As a verb, to show something clearly, or to appear; as an adjective, easy to see or understand.
usage: Patterns: manifest itself in/as something (a problem manifests itself as…); a manifest failure/lack. The noun “manifestation” means a sign or form of something. In casual modern use, “manifest” can mean to make something happen by believing in it.
examples: Stress can manifest itself in physical symptoms such as headaches.
Her talent for languages manifested early.
The policy was a manifest failure.
Anxiety often manifests as difficulty sleeping.
His frustration was manifest in his tone of voice.

definition: To control or influence someone or something cleverly and unfairly for your own advantage; also, to handle or move something skilfully.
usage: Collocations: manipulate people/data/figures/public opinion/the market. The negative sense is the most common. The adjective “manipulative” describes a person who manipulates others.
examples: He manipulated his friends into lending him money.
The company was accused of manipulating its sales figures.
Social media can be used to manipulate public opinion.
Surgeons use robotic arms to manipulate tiny instruments.
She's very manipulative; be careful what you tell her.

definition: Very small and not important; also, at the edge of a group or society.
usage: Collocations: a marginal increase/difference/improvement/role; marginal groups. The adverb “marginally” (marginally better) is common. To “marginalize” means to push people to the edge of society.
examples: There was only a marginal improvement in sales.
The new version is marginally faster than the old one.
He played a marginal role in the project.
The policy affects marginal communities the most.
The difference in price is marginal.

definition: To try to help two people or groups who disagree reach an agreement.
usage: Patterns: mediate between A and B; mediate a dispute/conflict/agreement. A “mediator” is a neutral third party; “mediation” is the process.
examples: The UN was asked to mediate between the two countries.
A teacher mediated the dispute between the students.
An independent expert will mediate the negotiations.
She often has to mediate between her parents.
The agreement was mediated by Norway.

definition: Of only average or below-average quality; not very good.
usage: Collocations: a mediocre performance/film/meal/student. It is clearly negative, more critical than “average”. The noun is “mediocrity”.
examples: The food was mediocre and overpriced.
After a mediocre first half, the team improved after the break.
He was a mediocre student but a brilliant businessman.
Critics described the sequel as mediocre.
Don't settle for mediocre work.

definition: An experienced person who advises and helps someone less experienced over a period of time; as a verb, to act as a mentor.
usage: Collocations: act as a mentor; a mentoring programme/scheme. The person being mentored is a “mentee”. It is common in workplaces and universities.
examples: My first manager was a great mentor to me.
The company runs a mentoring programme for new graduates.
She mentors young women in the tech industry.
Having a mentor can speed up your career development.
Each new teacher is assigned a mentor for the first year.

definition: The quality of being good and deserving praise or reward; also, an advantage or good feature. As a verb, to deserve something.
usage: Patterns: the merits of something; on merit (based on ability); judge something on its merits; merit attention/consideration/discussion. The adjective “meritocratic” describes systems rewarding ability.
examples: We discussed the merits of each proposal.
Promotion should be based on merit, not connections.
The idea has some merit, but it's too expensive.
The case merits further investigation.
Each application will be judged on its merits.

definition: A very important event or stage in the development or progress of something.
usage: Collocations: reach/hit/mark/celebrate a milestone; a major/significant milestone. Common in project management and in describing personal life events.
examples: Graduating from university is a major milestone.
The company reached the milestone of one million users.
The treaty marked an important milestone in the peace process.
Babies reach developmental milestones at different ages.
We celebrated the milestone with a team dinner.

definition: To copy the way someone speaks, moves, or behaves, often to make people laugh; also, to look or behave like something else.
usage: Past forms add “k”: mimicked, mimicking. Collocations: mimic someone's accent/voice; mimic the effects of something. As a noun, a mimic is someone good at copying others.
examples: He can mimic our teacher's voice perfectly.
Children learn language by mimicking adults.
The drug mimics the effects of a natural hormone.
Some insects mimic the appearance of leaves.
The software mimics human conversation.

definition: A wrong idea or belief, often based on faulty thinking or understanding.
usage: Collocations: a common/popular/widespread misconception; the misconception that…; correct/dispel a misconception.
examples: It's a common misconception that we only use 10 per cent of our brains.
The campaign aims to correct misconceptions about mental illness.
There's a widespread misconception that learning a language is only for the young.
Many misconceptions about the disease still exist.
The teacher addressed students' misconceptions before the exam.

definition: Not very large, expensive, or important; also, not talking much about your own achievements or abilities.
usage: Collocations: a modest increase/income/house/amount; a modest person. Applied to people, it is a compliment. The noun is “modesty”.
examples: There was a modest increase in sales this year.
They live in a modest flat on the outskirts of town.
She's very modest about her achievements.
The project was completed on a modest budget.
Don't be so modest; you did a great job.

definition: The force or speed that keeps an activity or process developing; in physics, the quantity of motion of a moving object.
usage: Collocations: gain/gather/build/lose/maintain momentum. It is common in politics, business, sport, and personal motivation.
examples: The campaign is gaining momentum.
We need to keep up the momentum after a good start.
The team lost momentum after their captain was injured.
Small daily wins help you build momentum.
The ball's momentum carried it into the net.

definition: Boring because it never changes and is always the same.
usage: Collocations: monotonous work/task/voice/routine/diet. The noun “monotony” means boring sameness. A “monotone” voice stays on one pitch.
examples: Factory work can be extremely monotonous.
The lecturer spoke in a monotonous voice.
Eating the same thing every day becomes monotonous.
The landscape was flat and monotonous.
She wanted to escape her monotonous routine.

definition: The level of confidence, enthusiasm, and motivation in a person or group, especially at a particular time.
usage: Collocations: boost/raise/lower/damage morale; low/high morale; staff/team morale. Don't confuse it with “moral” (relating to right and wrong).
examples: Staff morale is low after the redundancies.
The win boosted the team's morale.
Long hours and low pay damage morale.
The manager organized events to raise morale.
Morale among the troops remained high.

definition: Very ordinary and therefore not interesting.
usage: Collocations: mundane tasks/details/chores/life. It often contrasts everyday routine with something exciting.
examples: Most of my job involves mundane tasks like answering emails.
The film turns a mundane situation into something magical.
Even the most mundane details were recorded.
Automation can free workers from mundane chores.
She found joy in the mundane parts of life.

definition: Felt or done equally by two or more people towards each other; also, shared by two or more people.
usage: Collocations: mutual respect/trust/understanding/benefit/agreement; a mutual friend. “The feeling is mutual” means I feel the same about you. The adverb is “mutually” (mutually beneficial).
examples: Good relationships are based on mutual respect.
We met through a mutual friend.
The partnership is mutually beneficial.
They separated by mutual agreement.
“I don't like him.” “Don't worry, the feeling is mutual.”

definition: A very large number of things; countless.
usage: Used as an adjective (myriad options) or noun (a myriad of options). Both are accepted, though some traditional writers prefer the adjective. It is somewhat literary.
examples: The city offers myriad opportunities for young professionals.
There are a myriad of ways to learn a language.
The festival features myriad colours and sounds.
She juggled myriad responsibilities at work and home.
The internet gives access to a myriad of sources.

definition: Lacking experience or judgement, and therefore too willing to believe or trust others.
usage: Collocations: a naive question/assumption/belief/view; politically naive. Also spelled “naïve”. The noun is “naivety” or “naïveté”.
examples: It was naive of me to think the work would be easy.
He's naive about how business really works.
This may sound like a naive question, but how does it work?
Her naive trust in strangers worried her parents.
The plan was criticized as politically naive.

definition: A story or description of events; also, a particular way of explaining or presenting events that reflects a point of view.
usage: Collocations: a personal/historical/dominant narrative; challenge/shape/control the narrative. In politics and media, “the narrative” means the version of events people accept.
examples: The novel has a complex narrative structure.
The government is trying to control the narrative.
Her essay is a personal narrative about migration.
The documentary challenges the dominant narrative about the war.
Children practise writing short narratives.

definition: So small or unimportant that it is not worth considering.
usage: Collocations: a negligible effect/impact/amount/risk/difference. It is common in scientific and financial writing. Don't confuse it with “negligent” (careless).
examples: The risk of side effects is negligible.
The new tax will have a negligible impact on most families.
The difference between the two results was negligible.
Costs are negligible compared with the benefits.
The damage to the car was negligible.

definition: To discuss something formally in order to reach an agreement; also, to successfully get past an obstacle or deal with a difficult situation.
usage: Patterns: negotiate with someone; negotiate a deal/contract/salary/settlement. The second sense: negotiate a bend/obstacles/the system. The noun is “negotiation”.
examples: The union is negotiating with management over pay.
She negotiated a higher starting salary.
The two countries negotiated a ceasefire.
It took us an hour to negotiate the narrow mountain roads.
International students often have to negotiate complex visa rules.

definition: A feeling of sadness mixed with pleasure when you think about happy times in the past.
usage: Collocations: a wave/sense/feeling of nostalgia; nostalgia for something. The adjective “nostalgic” is common: “feel nostalgic about/for”. Advertisers often use nostalgia to sell products.
examples: Old photos filled her with nostalgia.
There's a lot of nostalgia for the music of the 1990s.
That song always brings a rush of nostalgia.
The film plays on our nostalgia for childhood.
He spoke with nostalgia about his student days.

definition: Important, interesting, or unusual enough to be noticed or mentioned.
usage: Collocations: a notable exception/example/achievement/feature; notable for something. The adverb “notably” introduces an important example: “several countries, notably Japan”.
examples: The report is notable for its honesty.
With a few notable exceptions, the reviews were positive.
It was a notable achievement for such a small company.
Several countries, notably Germany and Japan, have ageing populations.
The town is notable for its medieval architecture.

definition: Famous for something bad.
usage: Patterns: notorious for something; notorious criminal/case/area. Compare “famous” (neutral or positive) and “infamous” (similar to notorious). The adverb “notoriously” is common: “notoriously difficult”.
examples: The road is notorious for accidents.
He was one of the most notorious criminals of the century.
English spelling is notoriously difficult.
The city is notorious for its traffic jams.
The landlord was notorious for ignoring repairs.

definition: As an adjective, new, original, and different from anything known before.
usage: Collocations: a novel idea/approach/solution/method/virus. In academic writing, it highlights originality: “a novel approach to the problem”. As a noun, a novel is a long fictional book; “novelty” means newness or a cheap amusing object.
examples: The researchers have developed a novel method for detecting cancer.
Paying staff to exercise is a novel idea.
The study takes a novel approach to an old question.
A novel virus is one that has not been identified before.
Working from home was a novel experience for many people in 2020.

definition: A person who is new to an activity and has little experience.
usage: Used as a noun (a complete novice) or before another noun (a novice driver/user/cook). Synonyms: beginner, newcomer. Opposite: expert, veteran.
examples: I'm a complete novice when it comes to cooking.
The course is suitable for novices and experienced users alike.
Novice drivers are more likely to have accidents.
The app is designed with novice users in mind.
Even as a novice, she showed great talent.

definition: To care for and help someone or something grow and develop; as a noun, the care and upbringing a child receives.
usage: Collocations: nurture talent/creativity/a relationship/young people. “Nature versus nurture” is the debate about whether genes or environment shape us.
examples: Good schools nurture students' creativity.
The company nurtures young talent through its graduate programme.
Friendships need to be nurtured.
She nurtured the plants carefully through the winter.
Is intelligence a matter of nature or nurture?

definition: Not aware of something that is happening around you.
usage: Pattern: oblivious to/of something. It often describes someone absorbed in something else: “oblivious to the noise”.
examples: He was completely oblivious to the danger.
She sat reading, oblivious to the noise around her.
Many shoppers are oblivious of the real cost of fast fashion.
The driver seemed oblivious to the cyclists.
They were happily oblivious to the drama in the office.

definition: Not well known; also, difficult to understand. As a verb, to hide something or make it difficult to see or understand.
usage: Collocations: an obscure writer/reference/village; obscure the view/the truth/the issue. The noun “obscurity” appears in “fade into obscurity”.
examples: The film was based on an obscure novel from the 1950s.
The legal language is deliberately obscure.
Clouds obscured the view of the mountains.
Technical jargon can obscure the main point.
After one hit song, the band faded into obscurity.

definition: An idea, interest, or person that you think about constantly, often in an unhealthy way.
usage: Pattern: an obsession with something/someone. The verb “obsess (about/over)” and adjective “obsessed (with)” and “obsessive” are common.
examples: His obsession with football worries his wife.
Society's obsession with appearance can damage self-esteem.
Cleaning has become an obsession for her.
The company's obsession with growth led to poor decisions.
What started as a hobby turned into an obsession.

definition: Something that blocks your way or makes it difficult to make progress.
usage: Collocations: overcome/face/remove an obstacle; a major/main obstacle; an obstacle to success/progress/peace. An “obstacle course” is a series of physical challenges.
examples: Cost is the main obstacle to wider use of solar power.
She overcame many obstacles to become a doctor.
Language can be a major obstacle for new immigrants.
The biggest obstacle was finding enough funding.
Fear of failure is often the greatest obstacle to success.

definition: Suggesting that something bad is going to happen.
usage: Collocations: ominous signs/clouds/silence/warning. The adverb “ominously” is common: “The phone was ominously silent.”
examples: Dark, ominous clouds gathered over the hills.
There was an ominous silence after he spoke.
Economists see ominous signs of a recession.
The engine made an ominous noise.
The email from HR had an ominous subject line.

definition: The beginning of something, especially something unpleasant.
usage: Pattern: the onset of something (winter/a disease/symptoms/puberty/the crisis). It is common in medical and academic writing.
examples: The onset of the disease is usually gradual.
With the onset of winter, energy bills rise.
Early treatment can delay the onset of symptoms.
The onset of the pandemic changed everything.
Many people experience the onset of allergies in adulthood.

definition: Best or most effective in a particular situation.
usage: Collocations: optimal conditions/performance/level/solution/temperature. It is formal and technical; also “optimum”. The verb “optimize” means to make something as effective as possible.
examples: Plants need optimal conditions to grow well.
Seven to nine hours of sleep is optimal for most adults.
We're looking for the optimal solution, not just a quick fix.
The battery performs at an optimal temperature of 20 degrees.
Is working from home optimal for productivity?

definition: Shocking and morally unacceptable; also, very unusual and surprising, sometimes in an amusing way.
usage: Collocations: outrageous behaviour/prices/claims/costumes. The noun “outrage” means strong anger. Informally, “outrageous” can be playful: “an outrageous outfit”.
examples: The prices at the airport were outrageous.
His behaviour at the meeting was outrageous.
She made some outrageous claims about her rivals.
The comedian is known for his outrageous costumes.
It's outrageous that people are paid so little for such hard work.

definition: To examine and repair or improve a system or machine thoroughly; as a noun (/ˈəʊvəhɔːl/), a complete review and change.
usage: Collocations: overhaul the system/tax code/curriculum/an engine; a complete/major overhaul. Common in politics and business news.
examples: The government plans to overhaul the tax system.
The engine was completely overhauled.
The website needs a major overhaul.
Schools are overhauling the curriculum to include coding.
The new CEO overhauled the company's management structure.

definition: To watch and control a piece of work or an activity to make sure it is done correctly.
usage: Irregular: oversaw, overseen. Collocations: oversee a project/operations/construction/the process. The noun “oversight” means supervision, but also a mistake caused by not noticing something. Don't confuse it with “overlook”.
examples: She oversees a team of twenty engineers.
An independent body will oversee the election.
He was hired to oversee the construction of the new hospital.
Who oversees quality control in the factory?
The project was overseen by a senior manager.

definition: A typical model or pattern of something; also, a set of ideas and assumptions that form the basis of a theory or way of thinking.
usage: Collocations: a new paradigm; a paradigm shift (a fundamental change in approach); the dominant paradigm. It is common in academic and business writing. The “g” is silent.
examples: The internet caused a paradigm shift in how we communicate.
The study challenges the dominant paradigm in economics.
Remote work represents a new paradigm for many companies.
Her research offers a new paradigm for understanding memory.
Renewable energy requires a paradigm shift in policy.

definition: A situation or statement that seems impossible or contradictory but may be true.
usage: Patterns: the paradox is that…; a paradox of something. The adjective “paradoxical” and the adverb “paradoxically” are common: “Paradoxically, more choice can make people less happy.”
examples: It's a paradox that we have more ways to communicate but feel lonelier.
The paradox is that the harder you try to sleep, the harder it becomes.
Paradoxically, having too many options can make decisions harder.
The novel explores the paradox of wealth and unhappiness.
Economists call this the paradox of thrift.

definition: More important than anything else.
usage: Patterns: be paramount; of paramount importance; safety/security is paramount. It usually comes after the verb “be”.
examples: Patient safety is paramount.
Trust is of paramount importance in any relationship.
In this job, accuracy is paramount.
Protecting children's privacy must be paramount.
Customer satisfaction is paramount to our business.

definition: Not as important as the main part; also, at the edge of an area. In computing, a device connected to a computer.
usage: Collocations: a peripheral issue/role/concern; peripheral vision (what you see at the edges). As a noun: computer peripherals (keyboards, printers).
examples: Cost is a peripheral issue; the main problem is quality.
He played only a peripheral role in the scandal.
I saw something move in my peripheral vision.
The factory is located in a peripheral area of the city.
The shop sells laptops and peripherals.

definition: To make something, especially something bad, continue to exist.
