usage: Collocations: perpetuate stereotypes/myths/inequality/a cycle/violence. It is common in social science writing.
examples: Films that perpetuate stereotypes can be harmful.
Poverty tends to perpetuate itself across generations.
The myth has been perpetuated by the media.
The system perpetuates inequality.
We must break the cycle rather than perpetuate it.

definition: To continue trying to do something despite difficulties.
usage: Patterns: persevere with/in something; persevere despite difficulties. The noun “perseverance” is a common virtue word. Stress is on the last syllable: per-se-VERE.
examples: If you persevere with your studies, you'll see results.
She persevered despite many rejections.
Learning to play the piano requires you to persevere.
He persevered in his efforts to find a job.
Success comes to those who persevere.

definition: Directly relevant to the subject being considered.
usage: Collocations: a pertinent question/point/fact/information; pertinent to something. It is formal; “relevant” is the everyday equivalent.
examples: She asked several pertinent questions.
Please include only information pertinent to the case.
That's a very pertinent point.
The report omits some pertinent facts.
The issue is particularly pertinent to young people.

definition: Existing everywhere or spreading through every part of something, often in an unwanted way.
usage: Collocations: a pervasive influence/problem/sense/smell; pervasive corruption. It is common in social criticism. The verb “pervade” means to spread through.
examples: Smartphones have a pervasive influence on daily life.
Corruption is pervasive in the industry.
There was a pervasive sense of fear in the city.
Advertising has become pervasive online.
Gender bias remains pervasive in many workplaces.

definition: Expecting bad things to happen or believing that something will not succeed.
usage: Pattern: pessimistic about something. The opposite is “optimistic”. A “pessimist” always expects the worst; “pessimism” is the attitude.
examples: Economists are pessimistic about growth next year.
Don't be so pessimistic; you might get the job.
The doctor was pessimistic about his chances of recovery.
Young people are increasingly pessimistic about home ownership.
The report paints a pessimistic picture of the future.

definition: Extremely good, successful, or impressive; unusually great in size or degree.
usage: Collocations: phenomenal success/growth/performance/memory. It is strongly positive and common in speech. The adverb “phenomenally” intensifies: “phenomenally successful”.
examples: The book has been a phenomenal success.
She has a phenomenal memory for names.
The company has seen phenomenal growth in Asia.
The food at that restaurant is phenomenal.
His performance in the final was phenomenal.

definition: A likely mistake, problem, or danger that is not obvious at first.
usage: Usually plural: common/potential pitfalls; avoid the pitfalls of something. Common in advice and guides.
examples: This guide explains how to avoid common pitfalls when buying a house.
One pitfall of working from home is isolation.
Be aware of the potential pitfalls of borrowing money.
The article highlights the pitfalls of relying on a single source.
Learners often fall into the pitfall of translating word for word.

definition: A difficult, sad, or dangerous situation that someone is in.
usage: Collocations: the plight of refugees/the homeless/farmers; highlight/draw attention to someone's plight. It is common in news and charity contexts.
examples: The documentary highlights the plight of refugees.
Few people are aware of the plight of farmers in the region.
The charity draws attention to the plight of homeless young people.
Their plight worsened as the winter arrived.
The minister promised to address the plight of low-paid workers.

definition: Causing a strong feeling of sadness or emotion.
usage: Collocations: a poignant moment/reminder/story/scene/memory. Note the silent “g”. The noun is “poignancy”.
examples: The film ends with a poignant scene between father and son.
The memorial is a poignant reminder of the war.
Her speech was short but poignant.
It was a poignant moment when the old friends met again.
The letters tell a poignant story of separation.

definition: To divide people into two groups with completely opposite opinions.
usage: Collocations: polarize opinion/society/the debate; a polarizing figure/issue. British spelling also “polarise”. The noun is “polarization”.
examples: The referendum polarized the country.
Social media algorithms may polarize public opinion.
He's a polarizing figure: people either love him or hate him.
The debate has become increasingly polarized.
Issues like immigration tend to polarize voters.

definition: Dealing with problems in a sensible, practical way based on real conditions rather than theories or ideals.
usage: Collocations: a pragmatic approach/solution/decision/leader. It is usually positive. The noun “pragmatism” describes the attitude. In linguistics, “pragmatics” studies meaning in context.
examples: We need a pragmatic approach to the problem.
She's a pragmatic leader who focuses on results.
It was a pragmatic decision rather than an ideal one.
Being pragmatic, we chose the cheaper option.
The government took a pragmatic view of the situation.

definition: Not safe or secure; likely to fall, fail, or get worse.
usage: Collocations: a precarious position/situation/balance/existence; precarious employment/finances. “Precarious work” refers to insecure jobs like zero-hours contracts.
examples: Many gig workers are in precarious employment.
The vase was in a precarious position on the edge of the shelf.
The company's finances are precarious.
Climbers made their way along a precarious ledge.
Refugees often live a precarious existence.

definition: An earlier action, decision, or event that is used as an example or rule for later situations.
usage: Collocations: set/create/establish a precedent; without precedent; a dangerous precedent. In law, previous court decisions are precedents. The adjective “unprecedented” means never having happened before.
examples: The court's decision set an important precedent.
Giving in to their demands would set a dangerous precedent.
There is no precedent for a crisis of this size.
The judge relied on precedent in reaching her verdict.
Is there any historical precedent for this policy?

definition: Exact and accurate in every detail.
usage: Collocations: precise details/measurements/instructions/location; to be precise (used to give exact information). The noun is “precision” and the adverb “precisely” (also used to mean “exactly, you're right”).
examples: Please give precise instructions.
The meeting lasted two hours, or to be precise, two hours and ten minutes.
Scientists need precise measurements.
Nobody knows the precise number of victims.
“So you mean we should wait?” “Precisely.”

definition: To prevent something from happening, or to make it impossible.
usage: Patterns: preclude something; preclude someone from doing something. It is formal and common in legal and academic writing.
examples: His injury precludes him from playing this season.
Lack of time precluded any further discussion.
Being a student doesn't preclude you from working part-time.
The contract precludes us from working with competitors.
Financial constraints may preclude expansion.

definition: Most common, noticeable, or powerful.
usage: Collocations: the predominant view/language/colour/religion/factor. The adverb “predominantly” (mainly) is very common in academic writing.
examples: Spanish is the predominant language in the area.
The predominant view among experts is that prices will fall.
Blue is the predominant colour in the painting.
The town's population is predominantly elderly.
Cost was the predominant factor in our decision.

definition: Coming before a more important action or event, as a preparation.
usage: Collocations: preliminary results/findings/report/talks/round. In academic writing, it signals that results are early and may change.
examples: Preliminary results suggest the drug is effective.
Preliminary talks between the two companies have begun.
This is only a preliminary report.
The team was knocked out in the preliminary round.
After some preliminary remarks, the speaker got to the point.

definition: An idea or statement that is accepted as true and on which an argument or theory is based.
usage: Patterns: the premise that…; based on the premise; a false premise. The plural “premises” also means a building and its land (“on the premises”).
examples: The argument rests on the premise that people act rationally.
The film's basic premise is a man who never ages.
Your conclusion is based on a false premise.
We start from the premise that every child can learn.
Smoking is not allowed on the premises.

definition: Something that must exist or happen before something else is possible.
usage: Patterns: a prerequisite for/of something; a necessary prerequisite. Universities often list prerequisite courses that students must complete first.
examples: A degree is a prerequisite for this job.
Trust is a prerequisite for any successful partnership.
Basic algebra is a prerequisite for the course.
Peace is a prerequisite for economic development.
Fluency in English is no longer a prerequisite for the role.

definition: Respected and admired because of high quality, success, or importance.
usage: Collocations: a prestigious university/award/job/company/event. The noun “prestige” means respect and admiration.
examples: She studied at one of the most prestigious universities in the world.
He won a prestigious literary award.
Many graduates want to work for prestigious law firms.
The hotel is in a prestigious area of the city.
Being selected for the programme is very prestigious.

definition: Used to say that you think something is probably true, based on what you know.
usage: It can go at the start, middle, or end of a sentence. It is common in speech and writing for reasonable guesses. The verb “presume” means to suppose.
examples: Presumably, the meeting has been cancelled.
You'll presumably want to see the contract first.
He's not here, so presumably he's still at work.
The decision was presumably made to save money.
The new rules will, presumably, apply from next month.

definition: To be common or widespread at a particular time or place; also, to win or be successful after a struggle.
usage: Patterns: conditions/attitudes prevail; prevail over/against an opponent; common sense prevailed. The adjective “prevailing” means most common at present (prevailing winds/conditions/view).
examples: A sense of optimism prevailed at the conference.
In the end, common sense prevailed.
Justice will prevail.
The prevailing winds here come from the west.
They prevailed over a much stronger opponent.

definition: Skilled and experienced at doing something.
usage: Patterns: proficient in/at something; proficient in English/Excel/coding. The noun “proficiency” appears in language testing: “English proficiency”.
examples: Applicants must be proficient in English and French.
She became proficient at coding within a year.
You need to be proficient in Excel for this job.
It takes years to become truly proficient in a language.
The test measures how proficient students are in reading.

definition: Producing a large number or amount of something, such as works of art, goals, or offspring.
usage: Collocations: a prolific writer/author/composer/scorer/inventor. It is usually admiring.
examples: Agatha Christie was a prolific writer of detective novels.
He's the most prolific goalscorer in the club's history.
Mozart was remarkably prolific for such a short life.
Rabbits are prolific breeders.
She's a prolific poster on social media.

definition: To make something last longer.
usage: Collocations: prolong life/the agony/a conflict/a stay. The adjective “prolonged” means lasting a long time: “prolonged exposure to the sun”.
examples: Regular exercise may prolong your life.
Don't prolong the agony; just tell me the result.
Arguing will only prolong the meeting.
Prolonged exposure to loud noise can damage your hearing.
Proper storage can prolong the life of fresh food.

definition: Important and well known; also, easily seen or noticed.
usage: Collocations: a prominent figure/politician/role/position; a prominent feature/place. The noun “prominence” appears in “rise to prominence”.
examples: Several prominent politicians attended the event.
She played a prominent role in the campaign.
The statue stands in a prominent position in the square.
He has a very prominent nose.
The issue has become more prominent in recent years.

definition: The possibility that something will happen; also, the chances of future success (often plural).
usage: Patterns: the prospect of (doing) something; job/career/economic prospects; little/no prospect of. The adjective “prospective” means likely to become (prospective students/employers).
examples: The prospect of moving abroad excites me.
A degree improves your job prospects.
There's little prospect of an agreement soon.
Economic prospects for the region are poor.
She faced the prospect of losing her home.

definition: To cause a strong reaction, especially anger; also, to deliberately annoy someone to make them react.
usage: Collocations: provoke a reaction/debate/outrage/criticism/anger. The adjective “provocative” describes something meant to provoke; “thought-provoking” means making people think.
examples: The decision provoked angry protests.
Her article provoked a lively debate.
Don't let him provoke you.
The dog will only bite if it is provoked.
It was a thought-provoking documentary.

definition: Sensible and careful, especially in avoiding risks.
usage: Collocations: a prudent decision/approach/investment; it would be prudent to + verb. Common in financial contexts. The noun is “prudence”.
examples: It would be prudent to save some money for emergencies.
A prudent investor spreads the risk.
Given the weather, it seemed prudent to cancel the trip.
The bank takes a prudent approach to lending.
Was it prudent to sign the contract so quickly?

definition: Arriving or doing something at the expected or agreed time; not late.
usage: It is a positive personal quality. The noun “punctuality” is often mentioned in workplace rules. Some cultures value punctuality more strictly than others.
examples: She's always punctual for meetings.
Trains in Japan are famously punctual.
Please be punctual; the exam starts at nine sharp.
Employers value punctual, reliable staff.
He's never been very punctual.

definition: The act of trying to achieve something; also, the act of chasing someone. Also, an activity you spend time doing.
usage: Patterns: the pursuit of happiness/knowledge/excellence; in pursuit of something; leisure/outdoor pursuits (hobbies). The verb is “pursue”.
examples: The pursuit of happiness is a basic human right.
She moved to London in pursuit of a career in journalism.
The police were in hot pursuit of the stolen car.
Hiking is one of my favourite outdoor pursuits.
Universities are devoted to the pursuit of knowledge.

definition: To measure or express something as a number or amount.
usage: Common in academic and business writing: quantify the impact/risk/benefits. Often negative: “difficult/impossible to quantify”. Related: “quantitative”.
examples: It's difficult to quantify the benefits of education.
The study tries to quantify the cost of air pollution.
Can you quantify how much time you spend on email?
The damage is hard to quantify.
Researchers quantified the effect of sleep on test scores.

definition: Very new, different, and far-reaching; also, believing in extreme political or social change.
usage: Collocations: radical change/reform/idea/shift; a radical politician/group. The adverb “radically” (radically different) is common.
examples: The company needs radical change to survive.
The proposal is a radical departure from current policy.
His ideas were considered radical at the time.
Life today is radically different from fifty years ago.
The party has a radical wing that wants more extreme measures.

definition: Spreading or increasing quickly and in an uncontrolled way, especially something bad.
usage: Collocations: rampant inflation/corruption/crime/speculation/disease. It usually comes after the verb “be” or before the noun, and is almost always negative.
examples: Corruption is rampant in the construction industry.
The country suffered years of rampant inflation.
Speculation about his resignation is rampant.
Weeds were rampant in the neglected garden.
Misinformation ran rampant on social media during the crisis.

definition: A friendly relationship in which people understand each other and communicate well.
usage: Collocations: build/establish/develop a rapport (with someone); a good/close rapport. Common in teaching, sales, and healthcare. The final “t” is silent.
examples: Good teachers build a strong rapport with their students.
She quickly established a rapport with the clients.
There's a great rapport between the two presenters.
Small talk helps develop rapport before a negotiation.
Doctors who build rapport with patients get better results.

definition: Given or done by each of two people or groups to the other; mutual.
usage: Collocations: a reciprocal agreement/arrangement/relationship. The verb “reciprocate” means to respond in the same way. In grammar, “each other” is a reciprocal pronoun.
examples: The two countries have a reciprocal agreement on healthcare.
Friendship should be a reciprocal relationship.
The universities have a reciprocal exchange programme.
Respect is reciprocal; you have to give it to get it.
The two leaders made reciprocal visits last year.

definition: To make two ideas or situations that seem opposed exist together; also, to make people friendly again after an argument.
usage: Patterns: reconcile A with B; be reconciled with someone; reconcile yourself to something (accept it). In accounting, to reconcile accounts is to make records agree. The noun is “reconciliation”.
examples: It's hard to reconcile a full-time job with raising young children.
After years of not speaking, the brothers finally reconciled.
How can we reconcile economic growth with environmental protection?
She has reconciled herself to living alone.
The accountant reconciled the bank statements.

definition: To correct something that is wrong.
usage: Collocations: rectify a mistake/error/problem/situation/fault. It is formal and common in customer service and official communication.
examples: We apologize for the error and will rectify it immediately.
The company took steps to rectify the problem.
It's never too late to rectify a mistake.
The fault was rectified within an hour.
We must rectify the situation before it gets worse.

definition: No longer needed or useful; also, in British English, having lost your job because your employer no longer needs you.
usage: Collocations: make someone redundant; redundant words/information/equipment. The noun “redundancy” is used for job losses (redundancy pay). In writing, “redundant” words repeat meaning unnecessarily (“free gift”).
examples: Two hundred workers were made redundant when the factory closed.
New technology has made many skills redundant.
“Past history” is redundant because history is always past.
Remove any redundant information from your essay.
Thousands of jobs could become redundant because of automation.

definition: To prove that a statement, theory, or argument is wrong; also, to deny that something is true.
usage: Collocations: refute a claim/argument/theory/allegation. Strictly, “refute” means to prove false; using it simply to mean “deny” is common but criticized by some. The noun is “refutation”.
examples: The new data refutes the theory.
She refuted the allegations in a public statement.
In your essay, present the counter-argument and then refute it.
No one has been able to refute his argument.
The minister refuted claims that she had misled parliament.

definition: To say something again, especially for emphasis or clarity.
usage: Patterns: reiterate a point/commitment/position/that… It is formal and common in speeches and meetings: “I'd like to reiterate…”
examples: I'd like to reiterate how important this deadline is.
The minister reiterated her commitment to reform.
Let me reiterate: phones are not allowed in the exam.
He reiterated that he had done nothing wrong.
The report reiterates the need for more funding.

definition: Continuing strongly without stopping or becoming less intense.
usage: Collocations: relentless pressure/pace/criticism/rain/pursuit. It can be negative (relentless pressure) or admiring (relentless determination). The adverb is “relentlessly”.
examples: The relentless pace of work left him exhausted.
She faced relentless criticism from the media.
The rain was relentless all weekend.
His relentless determination finally paid off.
The company relentlessly focuses on customer service.

definition: A successful way of dealing with a problem; also, a treatment or medicine for an illness. As a verb, to correct or improve something.
usage: Collocations: a remedy for something; a home/herbal remedy; remedy a situation/problem. In law, a remedy is a way of correcting a wrong.
examples: Honey and lemon is a popular home remedy for sore throats.
There's no simple remedy for unemployment.
The government acted quickly to remedy the situation.
Sleep is often the best remedy for stress.
Customers have the right to seek a legal remedy.

definition: To cause someone or something to be in a particular state; also, to provide a service or to represent something in art or another form.
usage: Patterns: render something useless/obsolete/invalid; render someone speechless/unconscious; render a service/assistance. In computing, to render is to produce an image or video.
examples: The storm rendered the roads impassable.
New technology has rendered many jobs obsolete.
The news rendered her speechless.
He was paid for services rendered.
The software takes a few minutes to render the video.

definition: Famous and respected for a particular quality or achievement.
usage: Patterns: renowned for something; renowned as something; a world-renowned expert/chef. The noun is “renown”.
examples: The city is renowned for its architecture.
She's a world-renowned expert on climate change.
The restaurant is renowned for its seafood.
He was renowned as a brilliant speaker.
The university is renowned for its research.

definition: An unintended and usually bad effect of an action or event, often one that continues for a long time.
usage: Usually plural: serious/far-reaching/political/economic repercussions; repercussions for someone. Similar to “consequences” but stronger.
examples: The decision will have serious repercussions for the economy.
The scandal had political repercussions across Europe.
Students who cheat face repercussions.
Nobody foresaw the repercussions of the policy.
The repercussions of the crisis were felt for years.

definition: To copy something exactly; in research, to repeat a study to see if the same results are obtained.
usage: Collocations: replicate a study/experiment/result/success. “Replication” is central to science: results that cannot be replicated are doubtful.
examples: Other researchers have been unable to replicate the results.
The company hopes to replicate its success in Asia.
The experiment was replicated in three countries.
It's hard to replicate the taste of home cooking.
Viruses replicate inside host cells.

definition: Able to recover quickly from difficulties, shocks, or damage.
usage: Collocations: a resilient economy/community/person/material. The noun “resilience” is very common in psychology, business, and climate discussions (build resilience).
examples: Children are often surprisingly resilient.
The economy has proved resilient despite high inflation.
We need more resilient supply chains.
The community was resilient in the face of the disaster.
Bamboo is a strong and resilient material.

definition: Determined and firm in purpose; not easily changing your mind.
usage: Collocations: a resolute leader/stance/refusal; remain resolute. It is admiring and formal. The adverb is “resolutely”.
examples: She remained resolute in the face of criticism.
The president took a resolute stance against corruption.
He was resolute in his refusal to compromise.
Resolute action is needed to tackle the crisis.
They resolutely refused to give up.

definition: To have a special meaning or importance for someone because it relates to their own experience; also, of a sound, to continue loudly or deeply.
usage: Pattern: resonate with someone (an idea/message/story resonates with people). The adjective “resonant” describes deep, clear sounds.
examples: Her speech resonated with young voters.
The book's themes resonate with anyone who has moved abroad.
The message didn't resonate with customers.
His deep voice resonated through the hall.
Stories of hardship often resonate more than statistics.

definition: To stop someone or something from doing something, often by using physical force; also, to control your feelings or actions.
usage: Patterns: restrain someone (from doing something); restrain yourself; restrain spending/growth. The noun “restraint” means self-control or a limit. The adjective “restrained” means calm and controlled.
examples: Security guards restrained the angry fan.
I had to restrain myself from laughing.
The government is trying to restrain public spending.
She restrained the dog from chasing the cat.
His response was surprisingly restrained.

definition: To keep or continue to have something.
usage: Collocations: retain staff/customers/information/control/heat. It is more formal than “keep”. The noun “retention” appears in “staff retention” and “memory retention”.
examples: Companies struggle to retain talented staff.
Reviewing notes helps you retain information.
The town has retained much of its historic charm.
Clay soils retain water well.
The champion retained her title.

definition: To harm or attack someone because they have harmed or attacked you.
usage: Patterns: retaliate against someone; retaliate by doing something; retaliate for something. The noun “retaliation” is common in politics and trade (“in retaliation for”).
examples: The country retaliated by imposing tariffs on imports.
If you insult him, he'll retaliate.
The player was sent off for retaliating against a foul.
The attack was in retaliation for last week's bombing.
Employees should not fear being retaliated against for reporting problems.

definition: To find and bring back something; also, to get information from a computer or memory.
usage: Collocations: retrieve data/information/files/a lost item. The noun is “retrieval” (information retrieval).
examples: I managed to retrieve my phone from the lost property office.
The system can retrieve old files in seconds.
Divers retrieved the black box from the sea.
Some deleted data can still be retrieved.
Practice testing helps students retrieve information from memory.

definition: To change or improve something to make it more modern or attractive.
usage: Collocations: revamp a website/menu/image/system/store. As a noun: a major revamp. It is informal to neutral and common in business news.
examples: The café revamped its menu to attract younger customers.
The company is revamping its website.
The old station has been completely revamped.
The brand needs a revamp to stay relevant.
They revamped the training programme after poor feedback.

definition: To officially cancel a law, decision, licence, or permission.
usage: Collocations: revoke a licence/visa/permit/law/decision. It is formal and used in official and legal contexts. The noun is “revocation”.
examples: His driving licence was revoked after the accident.
The government revoked the controversial law.
Her visa was revoked without explanation.
The company's operating permit may be revoked.
You can revoke the app's access to your data at any time.

definition: Language designed to persuade or impress, often regarded as insincere or lacking meaningful content; also, the art of effective speaking or writing.
usage: Collocations: political/empty/campaign rhetoric; heated rhetoric. A “rhetorical question” is asked for effect, not for an answer. The adjective is “rhetorical”.
examples: Voters are tired of empty political rhetoric.
The rhetoric on both sides has become more aggressive.
His speech was full of rhetoric but short on detail.
Students study rhetoric to become better speakers.
It was a rhetorical question; I didn't expect an answer.

definition: Stiff and not able to bend; also, strict and not willing or able to change.
usage: Collocations: rigid rules/structure/schedule/thinking/hierarchy; a rigid material. The opposite is “flexible”. The noun is “rigidity”.
examples: The school's rules are too rigid.
A rigid schedule leaves no room for creativity.
The box is made of rigid plastic.
Rigid thinking makes it hard to solve new problems.
She was rigid with fear.

definition: Very careful, thorough, and exact; also, strict and demanding.
usage: Collocations: rigorous testing/research/analysis/standards/training. In academic contexts it is a high compliment. The noun “rigour” (US: rigor) is common: “academic rigour”.
examples: All new medicines go through rigorous testing.
The study was praised for its rigorous methodology.
Candidates face a rigorous selection process.
The course is academically rigorous.
Pilots undergo rigorous training before flying passengers.

definition: Strong, healthy, and unlikely to break or fail; also, of an argument or system, effective in many conditions.
usage: Collocations: a robust economy/system/defence/debate/evidence; robust health. In research, “robust” results stay the same under different tests. “A robust response” means a strong, firm one.
examples: The economy remains robust despite global uncertainty.
We need a robust system that won't crash under pressure.
The findings are robust across different age groups.
There was a robust debate about the proposal.
This phone case is robust enough to survive a fall.

definition: Basic and simple; not highly developed.
usage: Collocations: a rudimentary knowledge/understanding/form/tool. It often describes a minimal level of skill: “a rudimentary knowledge of French”.
examples: I have only a rudimentary knowledge of Spanish.
The camp had rudimentary facilities.
Early humans used rudimentary stone tools.
The robot can perform only rudimentary tasks.
Students need at least a rudimentary understanding of statistics.

definition: Determined to get what you want without caring about the harm you cause to others.
usage: Collocations: a ruthless dictator/businessman/competitor/efficiency. It can be admiring in some business contexts (“ruthless efficiency”), but is usually negative.
examples: The dictator was known for his ruthless treatment of opponents.
Big companies can be ruthless in crushing competition.
She's a ruthless negotiator.
Editing requires you to be ruthless with unnecessary words.
The team played with ruthless efficiency.

definition: Most important or most noticeable.
usage: Collocations: the salient points/features/facts/details. It is formal and common in academic and legal writing, especially in summaries.
examples: The report summarizes the salient points of the debate.
Let me outline the salient features of the plan.
The salient fact is that sales have fallen for three years.
Focus on the salient details, not the minor ones.
The most salient issue for voters is the cost of living.

definition: An official penalty or order, especially against a country; also, official permission or approval. As a verb, to approve or to punish officially.
usage: Collocations: impose/lift sanctions (on a country); economic/trade sanctions; without official sanction. Note the two opposite senses: permission and punishment.
examples: The UN imposed economic sanctions on the country.
Sanctions were lifted after the agreement was signed.
The strike did not have the union's official sanction.
The government refused to sanction the plan.
Players who break the rules face sanctions.

definition: Not available in large enough quantities; rare.
usage: Collocations: scarce resources/water/jobs/housing. The noun “scarcity” is a key economic term. The adverb “scarcely” means hardly. “Make yourself scarce” means to leave quickly.
examples: Water is becoming scarce in many parts of the world.
Good jobs are scarce in rural areas.
Governments must decide how to use scarce resources.
Fresh food was scarce during the war.
I could scarcely believe my eyes.

definition: A description of possible events or a situation that could happen in the future.
usage: Collocations: a worst-case/best-case/likely scenario; in this scenario. Plural: scenarios. Common in planning, business, and academic discussion.
examples: In the worst-case scenario, the project will be delayed by a year.
Let's imagine a scenario where prices double.
Economists modelled several different scenarios.
The best-case scenario is that we finish early.
Teachers use real-life scenarios in role-plays.

definition: To examine something very carefully to find information or mistakes.
usage: Collocations: scrutinize a document/proposal/someone's behaviour/the figures. British spelling also “scrutinise”. The noun “scrutiny” is common: “under scrutiny”, “close scrutiny”.
examples: The committee will scrutinize the proposal carefully.
Lawyers scrutinized every word of the contract.
Her spending was scrutinized by journalists.
Scientists scrutinize each other's work before publication.
Voters will scrutinize the budget closely.

definition: Happening smoothly without any obvious breaks, problems, or interruptions.
usage: Collocations: a seamless transition/experience/integration/service. It is popular in business and technology writing. The adverb is “seamlessly”.
examples: The new manager ensured a seamless transition.
The app offers a seamless shopping experience.
The devices work together seamlessly.
Moving between the two systems was seamless.
The dancers moved in a seamless, fluid motion.

definition: An opinion or feeling about something; also, emotional feelings such as tenderness or nostalgia.
usage: Collocations: public/anti-government/consumer/market sentiment; share a sentiment. The adjective “sentimental” means emotional, sometimes excessively. “Sentiment analysis” measures opinions in texts.
examples: Public sentiment is turning against the war.
Consumer sentiment improved last month.
I share your sentiments entirely.
There's no room for sentiment in business.
Anti-immigration sentiment has grown in some areas.

definition: Clever at understanding situations and making good judgements, especially for your own advantage.
usage: Collocations: a shrewd businessman/investor/move/guess/judge of character. It is generally admiring, though it can imply cunning.
examples: She's a shrewd businesswoman who rarely makes mistakes.
Buying the property before prices rose was a shrewd move.
I have a shrewd idea of who's behind this.
He's a shrewd judge of character.
The company made a shrewd investment in AI.

definition: To create conditions or a process that is similar to something real, usually for study or training; also, to pretend to have a feeling.
usage: Collocations: simulate conditions/an emergency/a flight/real-world situations. The noun “simulation” and “simulator” (a flight simulator) are common.
examples: The software simulates the effects of climate change.
Pilots train in machines that simulate real flights.
The exercise simulated a terrorist attack.
Role-plays simulate real-life conversations.
Scientists simulated conditions on Mars in the lab.

definition: Making you feel that something bad, harmful, or evil is happening or will happen.
usage: Collocations: a sinister motive/plot/figure/look/atmosphere. It often describes hidden bad intentions.
examples: There was something sinister about the way he smiled.
Police suspect a more sinister motive behind the attack.
The film has a dark, sinister atmosphere.
Nothing sinister happened; the lights just went out.
Critics see a sinister plan to control the media.

definition: To change or distort information or results so that they are not accurate or fair.
usage: Collocations: skew the results/data/figures/perception. The adjective “skewed” is common: “skewed results”, “a skewed view”. In statistics, skewed data is not evenly distributed.
examples: One extreme value can skew the average.
The small sample may have skewed the results.
Social media can skew our view of reality.
The survey was skewed towards older people.
Biased questions skew the data.

definition: To ask for something, such as money, help, or opinions, especially in a formal way.
usage: Collocations: solicit feedback/opinions/donations/advice/support. “Unsolicited” means not asked for (unsolicited advice/emails). In British English, a “solicitor” is a type of lawyer.
examples: The company solicits feedback from customers after every purchase.
Charities solicit donations online.
We solicited advice from several experts.
The magazine does not solicit articles from the public.
The council is soliciting opinions on the new plan.

definition: Advanced and complex in design or function; also, having a lot of experience of the world and of culture.
usage: Collocations: sophisticated technology/software/analysis/system; a sophisticated audience/taste. The noun is “sophistication”.
examples: The car is equipped with sophisticated safety technology.
Hackers are using increasingly sophisticated methods.
The film appeals to a sophisticated audience.
She has very sophisticated taste in wine.
The analysis was more sophisticated than previous studies.

definition: Small in number or amount and spread out over an area.
usage: Collocations: sparse population/vegetation/data/information. The adverb “sparsely” is common: “sparsely populated”, “sparsely furnished”.
examples: Vegetation is sparse in the desert.
Information about the accident is still sparse.
The region is sparsely populated.
The room was sparsely furnished with just a bed and a desk.
Data on the disease remains sparse.

definition: Happening naturally without being planned or forced; also, of a person, acting on sudden impulse.
usage: Collocations: a spontaneous decision/reaction/applause/trip/speech. In speaking tests, “spontaneous” speech is unprepared. The noun is “spontaneity”.
examples: The audience burst into spontaneous applause.
We made a spontaneous decision to drive to the beach.
She's fun and spontaneous.
The protest was spontaneous, not organized.
Spontaneous conversation is harder than prepared speech.

definition: Happening sometimes but not regularly or often.
usage: Collocations: sporadic fighting/violence/showers/outbreaks/attempts. The adverb is “sporadically”.
examples: There has been sporadic fighting near the border.
The forecast is for sporadic showers.
His attendance at classes was sporadic.
Sporadic cases of the disease are still reported.
She updates her blog sporadically.

definition: Of water or air, not moving and often smelling bad; of an economy or situation, not developing or growing.
usage: Collocations: stagnant water/wages/economy/growth/career. The verb “stagnate” and noun “stagnation” are common in economics.
examples: Mosquitoes breed in stagnant water.
Wages have remained stagnant for a decade.
The economy has been stagnant since the crisis.
She felt her career had become stagnant.
The air in the room was stagnant and stuffy.

definition: A publicly stated opinion or attitude about something; also, the way someone stands.
usage: Collocations: take/adopt a stance (on something); a firm/tough/neutral stance. In argumentative essays, you take a clear stance.
examples: The government has taken a tough stance on crime.
What's your stance on nuclear energy?
In your essay, make your stance clear from the start.
The company adopted a neutral stance in the debate.
The boxer took up a defensive stance.

definition: Very loyal and committed in your support for a person, organization, or belief.
usage: Collocations: a staunch supporter/ally/defender/critic/opponent. It comes before the noun. The adverb is “staunchly”.
examples: She is a staunch supporter of women's rights.
The two countries have been staunch allies for decades.
He was a staunch critic of the government.
My grandfather was a staunch defender of tradition.
The town is staunchly conservative.

definition: A fixed and oversimplified idea about what a particular type of person or thing is like.
usage: Collocations: a gender/racial/cultural stereotype; reinforce/challenge/break a stereotype. As a verb, “stereotype someone (as)”. The adjective is “stereotypical”.
examples: The advert reinforces gender stereotypes.
She challenges the stereotype that engineers are men.
Not all teenagers fit the stereotype of being lazy.
Older workers are often stereotyped as slow with technology.
Travel helps break down cultural stereotypes.

definition: A strong feeling of disapproval that most people in a society have about something, especially when it is unfair.
usage: Collocations: the stigma of/attached to something; reduce/remove/overcome stigma; social stigma. The verb “stigmatize” means to treat as shameful.
examples: There is still a stigma attached to mental illness.
The campaign aims to reduce the stigma around asking for help.
Many people feel the stigma of unemployment.
The social stigma of divorce has largely disappeared.
Talking openly can help overcome stigma.

definition: To encourage something to grow, develop, or become more active; also, to make someone interested or excited.
usage: Collocations: stimulate growth/the economy/demand/debate/interest/the brain. The adjective “stimulating” describes interesting conversation or work. The noun is “stimulation”; a “stimulus” is something that causes a reaction.
examples: The government cut taxes to stimulate the economy.
Good teachers stimulate students' curiosity.
The article stimulated a lively debate.
Puzzles can stimulate the brain.
It was a stimulating discussion.

definition: To state clearly and officially what must be done, especially as part of an agreement or rule.
usage: Patterns: stipulate that…; stipulate conditions/terms. It is formal and common in legal and contractual contexts. The noun is “stipulation”.
examples: The contract stipulates that payment must be made within 30 days.
The rules stipulate a maximum of two bags per passenger.
Her will stipulated that the house be sold.
The law stipulates minimum safety standards.
The scholarship stipulates that recipients return home after graduating.

definition: Requiring or using a lot of physical effort or energy.
usage: Collocations: strenuous exercise/activity/effort; strenuous denials/objections (very determined). Doctors often advise avoiding strenuous activity after surgery.
examples: Avoid strenuous exercise for two weeks after the operation.
Hiking at high altitude is strenuous.
Despite strenuous efforts, they couldn't save the business.
He made strenuous denials of any wrongdoing.
The job involves strenuous physical work.

definition: Very strict and precise, and having to be obeyed.
usage: Collocations: stringent rules/regulations/standards/requirements/controls. It is formal and stronger than “strict”.
examples: The industry is subject to stringent safety regulations.
Airlines have stringent rules about liquids in hand luggage.
The university has stringent entry requirements.
Food producers must meet stringent hygiene standards.
The government introduced more stringent controls on immigration.

definition: Based on personal feelings, opinions, or tastes rather than on facts.
usage: Collocations: a subjective judgement/opinion/view/experience. The opposite is “objective”. In academic writing, it is often a criticism of evidence.
examples: Taste in music is highly subjective.
Marking essays always involves some subjective judgement.
Pain is a subjective experience.
The review was too subjective to be useful.
Beauty is subjective; what one person loves, another hates.

definition: Having a lower rank or position; less important. As a noun, someone with a lower position at work.
usage: Patterns: subordinate to someone/something; a subordinate role/position. In grammar, a subordinate clause depends on a main clause (“because it rained”).
examples: She was always polite to her subordinates.
Personal interests should be subordinate to the needs of the team.
In this sentence, “because it rained” is a subordinate clause.
He refused to accept a subordinate role.
Managers should listen to their subordinates' ideas.

definition: Happening after something else.
usage: Collocations: subsequent years/events/studies/generations; subsequent to (formal: after). The adverb “subsequently” (later) is very common in formal writing.
examples: Subsequent studies confirmed the original results.
The first book was a success, but subsequent novels sold poorly.
He was arrested and subsequently released.
The policy affected subsequent generations.
Details will be announced in a subsequent email.

definition: To pay part of the cost of something to reduce its price for the buyer, usually as a government.
usage: Collocations: subsidize farmers/housing/public transport/education. British spelling also “subsidise”. The noun “subsidy” is very common in economics.
examples: The government subsidizes public transport in the capital.
Many countries subsidize farmers.
The company subsidizes meals in the staff canteen.
Should the state subsidize renewable energy?
Students receive subsidized accommodation in their first year.

definition: To provide evidence to prove that something is true.
usage: Collocations: substantiate a claim/allegation/argument. Often negative: “unsubstantiated rumours” (not proven). It is formal and common in academic and legal writing.
examples: You need data to substantiate your claim.
The allegations could not be substantiated.
She substantiated her argument with several case studies.
There is no evidence to substantiate the rumour.
Can you substantiate what you're saying?

definition: Expressed clearly in few words.
usage: Collocations: a succinct summary/explanation/answer/statement. It is close to “concise” and is a compliment. The adverb is “succinctly”.
examples: Give a succinct summary of the article.
Her answer was succinct and to the point.
He explained the problem succinctly.
The report is succinct but thorough.
Try to keep your conclusion succinct.

definition: To stop resisting something and give in to it, such as pressure, temptation, or illness; also, to die from an illness or injury.
usage: Pattern: succumb to something (temptation/pressure/an illness/injuries). Note the silent “b”. It is formal.
examples: I finally succumbed to temptation and ate the cake.
The government succumbed to pressure and dropped the plan.
He succumbed to his injuries in hospital.
Many small shops have succumbed to competition from online retailers.
Don't succumb to the pressure to buy things you don't need.

definition: Only on the surface, not deep or serious; of a person, not caring about serious matters.
usage: Collocations: a superficial wound/understanding/analysis/similarity/person. It is often critical. The adverb is “superficially”.
examples: He suffered only superficial injuries.
The essay offers a superficial analysis of the issue.
There's only a superficial similarity between the two cases.
Social media can encourage superficial relationships.
She thought he was charming but rather superficial.

definition: To replace something older or less useful.
usage: Often passive: be superseded by something. It is formal and common for technology, laws, and documents. Spelling note: it ends in “-sede”, not “-cede”.
examples: DVDs were superseded by streaming services.
This version supersedes all previous instructions.
The old law has been superseded by new legislation.
Fax machines were largely superseded by email.
The new guidelines supersede the 2018 policy.

definition: Something added to something else to improve or complete it; as a verb (/ˈsʌplɪment/), to add to something.
usage: Collocations: a dietary/vitamin supplement; supplement your income/diet. The adjective “supplementary” means additional (supplementary materials).
examples: Many people take vitamin D supplements in winter.
She supplements her income by teaching online.
The textbook is supplemented by online exercises.
Lectures are a supplement to, not a substitute for, reading.
There's a small supplement for a single room.

definition: To stop something from being seen, expressed, or developing; also, to end opposition by force.
usage: Collocations: suppress a laugh/yawn/emotions/information/a rebellion/the immune system. The noun is “suppression”.
examples: She tried to suppress a smile.
The government suppressed the protests violently.
The company was accused of suppressing negative research.
Some medicines suppress the immune system.
It's unhealthy to suppress your emotions all the time.

definition: To be greater or better than something or someone; to exceed.
usage: Collocations: surpass expectations/a record/a target/a rival. Common in business and sports news.
examples: Sales this year surpassed all expectations.
The film surpassed the record for opening-weekend earnings.
China has surpassed the US as the world's largest car market.
Her performance surpassed anything she had done before.
The student quickly surpassed her teacher.

definition: Easily influenced, affected, or harmed by something.
usage: Pattern: susceptible to something (disease/infection/pressure/flattery). It is common in medical and scientific contexts. The noun is “susceptibility”.
examples: Young children are more susceptible to infections.
Teenagers are particularly susceptible to peer pressure.
The region is susceptible to earthquakes.
Older computers are more susceptible to viruses.
He's very susceptible to flattery.

definition: To keep something going over a period of time; also, to suffer an injury or damage; to provide what is needed for life.
usage: Collocations: sustain growth/interest/a conversation/an effort; sustain injuries/damage/losses. The adjectives “sustained” (continued) and “sustainable” are related.
examples: It's hard to sustain motivation over a long course.
The driver sustained serious injuries in the crash.
The economy cannot sustain this level of growth.
The building sustained minor damage in the storm.
There's not enough food to sustain the population.

definition: Happening or moving quickly or immediately.
usage: Collocations: a swift response/reaction/action/recovery/decision. It is slightly more formal than “quick”. The adverb is “swiftly”.
examples: The government promised swift action.
We wish you a swift recovery.
The company's swift response prevented a crisis.
The decision was swift and unanimous.
She swiftly changed the subject.

definition: The combination of separate ideas, parts, or substances to form a whole; in chemistry, the production of a substance from simpler ones.
usage: Plural: syntheses. Collocations: a synthesis of ideas/research/styles. In academic writing, a literature review involves synthesis, not just summary. The verb is “synthesize”.
examples: The book is a synthesis of years of research.
Good essays show synthesis, not just a list of sources.
Her style is a synthesis of jazz and classical music.
Plants use sunlight for the synthesis of sugars.
The report offers a useful synthesis of current evidence.

definition: Real and able to be shown, seen, or felt; also, physically existing.
usage: Collocations: tangible results/benefits/evidence/progress/assets. The opposite is “intangible” (intangible benefits like reputation).
examples: The new system has brought tangible benefits.
We need tangible results, not promises.
There was a tangible sense of excitement in the room.
Property is a tangible asset.
Investors want to see tangible progress before investing more.

definition: A person's or animal's natural character and way of reacting to situations.
usage: Collocations: a calm/fiery/artistic temperament; by temperament. The adjective “temperamental” means having changeable moods, or (of a machine) unreliable.
examples: She has a calm temperament, which makes her a good nurse.
The two brothers have very different temperaments.
He was by temperament cautious.
Dogs of this breed have a gentle temperament.
My old car is a bit temperamental in cold weather.

definition: Very determined and not giving up easily; also, holding on firmly to something.
usage: Collocations: a tenacious player/journalist/fighter/grip. It is admiring. The noun is “tenacity”.
examples: She's a tenacious journalist who never gives up on a story.
The team put up a tenacious defence.
His tenacious grip on power lasted thirty years.
You need to be tenacious to succeed in sales.
The weeds were tenacious and hard to remove.

definition: To end something, or to come to an end.
usage: Collocations: terminate a contract/agreement/employment/pregnancy; a train terminates at a station (ends its journey). It is formal; the noun is “termination”.
examples: The company terminated his contract without notice.
Either party may terminate the agreement with a month's notice.
This train terminates at London King's Cross.
Her employment was terminated after the investigation.
The program terminated unexpectedly.

definition: A formal statement that something is true, especially one made in court; also, proof or evidence of something.
usage: Collocations: give testimony; witness testimony; a testimony to something (proof of a quality). “Testify” is the verb.
examples: The witness gave testimony in court.
The jury did not believe his testimony.
The building's survival is a testimony to its solid construction.
Her success is a testimony to her hard work.
Several victims gave testimony at the inquiry.

definition: Done completely and carefully, including every detail; of a person, careful to do things well.
usage: Collocations: a thorough investigation/check/understanding/search/review. The adverb “thoroughly” also means “completely”: “thoroughly enjoyed”. Don't confuse the spelling with “through” or “though”.
examples: The police carried out a thorough investigation.
You need a thorough understanding of grammar to teach it.
She's very thorough and rarely makes mistakes.
The car had a thorough check before the long trip.
We thoroughly enjoyed the evening.

definition: To accept or allow something you dislike or disagree with; also, to be able to bear something unpleasant.
usage: Patterns: tolerate behaviour/noise/heat/a drug; will not tolerate something. The adjective “tolerant” and noun “tolerance” (zero tolerance) are common.
examples: The school will not tolerate bullying.
I can't tolerate loud music when I'm working.
Some plants tolerate drought better than others.
Most patients tolerate the medication well.
A healthy society tolerates different opinions.

definition: Calm, quiet, and peaceful.
usage: Collocations: a tranquil setting/atmosphere/garden/lake/village. It is slightly literary. The noun is “tranquillity” (US: tranquility).
examples: The hotel is set in a tranquil garden.
We spent a tranquil afternoon by the lake.
The village is tranquil compared with the busy city.
Meditation helps create a tranquil state of mind.
The tranquil atmosphere made it a perfect place to study.

definition: To go beyond the usual limits of something.
usage: Collocations: transcend boundaries/borders/differences/cultures/generations. It is formal and often used in praise of art and ideas. The adjective “transcendent” means extraordinary.
examples: Music transcends language barriers.
Her films transcend cultural boundaries.
The issue transcends party politics.
Great literature transcends its time and place.
Their friendship transcended their political differences.

definition: Lasting only for a short time; temporary. Also, staying in a place only briefly.
usage: Collocations: a transient effect/feeling/population/phenomenon. It is formal; “temporary” or “short-lived” are more common.
examples: The side effects are usually mild and transient.
Fame can be transient.
The city has a large transient population of students.
Happiness from buying things is often transient.
The drop in prices was only transient.

definition: Clear enough to see through; also, open and honest, without secrets. Also, easy to notice or understand.
usage: Collocations: a transparent process/system/government; transparent glass/plastic; a transparent lie (obvious). The noun “transparency” is common in governance and business.
examples: The bottle is made of transparent plastic.
The selection process should be fair and transparent.
Companies should be transparent about their prices.
His excuse was a transparent attempt to avoid blame.
Voters want a more transparent government.

definition: Not important, serious, or valuable.
usage: Collocations: a trivial matter/issue/detail/mistake; trivial things. The verb “trivialize” means to make something seem less important than it is. “Trivia” are unimportant facts (a trivia quiz).
examples: Don't waste time on trivial details.
They argued over something completely trivial.
It may seem trivial, but small habits matter.
The error was trivial and easy to fix.
His problems seem trivial compared with hers.

definition: Involving a lot of sudden change, conflict, or disorder; of air or water, moving violently.
usage: Collocations: a turbulent period/history/year/relationship; turbulent waters/weather. The noun “turbulence” is common on flights.
examples: The country went through a turbulent period in the 1990s.
They had a turbulent relationship.
The boat struggled in the turbulent waters.
Markets have been turbulent this year.
The flight was turbulent, and several passengers felt sick.

definition: Seeming to be everywhere at the same time; very common.
usage: Collocations: ubiquitous smartphones/advertising/technology/coffee shops. It is formal and slightly humorous in everyday use. The noun is “ubiquity”.
examples: Smartphones have become ubiquitous.
Coffee chains are ubiquitous in city centres.
Plastic is ubiquitous in modern life.
Advertising is ubiquitous online.
The ubiquitous tourist with a selfie stick was everywhere.

definition: Agreed by everyone in a group.
usage: Collocations: a unanimous decision/vote/verdict/agreement; unanimous in their support. The adverb “unanimously” is common: “The proposal was approved unanimously.”
examples: The committee reached a unanimous decision.
The jury's verdict was unanimous.
The proposal was approved unanimously.
Critics were unanimous in their praise for the film.
There was unanimous support for the plan.

definition: Real but not immediately obvious; forming the basis of something.
usage: Collocations: the underlying cause/problem/reason/assumption/condition/message. In medicine, “underlying conditions” are existing health problems.
examples: We need to address the underlying causes of poverty.
Patients with underlying health conditions are at higher risk.
The underlying message of the film is hopeful.
What are the underlying assumptions of this model?
Stress may be the underlying reason for his headaches.

definition: To accept responsibility for a task or job and start doing it; also, to promise to do something.
usage: Irregular: undertook, undertaken. Collocations: undertake research/a project/a task/a study/a journey; undertake to do something (promise). The noun “undertaking” means a task or a promise.
examples: The university is undertaking a major research project.
She undertook a three-month journey across Africa.
He undertook to repay the money within a year.
The study was undertaken by a team of economists.
Writing a dictionary is a huge undertaking.

definition: Never having happened or existed before.
usage: Collocations: an unprecedented level/scale/rise/crisis/event/step. It is very common in news, sometimes overused. Related: “precedent”.
examples: The pandemic caused unprecedented disruption.
House prices have risen at an unprecedented rate.
The president took the unprecedented step of resigning.
The storm caused damage on an unprecedented scale.
These are unprecedented times for the industry.

definition: To separate threads that are tangled; also, to solve or explain something complicated, or to fail and fall apart.
usage: Patterns: unravel a mystery/the truth; a plan/agreement unravels (falls apart). British spelling doubles the l: unravelled, unravelling.
examples: Detectives are trying to unravel the mystery.
Scientists are slowly unravelling the secrets of the brain.
The peace deal began to unravel within weeks.
His life started to unravel after he lost his job.
The jumper unravelled when I pulled a loose thread.

definition: Not justified or necessary.
usage: Collocations: unwarranted criticism/interference/fears/intrusion/attention. The verb “warrant” means to justify.
examples: The criticism was completely unwarranted.
Your fears are unwarranted; the plan is safe.
They complained of unwarranted interference in their private lives.
The price increase seems unwarranted.
She received a lot of unwarranted attention from the press.

definition: A big change that causes a lot of confusion, worry, or problems.
usage: Collocations: political/social/economic/emotional upheaval; a period of upheaval. It is common in history and news writing.
examples: Moving house is a major upheaval.
The country went through years of political upheaval.
Technology has caused upheaval in the music industry.
Divorce causes emotional upheaval for children.
The company is in a period of upheaval after the merger.

definition: To support or defend a principle or law and make sure it continues; also, of a court, to confirm an earlier decision.
usage: Irregular: upheld. Collocations: uphold the law/values/rights/standards/a decision/a complaint.
examples: Judges must uphold the law.
The court upheld the original verdict.
The organization aims to uphold human rights.
Teachers should uphold high standards.
Her complaint was upheld by the ombudsman.

definition: To use something, especially for a practical purpose.
usage: British spelling also “utilise”. It is formal and sometimes considered unnecessarily inflated; “use” is often better in plain writing. The noun is “utilization”.
examples: The factory utilizes solar energy.
We need to utilize our resources more efficiently.
The app utilizes artificial intelligence to suggest recipes.
Students should utilize the library's online databases.
The space is poorly utilized.

definition: Greatest or most extreme; as a noun, the greatest possible amount.
usage: Collocations: of the utmost importance; the utmost care/respect; do your utmost (to do something). It is formal and emphatic.
examples: This matter is of the utmost importance.
Handle the samples with the utmost care.
We will do our utmost to help you.
I have the utmost respect for nurses.
She tried her utmost to finish on time.

definition: Not clear, detailed, or exact; also, of a person, not thinking or expressing themselves clearly.
usage: Collocations: a vague idea/memory/answer/promise/description; vague about something. The adverb “vaguely” is common: “vaguely remember”.
examples: The instructions were too vague to follow.
I have a vague memory of meeting her.
Politicians often give vague answers.
He was vague about his plans for the future.
The face looked vaguely familiar.

definition: Based on good reasoning or evidence; also, legally or officially acceptable for use.
usage: Collocations: a valid point/argument/reason/concern; a valid passport/ticket/licence. The noun “validity” is used in research (the validity of a test).
examples: That's a valid point.
Your passport must be valid for at least six months.
She had a valid reason for being absent.
The ticket is valid for one month.
Critics raised several valid concerns about the study.

definition: To prove that something is true or correct; also, to make something officially acceptable, or to recognize that someone's feelings are reasonable.
usage: Collocations: validate a theory/results/a method/a ticket/someone's feelings. In psychology, “validate feelings” means acknowledging them as legitimate. The noun is “validation”.
examples: Further studies are needed to validate the results.
Remember to validate your ticket before boarding.
The experiment validated the theory.
Good friends validate your feelings instead of dismissing them.
The new test has been validated in several countries.

definition: A new business or activity that involves risk; as a verb, to go somewhere unknown or dangerous, or to risk saying something.
usage: Collocations: a business/joint venture; venture capital (money invested in new companies); venture out/into; venture an opinion/guess.
examples: The restaurant was her first business venture.
The two firms formed a joint venture in China.
We didn't venture out because of the storm.
May I venture a suggestion?
Start-ups often rely on venture capital.

definition: To check or prove that something is true or correct.
usage: Collocations: verify information/someone's identity/the facts/a claim. The noun is “verification” (identity verification).
examples: Please verify your email address.
Journalists must verify their sources.
The bank needs to verify your identity.
The claims could not be independently verified.
Always verify information before sharing it online.

definition: Able to work successfully; practical. Also, able to survive or grow.
usage: Collocations: a viable option/alternative/solution/plan/business. Economically/commercially viable. The noun is “viability”.
examples: Electric cars are now a viable alternative to petrol cars.
Is the business commercially viable?
We need a viable plan, not just ideas.
Without funding, the project is not viable.
The seeds are still viable after ten years.

definition: Full of energy, life, and enthusiasm; of colours, bright and strong.
usage: Collocations: a vibrant city/culture/community/nightlife/economy; vibrant colours. It is positive and common in travel and marketing writing.
examples: Ho Chi Minh City has a vibrant street food culture.
The market is full of vibrant colours.
She has a vibrant personality.
The area has a vibrant arts scene.
Small businesses help create a vibrant local economy.

definition: Watching carefully and always ready to notice possible danger or problems.
usage: Patterns: remain/stay vigilant; vigilant about/against/for something. Common in safety warnings. The noun is “vigilance”.
examples: Passengers are asked to remain vigilant and report suspicious bags.
Parents need to be vigilant about what their children do online.
Stay vigilant against phishing emails.
A vigilant neighbour spotted the fire and called for help.
Doctors must be vigilant for early signs of infection.

definition: Strong, healthy, and full of energy; also, done with great force or determination.
usage: Collocations: vigorous exercise/activity/debate/campaign/opposition. The adverb is “vigorously”: “vigorously deny/defend”.
examples: Adults should do at least 75 minutes of vigorous exercise a week.
There was a vigorous debate about the new policy.
The company vigorously denied the allegations.
Stir the mixture vigorously.
Campaigners launched a vigorous protest against the plan.

definition: Almost completely; very nearly. Also, using computer technology rather than in person.
usage: Collocations: virtually impossible/identical/all/every/nothing. The newer sense: “meet virtually” (online). The adjective “virtual” means almost, or computer-based.
examples: It's virtually impossible to find a flat in the city centre.
The two products are virtually identical.
Virtually everyone in the class passed.
The conference was held virtually this year.
I knew virtually nothing about the subject.

definition: Absolutely necessary or extremely important; also, full of energy.
usage: Patterns: vital to/for something; it is vital that/to…; a vital role/part/link. “Vital signs” are measurements like pulse and breathing.
examples: Regular exercise is vital for good health.
It's vital that you keep your password secret.
Bees play a vital role in pollinating crops.
The nurse checked the patient's vital signs.
Clean water is vital to the community's survival.

definition: Producing very clear, strong images in the mind; of colours, very bright.
usage: Collocations: a vivid memory/description/dream/imagination; vivid colours. The adverb “vividly” is common: “I vividly remember…”
examples: I have a vivid memory of my first day at school.
The book gives a vivid description of life in the 1920s.
Children have vivid imaginations.
The painting uses vivid colours.
She vividly remembers the night of the earthquake.

definition: Likely to change suddenly and unexpectedly, especially for the worse; of a person, likely to become angry quickly.
usage: Collocations: a volatile market/situation/temper/price; volatile substances (evaporate easily). The noun is “volatility”. American pronunciation: /ˈvɑːlətl/.
examples: Cryptocurrency prices are extremely volatile.
The political situation remains volatile.
He has a volatile temper.
Oil prices have been volatile this year.
Petrol is a volatile liquid.

definition: Done because you choose to, not because you must; also, done without payment.
usage: Collocations: voluntary work/organization/redundancy/participation. The opposite is “compulsory/mandatory”. A “volunteer” does voluntary work.
examples: She does voluntary work at a local hospital.
Participation in the survey is voluntary.
The company offered voluntary redundancy to older staff.
Voluntary organizations rely on donations.
Attendance at the extra classes is completely voluntary.

definition: To gradually become weaker, smaller, or less important.
usage: Typical subjects: interest, popularity, influence, enthusiasm, power. The phrase “on the wane” means decreasing. The moon “waxes and wanes”.
examples: Public interest in the story has started to wane.
His influence waned after he left office.
My enthusiasm for running waned after a few weeks.
The popularity of cable TV is on the wane.
The moon is waning.

definition: To make an action necessary or appropriate; as a noun, a legal document allowing the police to do something.
usage: Verb: warrant attention/investigation/concern. Noun: a search/arrest warrant. The adjective “unwarranted” means unjustified.
examples: The situation warrants further investigation.
The results don't warrant such an expensive treatment.
Police obtained a warrant to search the house.
A judge issued a warrant for his arrest.
Nothing she did warranted such harsh criticism.

definition: Careful and cautious because you think something might be dangerous or cause problems.
usage: Pattern: wary of something/someone (wary of strangers/scams/investing). The adverb is “warily”. Compare “weary” (tired).
examples: Be wary of emails asking for your password.
Investors are wary of putting money into new markets.
The cat was wary of strangers.
I'm wary of making promises I can't keep.
Consumers have grown wary of fake online reviews.

definition: Existing or happening in many places or among many people.
usage: Collocations: widespread support/use/belief/damage/concern/protests. It is common in academic and news writing.
examples: The storm caused widespread damage.
There is widespread support for the new law.
Smartphone use is now widespread among older people.
The decision caused widespread anger.
It's a widespread belief that carrots improve your eyesight.

definition: To have and use power or influence; also, to hold and use a weapon or tool.
usage: Collocations: wield power/influence/authority/control; wield a sword/knife. It is common in political writing.
examples: Tech giants wield enormous power over our lives.
The prime minister wields considerable influence.
The attacker was wielding a knife.
Social media influencers wield real influence over young consumers.
She wields authority with fairness.

definition: To be strong enough not to be harmed or affected by something.
usage: Irregular: withstood. Collocations: withstand pressure/heat/an earthquake/criticism/the test of time.
examples: The building is designed to withstand earthquakes.
The bridge withstood the storm.
Her theory has withstood decades of criticism.
These plants can withstand very low temperatures.
Good design withstands the test of time.

definition: A difficult or unlucky situation or period of time.
usage: Collocations: face/overcome adversity; in the face of adversity. It is uncountable in most uses and often appears in inspiring stories.
examples: She showed great courage in the face of adversity.
Many successful people have overcome adversity.
The team pulled together in times of adversity.
Adversity can make people stronger.
His childhood was marked by poverty and adversity.

definition: A natural liking for or understanding of someone or something; also, a close similarity or connection.
usage: Patterns: an affinity for/with someone or something; a natural affinity. It is slightly formal.
examples: She has a natural affinity for languages.
I felt an immediate affinity with him.
Children often have an affinity with animals.
There is a strong affinity between the two cultures.
He had little affinity for city life.

definition: A large amount of work or tasks that should have been done already and are still waiting.
usage: Collocations: a backlog of cases/orders/emails/work; clear/reduce a backlog. Common in workplace and public service contexts.
examples: After my holiday, I had a huge backlog of emails.
The courts are struggling with a backlog of cases.
The factory hired extra staff to clear the backlog of orders.
Hospitals face a backlog of operations after the pandemic.
The visa office has a backlog of six months.

definition: To make someone or something seem unimportant or of little value.
usage: Typical objects: someone's achievements/efforts/feelings/opinions. It is always negative and suggests disrespect.
examples: Don't belittle her achievements; she worked hard for them.
He constantly belittled his staff in front of others.
I'm not trying to belittle your problems.
Bullies often belittle others to feel powerful.
She felt belittled by his comments.

definition: Saying what you think directly and honestly, without trying to be polite; also, of a knife or pencil, not sharp.
usage: Collocations: a blunt question/answer/message/assessment; to be blunt (= to be honest). The adverb “bluntly” is common: “to put it bluntly”.
examples: To be blunt, your essay needs a lot of work.
She's very blunt, but she's always honest.
This knife is too blunt to cut tomatoes.
To put it bluntly, we're running out of money.
His blunt comments offended some people.

definition: Quick and energetic; also, of weather, cold and fresh, and of business, busy.
usage: Collocations: a brisk walk/pace; brisk business/trade; a brisk wind/morning; a brisk manner (efficient, slightly unfriendly).
examples: We went for a brisk walk after lunch.
Business at the market was brisk.
It was a brisk autumn morning.
She spoke in a brisk, businesslike way.
Walk at a brisk pace for at least 30 minutes a day.

definition: To love, protect, and care for someone or something that is important to you; also, to keep a memory or hope in your mind.
usage: Collocations: cherish memories/moments/friendships/freedom/a dream. The adjective “cherished” means much loved (a cherished possession).
examples: I'll always cherish the memories of our trip.
Cherish the time you have with your grandparents.
This watch is my most cherished possession.
We should cherish our freedom.
She cherished the hope that he would return.

definition: Moving or doing things in an awkward way and often dropping or breaking things; also, done without skill or tact.
usage: Collocations: a clumsy person/movement/attempt/apology/design. The noun is “clumsiness”.
examples: I'm so clumsy; I've broken another glass.
He made a clumsy attempt to apologize.
The translation is accurate but clumsy.
My clumsy fingers kept hitting the wrong keys.
The design looks clumsy compared with newer models.

definition: A strong feeling of sympathy for people who are suffering, and a wish to help them.
usage: Collocations: show/feel compassion; compassion for someone. The adjective is “compassionate” (compassionate leave = time off for a family death or illness).
examples: Nurses treat patients with compassion.
She felt deep compassion for the refugees.
We need leaders who show compassion.
His story moved the audience to compassion.
She was given compassionate leave after her father died.

definition: Too proud of yourself and your abilities.
usage: It is a strong criticism of someone's character. Synonyms: arrogant, vain, big-headed (informal). The noun “conceit” means excessive pride.
examples: He's talented but terribly conceited.
I don't want to sound conceited, but I think I did well.
Success made her conceited.
Nobody likes a conceited colleague.
His conceited attitude annoyed the rest of the team.

definition: Behaving as though you are more important or intelligent than other people.
usage: Patterns: condescending to/towards someone; a condescending tone/attitude/smile. Synonym: patronizing. The verb is “condescend”.
examples: I hate it when people are condescending to me.
He spoke in a condescending tone.
Her condescending attitude annoyed the other students.
Don't be condescending; I understand the problem.
The manager's condescending comments upset the staff.

definition: A confusing and difficult problem or question.
usage: Collocations: face a conundrum; a real/moral/ethical conundrum. It is slightly informal or playful, similar to “puzzle” or “dilemma”.
examples: How to fund healthcare for an ageing population is a real conundrum.
Choosing between two great job offers was quite a conundrum.
The data presents scientists with a conundrum.
Parents face the conundrum of how much screen time to allow.
That's the conundrum: we need more staff but have no budget.

definition: To reach the highest point, final result, or climax after a gradual development.
usage: Pattern: culminate in/with something. The noun “culmination” means the final result of a long process.
examples: Years of protests culminated in a change of government.
The course culminates in a final project.
Their rivalry culminated in a dramatic final.
The festival culminates with a huge fireworks display.
The award was the culmination of years of hard work.

definition: Unhappy and disappointed, especially after a failure.
usage: Collocations: look/feel/seem dejected; dejected fans/players. Synonyms: downhearted, despondent. The noun is “dejection”.
examples: The players looked dejected after losing the final.
She felt dejected when her application was rejected.
Dejected fans left the stadium in silence.
He sat alone, looking dejected.
Don't be dejected; you'll get another chance.

definition: To destroy or badly damage something; also, to make someone extremely shocked and upset.
usage: Often passive or as an adjective: be devastated by news (very upset); devastating effects/news/impact. The noun is “devastation”.
examples: The earthquake devastated the city.
She was devastated by the news of his death.
The floods have had a devastating impact on farmers.
Losing the final was devastating for the team.
The industry was devastated by the recession.

definition: To move away from the main subject when speaking or writing.
