usage: Common phrases: “But I digress” (used to return to the main point); digress from the topic. The noun “digression” means a section that moves away from the topic.
examples: Sorry, I'm digressing; let's get back to the main point.
The professor often digresses during lectures.
But I digress. Where was I?
Try not to digress from the question in your essay.
He digressed into a long story about his childhood.

definition: A feeling of shock, worry, and disappointment; as a verb, to make someone feel this.
usage: Patterns: to someone's dismay; in/with dismay; be dismayed at/by something. It is slightly formal.
examples: To my dismay, the shop had already closed.
Fans reacted with dismay to the news.
She was dismayed by the poor results.
Teachers expressed dismay at the cuts.
He looked at the bill in dismay.

definition: Showing that you think something or someone is not important or not worth considering.
usage: Pattern: dismissive of someone/something; a dismissive attitude/tone/wave. The verb “dismiss” means to reject an idea or end someone's employment.
examples: The manager was dismissive of my suggestions.
She gave a dismissive wave of her hand.
Don't be so dismissive of other people's feelings.
His dismissive tone upset the students.
Experts were initially dismissive of the theory.

definition: Extremely worried, upset, or anxious, so that you cannot think clearly.
usage: It describes intense distress, stronger than “upset”. Typical contexts: losing a child, a pet, or a loved one.
examples: The distraught mother searched everywhere for her son.
He was distraught when his dog went missing.
Distraught relatives waited for news at the airport.
She was too distraught to speak.
The family is distraught after the accident.

definition: Extremely happy and excited, especially because of a success.
usage: Patterns: elated at/by/about something. It is stronger than “happy”. The noun is “elation”.
examples: She was elated when she got the scholarship.
The team was elated by their victory.
I felt elated after finishing the marathon.
Elated fans celebrated in the streets.
He was elated at the news of his promotion.

definition: To make a story more interesting by adding details that may not be true; also, to decorate something.
usage: Collocations: embellish a story/account/the truth; embellished with beads/gold. The noun is “embellishment”.
examples: He tends to embellish his stories to make them funnier.
The dress was embellished with tiny pearls.
Don't embellish your CV; employers will check.
Her account of the trip was slightly embellished.
The ceiling is embellished with gold leaf.

definition: Making people feel love or affection.
usage: Collocations: an endearing quality/habit/smile/personality. The verb “endear” is used in “endear yourself to someone” (make them like you).
examples: His shyness is one of his most endearing qualities.
She has an endearing habit of humming while she works.
The film's characters are flawed but endearing.
The puppy's clumsiness was endearing.
Her honesty endeared her to the voters.

definition: So interested in something that you do not notice anything else.
usage: Pattern: engrossed in something (a book/work/conversation/game). The adjective “engrossing” describes something very interesting.
examples: She was so engrossed in her book that she missed her stop.
The children were engrossed in the film.
He was engrossed in conversation and didn't see me.
I got so engrossed in my work that I forgot to eat.
The students were engrossed in the experiment.

definition: Very annoyed and frustrated, especially because you cannot do anything to change a situation.
usage: Patterns: exasperated by/with/at someone or something. The adjective “exasperating” describes what causes the feeling. The noun is “exasperation”.
examples: The teacher was exasperated by the students' constant chatter.
“How many times do I have to tell you?” she said, exasperated.
Customers are exasperated with the slow service.
He gave an exasperated sigh.
Dealing with the bank's bureaucracy left me exasperated.

definition: Making you feel extremely happy, excited, and full of energy.
usage: Collocations: an exhilarating experience/ride/feeling/game. The adjective “exhilarated” describes the person; the noun is “exhilaration”.
examples: Skydiving was an exhilarating experience.
The roller coaster ride was exhilarating.
It was an exhilarating match from start to finish.
There's nothing as exhilarating as finishing your first marathon.
Moving to a new city was both frightening and exhilarating.

definition: Likely to change your opinions, feelings, or loyalties suddenly and often.
usage: Collocations: fickle fans/consumers/voters/weather/fortune. It is usually critical.
examples: Football fans can be fickle.
Consumers are fickle and quickly switch brands.
The weather in Britain is notoriously fickle.
Fame is fickle; one day you're a star, the next you're forgotten.
Voters proved fickle at the last election.

definition: A natural ability to do something well; also, a stylish, original quality.
usage: Patterns: a flair for something (languages/design/business); with flair. Don't confuse it with “flare” (a sudden flame).
examples: She has a real flair for languages.
He dresses with flair.
The job requires creativity and a flair for design.
The chef cooks traditional dishes with a modern flair.
She showed a flair for business from a young age.

definition: A state of great excitement, activity, or emotion that is difficult to control.
usage: Collocations: a media/buying/feeding/shopping frenzy; in a frenzy. The adjective “frenzied” means wild and uncontrolled.
examples: The news caused a media frenzy.
There was a buying frenzy before the price increase.
The crowd worked itself into a frenzy.
Black Friday sales lead to a shopping frenzy.
She cleaned the house in a frenzy before the guests arrived.

definition: To worry continuously about something, often unnecessarily.
usage: Pattern: fret about/over something. Past forms double the t: fretted, fretting. It is informal and often used in the negative: “Don't fret.”
examples: Don't fret; everything will be fine.
She fretted about the exam all week.
Parents often fret over their children's screen time.
There's no point fretting about things you can't change.
He spent the night fretting over the decision.

definition: Very serious, worrying, or unpleasant; also, looking serious and unfriendly.
usage: Collocations: a grim reality/outlook/picture/warning; grim news; a grim expression. “Grim determination” means determination despite difficulty.
examples: The economic outlook is grim.
The report paints a grim picture of the health service.
She had a grim expression on her face.
They carried on with grim determination.
The weather has been grim all week.

definition: A feeling of anger or dislike towards someone because of something they did in the past.
usage: Collocations: hold/bear a grudge (against someone); an old grudge. The adverb “grudgingly” means unwillingly (grudgingly admit).
examples: He still holds a grudge against his old boss.
Life's too short to hold grudges.
I don't bear any grudge against her.
The rivalry started with a personal grudge.
She grudgingly admitted that he was right.

definition: To argue about the price of something, especially in a market.
usage: Patterns: haggle over/about the price; haggle with a seller. In some cultures haggling is expected; in others it may seem rude.
examples: Tourists are expected to haggle in the market.
We haggled over the price for twenty minutes.
I'm terrible at haggling.
She haggled with the taxi driver before getting in.
In most shops here, prices are fixed and you can't haggle.

definition: A situation that is annoying because it involves difficulty or effort; as a verb, to keep annoying someone.
usage: Collocations: a real hassle; it's a hassle to + verb; hassle-free; hassle someone (about something). It is informal.
examples: Renewing a passport can be a real hassle.
It's too much hassle to cook tonight; let's order food.
Online banking makes paying bills hassle-free.
Stop hassling me; I'll do it later.
Travelling with young children can be a hassle.

definition: Very busy and full of activity, often in a slightly stressful way.
usage: Collocations: a hectic schedule/day/week/lifestyle/pace. It is common in everyday speech.
examples: I've had a hectic week at work.
Her hectic schedule leaves little time for friends.
Life in a big city can be hectic.
The days before the wedding were hectic.
After a hectic morning, I finally had lunch at three.

definition: To make someone feel ashamed, foolish, or less respected, especially in front of others.
usage: The adjectives “humiliating” (a humiliating defeat) and “humiliated” (feel humiliated) are common. The noun is “humiliation”.
examples: The teacher humiliated him in front of the whole class.
It was a humiliating defeat for the champions.
She felt humiliated when her mistake was made public.
Never humiliate an employee in public.
The team suffered a humiliating 6-0 loss.

definition: A feeling that something is true or will happen, even without clear evidence.
usage: Collocations: have a hunch (that…); follow/act on a hunch; my hunch is that… As a verb, to hunch means to bend your back and shoulders forward.
examples: I had a hunch that she would say yes.
The detective followed a hunch and solved the case.
My hunch is that prices will fall next year.
Acting on a hunch, I checked the back door.
Don't sit hunched over your laptop for hours.

definition: Angry because you feel you have been treated unfairly or insulted.
usage: Patterns: indignant at/about/over something. The noun “indignation” suggests moral anger at injustice.
examples: She was indignant at the suggestion that she had cheated.
Residents are indignant about the rise in parking fees.
“I've never been late in my life!” he said, indignant.
Customers wrote indignant letters to the company.
Local residents are indignant over the closure of the library.

definition: To make someone extremely angry.
usage: The adjectives “infuriating” (an infuriating habit) and “infuriated” (feel infuriated) are very common. It is stronger than “annoy”.
examples: His constant lateness infuriates me.
The decision infuriated local residents.
It's infuriating when the Wi-Fi keeps dropping.
She was infuriated by his rude reply.
Nothing infuriates me more than people who don't listen.

definition: Eager to learn and find out about things, sometimes in a way that seems too curious.
usage: Collocations: an inquisitive mind/child/nature. It is usually positive (curious) but can suggest nosiness.
examples: Young children are naturally inquisitive.
She has an inquisitive mind and asks great questions.
My inquisitive neighbour always wants to know where I'm going.
Good scientists are inquisitive and sceptical.
The inquisitive cat explored every corner of the room.

definition: A natural skill or ability to do something well, or a clever way of doing something.
usage: Patterns: have a knack for/of (doing) something; get the knack of something; there's a knack to it. It is informal. The “k” is silent.
examples: She has a knack for making people feel comfortable.
It took me a while to get the knack of using chopsticks.
There's a knack to opening this jar.
He has a knack of saying the wrong thing.
Some people have a knack for languages.

definition: Large, generous, and expensive; as a verb, to give a lot of something to someone.
usage: Collocations: a lavish party/wedding/lifestyle/gift; lavish praise/attention on someone. It can be admiring or critical.
examples: They threw a lavish party for their anniversary.
The celebrity lives a lavish lifestyle.
Critics lavished praise on the young director.
The hotel has lavish rooms with marble bathrooms.
Grandparents often lavish gifts on their grandchildren.

definition: The amount of freedom someone has to act or make decisions; also, extra time, space, or money.
usage: Collocations: give someone leeway; some/little/considerable leeway; leeway to do something.
examples: Teachers have some leeway in how they cover the curriculum.
Our manager gives us a lot of leeway.
We have a little leeway in the budget.
Build some leeway into your schedule in case of delays.
The new law leaves little leeway for interpretation.

definition: A short period of calm or reduced activity; as a verb, to make someone calm or sleepy, or make them feel falsely safe.
usage: Collocations: a lull in the conversation/fighting/trading; lull someone to sleep; lull someone into a false sense of security.
examples: There was a brief lull in the conversation.
During a lull in the fighting, civilians escaped.
The sound of the rain lulled me to sleep.
Don't let an easy start lull you into a false sense of security.
Sales often experience a lull after Christmas.

definition: To try to change or influence something that is not your responsibility, in an annoying way.
usage: Patterns: meddle in/with something. It is negative. The adjective “meddling” describes someone who interferes.
examples: Stop meddling in my private life.
Don't meddle with the settings; you might break something.
Politicians shouldn't meddle in judicial decisions.
Her meddling mother-in-law causes constant tension.
He accused foreign governments of meddling in the election.

definition: A small accident or piece of bad luck that does not have serious results.
usage: Collocations: a minor mishap; without mishap. It is lighter than “accident” or “disaster”.
examples: Apart from a few minor mishaps, the trip went well.
The wedding went ahead without mishap.
There was a slight mishap with the cake.
A technical mishap delayed the broadcast.
Kitchen mishaps are part of learning to cook.

definition: Very important, especially because of effects on the future.
usage: Collocations: a momentous decision/event/occasion/day/change. Don't confuse it with “momentary” (lasting a moment).
examples: Leaving home for university is a momentous step.
It was a momentous day in the country's history.
The election result was momentous.
Signing the treaty was a momentous occasion.
She made the momentous decision to start her own company.

definition: To keep criticizing someone or asking them to do something in an annoying way; also, of a worry, to trouble you continuously.
usage: Patterns: nag someone to do something; nag someone about something; a nagging doubt/feeling/pain (that won't go away).
examples: My mum keeps nagging me to tidy my room.
Stop nagging; I'll do it later.
I had a nagging feeling that I'd forgotten something.
He nagged his parents for a new phone.
A nagging injury kept her out of the team.

definition: Calm and relaxed, and seeming not to care or be worried.
usage: Collocations: a nonchalant attitude/shrug/manner. It can suggest real calm or a pretence of not caring. The adverb is “nonchalantly”.
examples: He seemed nonchalant about the exam, but he was secretly nervous.
She gave a nonchalant shrug.
His nonchalant attitude to money worries his wife.
He walked in nonchalantly, two hours late.
Try to look nonchalant when you ask for a pay rise.

definition: Something or someone that annoys you or causes problems.
usage: Collocations: a real nuisance; make a nuisance of yourself; a public nuisance (legal). “It's a nuisance having to…” is a common pattern.
examples: The noise from the building site is a real nuisance.
It's a nuisance having to change trains twice.
Pigeons have become a nuisance in the city centre.
Stop making a nuisance of yourself.
Spam calls are a constant nuisance.

definition: A very unpleasant and painful or difficult experience.
usage: Collocations: go through/survive/face an ordeal; a terrible/long ordeal. It is often used for frightening events or difficult processes.
examples: The hostages spoke about their terrible ordeal.
Getting a visa was a real ordeal.
She's still recovering from the ordeal.
The long flight with two toddlers was an ordeal.
Survivors described their ordeal to reporters.

definition: Confused and worried because you cannot understand something.
usage: Patterns: perplexed by/at something; a perplexed look/expression. The verb “perplex” and adjective “perplexing” (confusing) are related.
examples: She looked perplexed by the question.
Doctors were perplexed by his symptoms.
He gave me a perplexed look.
I'm perplexed as to why they cancelled the event.
Many students were perplexed by the new grading system.

definition: To annoy someone by repeatedly asking them for something or interrupting them.
usage: Patterns: pester someone for something; pester someone to do something; pester someone with questions. “Pester power” is children's ability to make parents buy things.
examples: The kids pestered me for ice cream all afternoon.
Journalists pestered her with questions.
Stop pestering your sister.
He pestered his boss to give him a pay rise.
Advertisers rely on children's pester power.

definition: Unimportant and trivial; also, caring too much about small, unimportant things in an unkind way.
usage: Collocations: petty arguments/details/crime/jealousy; petty cash (small amounts of money for minor expenses). Calling someone petty is a criticism.
examples: Let's not argue over petty details.
He was arrested for petty theft.
Don't be so petty; it's only a few pounds.
The office is full of petty rivalries.
Pay for the coffee out of petty cash.

definition: To fall very quickly and suddenly from a high level or position.
usage: Typical subjects: prices, sales, temperatures, profits, popularity. It is stronger than “fall” and common in news and graph descriptions.
examples: Share prices plummeted after the announcement.
Temperatures plummeted overnight.
The president's popularity has plummeted.
Sales of DVDs plummeted as streaming grew.
The plane plummeted into the sea.

definition: To think carefully about something for a period of time.
usage: Patterns: ponder a question/problem; ponder over/on something; ponder whether/how… It is slightly literary.
examples: She pondered the question for a moment.
I've been pondering whether to change jobs.
The film leaves viewers pondering its meaning.
He sat by the window, pondering his future.
Philosophers have long pondered the nature of happiness.

definition: Likely to suffer from something or do something, usually bad; also, lying flat facing downwards.
usage: Patterns: prone to something (injury/illness/mistakes/flooding); prone to do something. Compounds: accident-prone, error-prone, flood-prone.
examples: This area is prone to flooding.
I'm prone to headaches when I don't sleep enough.
He's accident-prone and always has a bruise somewhere.
Tired people are more prone to mistakes.
Older buildings are prone to damp.

definition: Unusual in an interesting or attractive way.
usage: Collocations: a quirky style/sense of humour/café/character. It is usually positive. A “quirk” is a strange habit or feature.
examples: The café has a quirky interior full of old furniture.
She has a quirky sense of humour.
The film is full of quirky characters.
It's a quirky little town with lots of independent shops.
One of his quirks is that he never wears socks.

definition: Doing something dangerous without thinking about the possible results.
usage: Collocations: reckless driving/behaviour/spending/disregard. The adverb is “recklessly”. Legal phrase: “reckless driving”.
examples: He was arrested for reckless driving.
Reckless spending left them in debt.
It was reckless to swim so far from the shore.
The bank was criticized for reckless lending.
Teenagers sometimes behave recklessly.

definition: To enjoy something very much or look forward to it; as a noun, great enjoyment, or a sauce served with food.
usage: Patterns: relish the chance/challenge/opportunity; relish doing something; not relish the idea/prospect (dislike). With relish = with great enjoyment.
examples: She relishes a good challenge.
I don't relish the idea of working this weekend.
He ate his dinner with relish.
The team is relishing the chance to play in the final.
Nobody relishes the prospect of moving house.

definition: To talk, write, or think about pleasant experiences from the past.
usage: Pattern: reminisce about something. The adjective “reminiscent (of)” means reminding you of something.
examples: We spent the evening reminiscing about our school days.
My grandparents love to reminisce about the old days.
Old friends reminisced over coffee.
Looking at photos made her reminisce about her childhood.
The song is reminiscent of the 1980s.

definition: To feel angry and upset about something you think is unfair.
usage: Patterns: resent someone/something; resent (someone) doing something. The adjective “resentful” and noun “resentment” are common.
examples: She resents being treated like a child.
Many workers resent the new rules.
I resent the suggestion that I'm lazy.
He resented his brother's success.
Unfair treatment breeds resentment.

definition: Good at finding clever ways to solve problems or deal with difficult situations.
usage: It is a strong compliment, often used in job references and stories of survival. The noun is “resourcefulness”.
examples: She's resourceful and always finds a solution.
Resourceful students find ways to study even without textbooks.
The stranded hikers were resourceful enough to build a shelter.
Employers want resourceful people who don't need constant supervision.
Being resourceful is essential when travelling on a budget.

definition: Careless and not done with enough attention; also, of clothes, loose and untidy.
usage: Collocations: sloppy work/writing/mistakes/thinking; a sloppy jumper. It is informal and critical.
examples: The report was full of sloppy mistakes.
Sloppy handwriting can cost you marks.
The team's defending was sloppy.
Don't be sloppy; check your work carefully.
He wore a sloppy old jumper around the house.

definition: Too pleased with yourself because of something you have done or have, in an annoying way.
usage: Collocations: a smug smile/expression/look; smug about something. It is clearly critical.
examples: He had a smug smile on his face after winning the argument.
Don't look so smug; you only won by luck.
She was smug about getting the best marks in the class.
The ending of the film felt a bit smug.
I hate his smug attitude.

definition: A problem or difficulty, especially a small or unexpected one.
usage: Collocations: hit/run into a snag; the only snag is…; there's a snag. It is informal. As a verb, to snag means to catch on something sharp, or informally, to get something.
examples: The plan sounds great; the only snag is the cost.
We hit a snag when the supplier went bankrupt.
There's a snag: the venue is already booked.
I snagged my jumper on a nail.
The project ran into a few snags but finished on time.

definition: To rise very quickly to a high level; also, to fly high in the air.
usage: Typical subjects: prices, temperatures, profits, demand, popularity, birds. The adjective “soaring” is common: “soaring prices”.
examples: House prices have soared in recent years.
Temperatures soared to 40 degrees.
Demand for electric cars has soared.
An eagle soared above the valley.
Soaring energy costs are hurting families.

definition: Serious, sad, and without humour; also, of colours, dark and dull.
usage: Collocations: a sombre mood/atmosphere/occasion/tone; sombre colours. American spelling: “somber”.
examples: The mood at the funeral was sombre.
The minister spoke in a sombre tone about the disaster.
Guests wore sombre colours.
It was a sombre occasion for the whole town.
The report reached a sombre conclusion.

definition: To waste money, time, or opportunities in a foolish way.
usage: Collocations: squander money/an opportunity/a chance/a lead/resources. It is critical.
examples: He squandered his inheritance on gambling.
Don't squander this opportunity.
The team squandered a two-goal lead.
Public money should not be squandered on vanity projects.
She regrets squandering her time at university.

definition: The physical or mental strength to continue doing something for a long time.
usage: Collocations: build up/improve stamina; physical/mental stamina; lack stamina. It is uncountable.
examples: Running every day helps build stamina.
Marathon runners need great stamina.
Writing a thesis requires mental stamina.
I don't have the stamina to stay up all night anymore.
Swimming improves strength and stamina.

definition: Determined not to change your opinion or behaviour, even when you should; also, difficult to remove or deal with.
usage: Collocations: a stubborn child/refusal/streak; stubborn stains/problems/inflation. Synonym: obstinate. It can be negative or, occasionally, admiring.
examples: He's too stubborn to admit he's wrong.
She has a stubborn streak.
This detergent removes stubborn stains.
Inflation has proved stubborn.
My grandfather is stubborn but kind.

definition: A sudden large increase; as a verb, to increase suddenly or to move forward quickly in a large mass.
usage: Collocations: a surge in demand/prices/popularity/cases; a surge of emotion; surge forward. A “power surge” is a sudden increase in electricity.
examples: There has been a surge in demand for online courses.
Prices surged after the announcement.
She felt a surge of anger.
The crowd surged towards the stage.
A power surge damaged the computer.

definition: Careful not to say or do things that might upset or embarrass people.
usage: Collocations: a tactful way/reply/comment. The opposite is “tactless”. The noun “tact” means this skill.
examples: Is there a tactful way to tell him his idea won't work?
She gave a tactful reply to an awkward question.
You need to be tactful when giving feedback.
It wasn't very tactful to mention her ex-husband.
Diplomats must be tactful.

definition: Careful with money and not wasteful.
usage: It is generally positive (sensible), similar to “frugal”. A “thrift shop” (US) sells second-hand goods for charity.
examples: My grandmother was thrifty and never wasted food.
Thrifty shoppers wait for the sales.
Living abroad on a small budget taught me to be thrifty.
They're thrifty, but they spend money on travel.
Thrifty habits helped them save for a house.

definition: Difficult to control or behaving badly; also, of hair, untidy and hard to manage.
usage: Collocations: unruly behaviour/children/crowds/passengers; unruly hair.
examples: The teacher struggled to control the unruly class.
An unruly passenger was removed from the flight.
Police dispersed the unruly crowd.
She tied back her unruly curly hair.
Unruly behaviour will not be tolerated.

definition: Positive, cheerful, and optimistic.
usage: Collocations: an upbeat mood/tone/message/assessment/song. It is informal to neutral and common in business and media.
examples: The manager was upbeat about the company's prospects.
The song has an upbeat rhythm.
Despite the bad news, she remained upbeat.
The report struck an upbeat tone.
Investors were upbeat after strong sales figures.

definition: To express a strong negative feeling, especially anger, often to someone not responsible; as a noun, an opening that lets air or gas out.
usage: Patterns: vent your anger/frustration (on someone); just need to vent. Informally, “vent” means to talk about frustrations to feel better.
examples: Sorry, I just need to vent for a minute.
He vented his frustration on his colleagues.
Social media gives people a place to vent their anger.
Don't block the air vents.
She vented about her terrible day at work.

definition: A sudden wish or idea, especially one that cannot be reasonably explained.
usage: Common phrases: on a whim; at the whim of someone; a passing whim. It suggests unplanned, impulsive behaviour.
examples: We booked the trip on a whim.
Workers shouldn't be at the whim of their managers.
Her interest in painting was just a passing whim.
He changes the rules according to his whims.
On a whim, she dyed her hair blue.

definition: Slightly sad because you are thinking about something you would like to have or have lost.
usage: Collocations: a wistful smile/look/tone/song. The adverb is “wistfully”. It is gentle and literary.
examples: She gave a wistful smile as she looked at the old photos.
He spoke wistfully of his youth.
The song has a wistful, nostalgic tone.
There was a wistful look in her eyes.
I felt a little wistful leaving my hometown.

definition: Able to say clever and funny things.
usage: Collocations: a witty remark/speech/writer/reply/conversation. The noun “wit” means this ability; “witticism” is a witty remark.
examples: She's intelligent and witty.
He made a witty remark that made everyone laugh.
The book is full of witty observations.
Her speech was short, warm, and witty.
Oscar Wilde was famous for his witty sayings.

definition: To want something very much, especially something difficult or impossible to get.
usage: Patterns: yearn for something; yearn to do something. The noun “yearning” means a strong desire. It is literary.
examples: She yearned for a quieter life in the countryside.
Many immigrants yearn to return home.
He yearned for his family's approval.
The people yearned for freedom.
I've always yearned to travel the world.

definition: As an adjective or noun, the total formed by combining several amounts; as a verb (/ˈægrɪgeɪt/), to combine into a total.
usage: Collocations: aggregate demand/data/score/figures; in aggregate. In sport, “on aggregate” means total score over two matches. Common in economics and statistics.
examples: Aggregate demand fell during the recession.
The data was aggregated to protect individual privacy.
The team won 4-2 on aggregate.
In aggregate, the changes had a positive effect.
The website aggregates news from different sources.

definition: Similar in some ways, so that a comparison can be made.
usage: Pattern: analogous to/with something. It is formal and common in academic writing. The noun is “analogy”.
examples: The heart is analogous to a pump.
The situation is analogous to the financial crisis of 2008.
Learning a language is in some ways analogous to learning music.
The two processes are analogous.
The brain's networks are loosely analogous to computer circuits.

definition: Relating to the relationship between a cause and its effect.
usage: Collocations: a causal link/relationship/connection/factor. In research, correlation does not prove a causal relationship. Don't confuse it with “casual”.
examples: There is no evidence of a causal link between the two.
The study cannot prove a causal relationship.
Smoking is a causal factor in lung cancer.
Researchers are investigating the causal connection.
Correlation is not the same as a causal relationship.

definition: To mention something as an example or reason; also, to refer to a source in academic writing.
usage: Collocations: cite a source/study/example/reason; widely cited. The noun “citation” is a reference to a source. Don't confuse it with “site” or “sight”.
examples: Always cite your sources in academic essays.
She cited lack of time as the reason for quitting.
The paper has been widely cited by other researchers.
Can you cite any examples to support your argument?
The minister cited rising costs to justify the decision.

definition: To happen at the same time as something else; also, to be the same or similar.
usage: Pattern: coincide with something. The noun “coincidence” means a surprising chance event.
examples: The festival coincides with the school holidays.
Her visit coincided with my birthday.
Our views on the issue coincide.
The rise in crime coincided with cuts to policing.
The book's release was timed to coincide with the film.

definition: To collect information from different sources and arrange it into a list, report, or book.
usage: Collocations: compile a list/report/database/statistics. A “compilation” is a collection (a compilation album). In computing, to compile is to convert code into a program.
examples: Compile a list of all the sources you used.
The report was compiled by a team of experts.
We compiled statistics from several surveys.
She compiled a database of local businesses.
The data took months to compile.

definition: Relating to ideas and principles rather than to practical details.
usage: Collocations: a conceptual framework/model/understanding/art. In research, a “conceptual framework” explains how key ideas relate. The noun is “concept”.
examples: The study is based on a clear conceptual framework.
Students need a conceptual understanding of maths, not just formulas.
Conceptual art focuses on ideas rather than appearance.
The project is still at the conceptual stage.
There's a conceptual difference between equality and equity.

definition: Happening or existing at the same time.
usage: Collocations: concurrent events/sessions/sentences/users. The adverb “concurrently” is common: “run concurrently”. In law, concurrent sentences are served at the same time.
examples: The conference has several concurrent sessions.
He is serving two concurrent prison sentences.
The two projects ran concurrently.
The software supports up to 100 concurrent users.
Concurrent changes in technology and culture transformed the industry.

definition: To form or make up something; also, to be considered as something.
usage: Patterns: constitute a threat/risk/breach/majority; constitute X per cent of something. It is formal; the noun “constitution” has related meanings.
examples: Women constitute over half of the workforce.
This behaviour may constitute a breach of contract.
What constitutes a healthy diet?
The new rules constitute a major change in policy.
Such actions could constitute a threat to national security.

definition: If two things correlate, there is a relationship between them so that one changes when the other changes.
usage: Patterns: correlate with something; be correlated with; positively/negatively/strongly correlated. The noun “correlation” is key in statistics; correlation does not prove causation.
examples: Income is strongly correlated with health.
Sleep quality correlates with academic performance.
Screen time was negatively correlated with wellbeing.
The two variables do not correlate.
Researchers correlated the survey answers with test scores.

definition: To reach an answer or conclusion by thinking carefully about the known facts.
usage: Patterns: deduce something from something; deduce that… The noun “deduction” also means an amount taken away (tax deductions).
examples: From the evidence, the detective deduced that the thief knew the victim.
Can we deduce anything from these results?
I deduced from her tone that she was upset.
Scientists deduced the age of the rocks from their composition.
It's easy to deduce the ending of the film.

definition: Relating to the structure of populations, such as age, gender, and income; as a noun, a particular group of people.
usage: Collocations: demographic change/trends/data; a target demographic; the 18–25 demographic. The noun “demographics” means population statistics.
examples: Japan faces serious demographic challenges.
The app is popular among a younger demographic.
Demographic changes will affect healthcare spending.
Advertisers target specific demographics.
The survey collected basic demographic information.

definition: To get something from something else; also, to come from or develop from something.
usage: Patterns: derive pleasure/benefit/income from something; be derived from (originate in). The adjective “derivative” means copied or not original.
examples: Many English words are derived from Latin.
She derives great pleasure from gardening.
The company derives most of its income from advertising.
Aspirin was originally derived from tree bark.
What benefits can students derive from studying abroad?

definition: Equal in value, amount, meaning, or importance; as a noun, something that is equal to something else.
usage: Patterns: equivalent to something; the equivalent of something; an equivalent qualification. Common in comparisons and translations.
examples: The prize is equivalent to a year's salary.
There's no exact English equivalent for this Vietnamese word.
A bachelor's degree or equivalent is required.
He drinks the equivalent of ten cups of coffee a day.
The two qualifications are roughly equivalent.

definition: To use known facts to make estimates or conclusions about something unknown or in the future.
usage: Patterns: extrapolate from something; extrapolate trends/results/data. It is common in research, often with caution about small samples.
examples: It's risky to extrapolate from such a small sample.
If we extrapolate current trends, the population will double by 2050.
The findings cannot be extrapolated to other countries.
Scientists extrapolated future temperatures from historical data.
Don't extrapolate too much from one bad day.

definition: To develop a plan, idea, or theory carefully; also, to express something clearly and exactly.
usage: Collocations: formulate a plan/policy/strategy/hypothesis/question/response. The noun “formulation” and “formula” are related.
examples: The government is formulating a new energy policy.
Researchers formulated a hypothesis based on earlier studies.
It took her a moment to formulate a reply.
We need to formulate a clear strategy.
The question was badly formulated.

definition: To make a general statement based on limited facts or examples; also, to apply something to a wider range.
usage: Patterns: generalize about something; generalize from something to something. Results that “generalize” apply beyond the original sample. The noun “generalization” often appears in “sweeping generalizations”.
examples: It's dangerous to generalize about whole nations.
You can't generalize from one person's experience.
These findings may not generalize to older adults.
Try not to generalize in your essay; give specific examples.
Saying all teenagers are lazy is a sweeping generalization.

definition: A set of beliefs or principles, especially one on which a political or economic system is based.
usage: Collocations: political/religious/dominant ideology; left-wing/right-wing ideology. The adjective “ideological” is common (ideological differences).
examples: The two parties have very different ideologies.
Decisions should be based on evidence, not ideology.
The war was fought over ideology as much as territory.
The book examines the ideology behind the movement.
Ideological differences made cooperation difficult.

definition: Stopping and starting repeatedly; not continuous.
usage: Collocations: intermittent rain/showers/problems/fasting/connection. The adverb is “intermittently”.
examples: The forecast is for intermittent showers.
We've had intermittent problems with the Wi-Fi.
Intermittent fasting has become popular.
She suffers from intermittent back pain.
The phone signal here is intermittent.

definition: Always, or almost always, without change.
usage: It is formal and usually goes before the main verb or at the start of a sentence. The adjective “invariable” is less common.
examples: He invariably arrives late.
Cheap products invariably break quickly.
Invariably, the most popular courses fill up first.
Her advice is invariably sensible.
Such projects invariably cost more than expected.

definition: The set of methods and principles used in a particular study or activity.
usage: Collocations: research methodology; the methodology section; a robust/flawed methodology. In dissertations, the methodology chapter explains and justifies how research was done.
examples: The methodology section explains how the data was collected.
Critics questioned the study's methodology.
Students take a course in research methodology.
The company uses an agile methodology for software development.
A flawed methodology can invalidate the results.

definition: A limit or rule that defines how something can be done; in maths and science, a measurable factor.
usage: Usually plural: within the parameters of; set/define/establish the parameters. In computing, a parameter is a value passed to a function.
examples: We must work within the parameters of the budget.
The research parameters were set by the funding body.
Adjust the parameters to see how the results change.
Let's define the parameters of the project first.
The model includes several key parameters.

definition: Relating to the quality or nature of something rather than to numbers.
usage: Collocations: qualitative research/data/analysis/methods. It contrasts with “quantitative”. Interviews and observations are typical qualitative methods.
examples: The study used qualitative methods such as interviews.
Qualitative data helps explain why people behave as they do.
There's a qualitative difference between the two products.
She specializes in qualitative research.
We combined qualitative and quantitative analysis.

definition: Relating to amounts and numbers that can be measured.
usage: Collocations: quantitative research/data/analysis/methods/easing. It contrasts with “qualitative”. Surveys and statistics are typical quantitative methods.
examples: Quantitative research uses statistics to test hypotheses.
We collected quantitative data through an online survey.
The course teaches quantitative skills for business.
Quantitative results showed a 20 per cent improvement.
Central banks used quantitative easing to support the economy.

definition: To improve something by making small changes; also, to make a substance pure.
usage: Collocations: refine a method/skill/technique/argument/search; refined sugar/oil. The adjective “refined” also means elegant and polite.
examples: Use filters to refine your search results.
She spent months refining her technique.
The team refined the design after user testing.
Oil is refined into petrol.
Refined sugar has little nutritional value.

definition: Relating to each of the people or things mentioned separately.
usage: Usually before a plural noun: their respective homes/roles/fields. The adverb “respectively” matches items in order: “A and B scored 80 and 90, respectively.”
examples: After the party, we all went back to our respective homes.
The two scientists are leaders in their respective fields.
The players returned to their respective clubs.
Tom and Sara are 25 and 30, respectively.
Each manager is responsible for their respective team.

definition: A wide range of related ideas, qualities, or opinions; in physics, the range of colours or frequencies.
usage: Collocations: a wide/broad spectrum; across the political spectrum; at both ends of the spectrum; on the autism spectrum. Plural: spectra or spectrums.
examples: Politicians from across the political spectrum supported the bill.
The course covers a broad spectrum of topics.
At the other end of the spectrum are people who never use social media.
Rainbows show the colour spectrum of light.
The disorder exists on a spectrum, from mild to severe.

definition: To combine different ideas, information, or substances to form a new whole; in chemistry, to produce a substance by chemical reactions.
usage: Collocations: synthesize information/research/findings/ideas. British spelling also “synthesise”. A “synthesizer” is an electronic music instrument.
examples: A good literature review synthesizes previous research.
Students must synthesize information from several sources.
Plants synthesize sugar from sunlight.
The drug was first synthesized in the 1950s.
She synthesized the team's ideas into a single plan.

definition: Based on theories and ideas rather than practice or experience; also, possible in theory but not proven.
usage: Collocations: a theoretical framework/approach/model/physics; a theoretical possibility. The adverb “theoretically” means in theory. Opposite: practical, empirical.
examples: The course combines theoretical knowledge with practical skills.
The paper proposes a new theoretical model.
It's a theoretical possibility, but very unlikely.
Theoretically, the plan should work.
She works in theoretical physics.

definition: The curved path of a moving object; also, the direction in which something develops over time.
usage: Collocations: career trajectory; growth trajectory; on an upward/downward trajectory; the trajectory of a ball/missile.
examples: Her career has followed an impressive trajectory.
The company is on an upward trajectory.
Scientists calculated the trajectory of the asteroid.
Current emissions put us on a dangerous trajectory.
The ball's trajectory took it just over the bar.

definition: To support or form the basis of an idea, argument, or system.
usage: Often passive: be underpinned by something. Past forms double the n: underpinned. It is common in academic and policy writing.
examples: Strong evidence underpins the new guidelines.
Trust underpins every successful relationship.
The theory is underpinned by decades of research.
What values underpin the company's culture?
Investment in education underpins long-term growth.

definition: The quality of being logically or factually sound; also, the state of being legally or officially acceptable.
usage: Collocations: question/challenge/test the validity of something; the validity of an argument/claim/study/passport. In research, validity means a test measures what it claims to measure.
examples: Critics questioned the validity of the survey.
The validity of the contract is being challenged in court.
The study's validity depends on its sample.
Check the validity of your passport before booking.
There's some validity in what she says.

definition: Likely to change often; as a noun, a factor that can change, especially in a study or calculation.
usage: Collocations: variable weather/quality/rates; an independent/dependent variable; control for variables. Very common in research and maths.
examples: The quality of the service is highly variable.
Age and income were the main variables in the study.
Mortgages with variable interest rates can be risky.
The weather in spring is very variable.
Researchers controlled for other variables such as gender.

definition: Although; used to add a fact that slightly limits what you have just said.
usage: It is formal and usually introduces a phrase, not a full clause: “a significant, albeit small, improvement”. It is common in academic writing.
examples: Prices rose, albeit slowly.
The results were positive, albeit based on a small sample.
She accepted the offer, albeit reluctantly.
It was a significant, albeit temporary, improvement.
The plan worked, albeit not as well as we hoped.

definition: For this reason; therefore. Also, from this time.
usage: It is formal and common in academic writing. It is often followed by a noun phrase: “hence the name”. “Two years hence” (from now) is old-fashioned.
examples: The data was incomplete; hence, the results are uncertain.
The town is near a hot spring, hence its name.
Costs have risen, hence the increase in prices.
He was ill, hence his absence.
The sample was small and hence not representative.

definition: As a result of the action just mentioned.
usage: It is formal and usually followed by an -ing form: “…, thereby reducing costs.” Common in academic and legal writing.
examples: The company cut its workforce, thereby reducing costs.
Exercise improves blood flow, thereby boosting brain function.
She signed the contract, thereby agreeing to its terms.
The new road bypasses the town, thereby easing congestion.
He missed the deadline, thereby losing the funding.

definition: In spite of what has just been said; however.
usage: It can start a sentence or come at the end: “It was difficult; nonetheless, we finished.” It is slightly formal. Similar to “nevertheless”.
examples: The task was difficult. Nonetheless, we finished on time.
The film is long but enjoyable nonetheless.
Prices are high; nonetheless, demand remains strong.
He was tired but kept working nonetheless.
The study has limitations. It is, nonetheless, an important contribution.

definition: An official examination of an organization's accounts or of how something is being done; as a verb, to carry out such an examination.
usage: Collocations: carry out/conduct an audit; a financial/internal/external/energy audit. An “auditor” performs audits.
examples: The company's accounts are audited every year.
An internal audit revealed serious problems.
We carried out an energy audit of the building.
The auditors found several errors in the accounts.
The government ordered an audit of public spending.

definition: A point where a process or traffic slows down because there is not enough capacity.
usage: Collocations: a production/traffic/supply bottleneck; identify/remove/ease a bottleneck. Common in business and project management.
examples: Approval from head office is the main bottleneck in the process.
The narrow bridge creates a traffic bottleneck.
Supply chain bottlenecks caused delays.
We need to identify the bottlenecks in our workflow.
Hiring more staff eased the bottleneck.

definition: A possible future event that might cause problems, or a plan for dealing with it.
usage: Collocations: a contingency plan/fund/budget; prepare for every contingency. Common in business and project management.
examples: We need a contingency plan in case the supplier fails.
The budget includes a contingency fund for unexpected costs.
Good planners prepare for every contingency.
The airline has contingency arrangements for bad weather.
Add ten per cent contingency to your project budget.

definition: To develop a wider range of products, interests, or investments, especially to reduce risk.
usage: Patterns: diversify into something; diversify your investments/income/skills. The noun is “diversification”.
examples: The company diversified into renewable energy.
Investors should diversify to reduce risk.
Farmers are diversifying by opening shops and cafés.
The economy needs to diversify away from oil.
Diversify your income so you don't depend on one client.

definition: To reduce the number of employees in a company; also, to move to a smaller home or reduce the size of something.
usage: It is a business euphemism for cutting jobs. In everyday life, older people often “downsize” to a smaller house.
examples: The company downsized and cut 500 jobs.
After the children left home, they downsized to a flat.
Many firms downsized during the recession.
She lost her job when the department was downsized.
We're downsizing our office to save on rent.

definition: Fairness and justice, especially in giving people what they need; in finance, the value of shares or of a property minus debts.
usage: Collocations: equity and inclusion; health/educational equity; private equity; home equity. “Equity” differs from “equality”: equity means fairness according to need.
examples: The policy aims to improve equity in education.
Equity means giving people what they need to succeed, not identical treatment.
Private equity firms bought the company.
They have built up a lot of equity in their house.
The investors took an equity stake in the start-up.

definition: The total amount of money spent by a government, organization, or person; also, the use of energy or time.
usage: Collocations: public/government/capital expenditure; expenditure on something; cut/increase expenditure. It is formal; “spending” is the everyday word.
examples: Government expenditure on health has increased.
We need to reduce expenditure on travel.
Public expenditure was cut during the crisis.
Keep a record of all your monthly expenditure.
The task required a huge expenditure of time and energy.

definition: A statement about what is likely to happen, based on information; as a verb, to predict.
usage: Collocations: a weather/sales/economic forecast; forecast growth/rain. Past forms: forecast or forecasted.
examples: The weather forecast says it will rain tomorrow.
Economists forecast growth of two per cent next year.
Sales were lower than forecast.
The company revised its profit forecast.
Heavy snow is forecast for the weekend.

definition: A person who currently holds an official position; as an adjective, currently holding a position. Also, necessary as a duty.
usage: Collocations: the incumbent president/mayor; defeat the incumbent; it is incumbent on/upon someone to do something (formal: it is their duty).
examples: The incumbent president is seeking a second term.
She defeated the incumbent by a narrow margin.
It is incumbent on all of us to protect the environment.
New companies struggle to compete with incumbent firms.
The incumbent mayor promised more parks.

definition: The detailed organization of a complicated activity; in business, the management of transporting and storing goods.
usage: It takes a plural or singular verb. Collocations: the logistics of something; a logistics company/manager. The adjective is “logistical” (logistical problems).
examples: Organizing the logistics of a wedding takes months.
The company works in logistics and transport.
We need to think about the logistics of moving the office.
Problems with logistics delayed the aid deliveries.
Online shopping depends on efficient logistics.

definition: The joining together of two or more companies or organizations into one.
usage: Collocations: a merger between/of A and B; announce/approve/block a merger; mergers and acquisitions (M&A). The verb is “merge”.
examples: The merger created the largest bank in the country.
Regulators blocked the proposed merger.
Hundreds of jobs were lost after the merger.
The two universities announced a merger.
She works in mergers and acquisitions.

definition: Complete control of the supply of a product or service by one company or group; also, exclusive possession of something.
usage: Patterns: a monopoly on/of something; have/hold/break a monopoly. “Nobody has a monopoly on wisdom” means no one is always right.
examples: The company has a monopoly on the local water supply.
Governments try to prevent monopolies.
The state broke up the telecom monopoly.
No political party has a monopoly on good ideas.
Monopolies can lead to higher prices for consumers.

definition: A specialized area of the market or of an activity; also, a role or position that suits someone well.
usage: Collocations: a niche market/product/audience; find your niche; carve out a niche. It is also pronounced /nɪtʃ/, especially in American English.
examples: The company serves a niche market of vintage car owners.
She finally found her niche as a science writer.
Small brands can carve out a niche against big competitors.
The magazine has a niche audience.
Vegan cheese was once a niche product.

definition: To pay another company or people outside your organization to do work instead of doing it yourself.
usage: Patterns: outsource something to a company/country. The noun is “outsourcing”. Common in business and economics discussions about jobs.
examples: Many companies outsource their customer service to other countries.
We outsource our IT support.
Outsourcing can reduce costs but affect quality.
The council outsourced rubbish collection to a private firm.
Small businesses often outsource accounting.

definition: A collection of examples of someone's work; also, a set of investments, products, or responsibilities.
usage: Collocations: a design/student portfolio; an investment/product portfolio; a minister's portfolio (area of responsibility). A “portfolio career” combines several part-time jobs.
examples: Designers need a strong portfolio to get jobs.
She has a diverse investment portfolio.
The company plans to expand its product portfolio.
Students submit a portfolio of work at the end of the course.
He was given the education portfolio in the new government.

definition: A period when a country's economy is not successful, trade and industry decline, and unemployment rises.
usage: Collocations: go into/enter/come out of a recession; a deep/global recession. Technically, two consecutive quarters of negative growth. The verb “recede” is related.
examples: The economy went into recession last year.
Many businesses closed during the recession.
Economists fear a global recession.
Unemployment rose sharply in the recession.
The country is slowly coming out of recession.

definition: The income that a company or government receives regularly.
usage: Collocations: generate/increase revenue; advertising/tax/sales revenue; a source of revenue. Often plural: revenues.
examples: The company's revenue grew by 15 per cent.
Advertising is the main source of revenue for the website.
Tax revenues fell during the recession.
Tourism generates significant revenue for the city.
The new product line boosted revenues.

definition: Able to grow or be made larger without losing effectiveness.
usage: Collocations: a scalable business/model/system/solution. Very common in start-up and technology language. The noun is “scalability”; the verb “scale up”.
examples: Investors look for scalable business models.
The software is scalable to millions of users.
We need a scalable solution, not a temporary fix.
Online courses are more scalable than classroom teaching.
Is your idea scalable beyond your local area?

definition: A person or group with an interest in a business, project, or decision and who is affected by it.
usage: Collocations: key/external/internal stakeholders; consult/engage stakeholders. Common in business, project management, and public policy.
examples: We consulted all key stakeholders before making the decision.
Employees, customers, and suppliers are all stakeholders.
The project involves many different stakeholders.
Stakeholder feedback shaped the final plan.
Parents are important stakeholders in education.

definition: To make a system or organization simpler and more efficient; also, to give something a smooth shape so it moves easily through air or water.
usage: Collocations: streamline a process/procedure/operations/the application system. The adjective “streamlined” means efficient or smoothly shaped.
examples: The new software will streamline the ordering process.
The company streamlined its operations to cut costs.
We need to streamline the application procedure.
Fish have streamlined bodies for fast swimming.
A streamlined team can make decisions faster.

definition: An amount of something that is more than what is needed; in finance, the amount by which income is greater than spending.
usage: Collocations: a budget/trade surplus; surplus food/stock/energy; in surplus. The opposite in finance is “deficit”.
examples: The country has a large trade surplus.
Supermarkets donate surplus food to charities.
The government ran a budget surplus last year.
Solar panels can sell surplus energy back to the grid.
There's a surplus of teachers in some subjects.

definition: The total value of goods or services sold by a company in a period; also, the rate at which employees leave and are replaced.
usage: Collocations: annual turnover; staff/employee turnover; high/low turnover. In British English, “turnover” often means total sales; in American English, “revenue” is more common.
examples: The company has an annual turnover of £5 million.
High staff turnover is costly for businesses.
The restaurant industry has a high turnover of workers.
Turnover increased by 10 per cent this year.
Better pay helped reduce employee turnover.

definition: To produce or provide a result, profit, or crop; also, to give way to pressure or to other traffic. As a noun, the amount produced.
usage: Collocations: yield results/benefits/a profit/information; crop yield; yield to pressure/temptation. In finance, “yield” is the income from an investment.
examples: The research yielded some surprising results.
New farming methods have increased crop yields.
The government refused to yield to pressure.
The investment yields a return of five per cent a year.
Drivers must yield to pedestrians at crossings.

definition: Very determined not to change your opinion or decision.
usage: Patterns: adamant that…; adamant about something. It usually follows “be”. The adverb is “adamantly”.
examples: She was adamant that she had locked the door.
He is adamant about not moving abroad.
The minister remains adamant that taxes will not rise.
My parents were adamant: no phones at dinner.
Despite the evidence, he adamantly denied any wrongdoing.

definition: Having a natural ability to do something skilfully.
usage: Patterns: adept at/in (doing) something. It is slightly formal. Synonyms: skilled, proficient.
examples: She's adept at handling difficult customers.
Children are adept at using new technology.
He became adept in several programming languages.
Politicians are adept at avoiding direct answers.
You'll need to be adept at managing your time.

definition: Able to move quickly and easily; also, able to think quickly or adapt to change.
usage: Collocations: an agile player/mind/company; agile methods (a flexible project management approach in software). The noun is “agility”.
examples: Cats are extremely agile animals.
Small companies can be more agile than large ones.
Even at 80, she has an agile mind.
The team uses agile methods to develop software.
Goalkeepers need to be strong and agile.

definition: To make someone feel that they do not belong or are no longer supported; to make someone less friendly towards you.
usage: Patterns: alienate someone (from something); alienate voters/customers/friends. The noun “alienation” is common in sociology.
examples: The new policy alienated many loyal voters.
His rude behaviour alienated his colleagues.
Many young people feel alienated from politics.
Raising prices too much could alienate customers.
She didn't want to alienate her family by moving away.

definition: To mention something or someone indirectly.
usage: Pattern: allude to something. The noun “allusion” is an indirect reference, often in literature. Don't confuse it with “elude” (escape).
examples: She alluded to problems in her marriage but gave no details.
The title alludes to a famous poem.
He didn't mention her by name, but he clearly alluded to her.
The speech alluded to recent political scandals.
Many of his lyrics allude to classic novels.

definition: Showing care and concern for others' wellbeing without expecting any personal benefit.
usage: Collocations: altruistic behaviour/motives/acts. The noun “altruism” is common in ethics and psychology.
examples: Her motives for volunteering were entirely altruistic.
Donating a kidney to a stranger is a truly altruistic act.
Some scientists ask whether animals show altruistic behaviour.
Few business decisions are purely altruistic.
Altruistic people often report higher levels of happiness.

definition: To make someone feel angry or hostile towards you.
usage: British spelling also “antagonise”. Related: “antagonist” (an opponent; in fiction, the main enemy) and “antagonistic” (hostile).
examples: He didn't want to antagonize his new boss.
The remarks antagonized many voters.
Try not to antagonize the neighbours.
The government's actions antagonized its allies.
There's no need to antagonize people unnecessarily.

definition: To make someone less angry or stop them from attacking by giving them what they want.
usage: Typical objects: critics, voters, shareholders, protesters. “Appeasement” refers especially to giving in to aggressive powers to avoid war, often seen negatively.
examples: The company cut prices to appease angry customers.
The concession was made to appease critics.
Nothing seemed to appease the protesters.
She tried to appease her crying baby with a toy.
Historians criticize attempts to appease dictators.

definition: Quick to understand situations and use them to your advantage.
usage: Collocations: an astute observer/businesswoman/investor/move/observation. It is admiring, similar to “shrewd”.
examples: She's an astute businesswoman.
That was a very astute observation.
An astute investor bought shares before the price rose.
His astute questions impressed the interviewers.
Astute readers will notice the clues early in the novel.

definition: Showing a willingness to take risks or surprising boldness, sometimes in a way that seems rude.
usage: Collocations: an audacious plan/attempt/move/goal. It can be admiring (bold) or critical (cheeky). The noun is “audacity” (“He had the audacity to…”).
examples: It was an audacious plan to climb the mountain in winter.
The thieves carried out an audacious robbery in daylight.
The company has set an audacious goal of zero emissions by 2030.
Asking for a pay rise after one week was audacious, to say the least.
Her audacious design surprised the judges.

definition: Very ordinary and lacking originality, and therefore boring.
usage: Collocations: banal conversation/remarks/lyrics/plot. The noun is “banality”. Pronunciation varies; /bəˈnɑːl/ is common in British English.
examples: The song's lyrics are rather banal.
We made banal conversation about the weather.
Critics described the film's plot as banal.
His speech was full of banal clichés.
Even banal daily tasks can be meaningful.

definition: Kind and helpful, wanting to do good things for others.
usage: Collocations: a benevolent ruler/smile/society/fund. “A benevolent dictator” is an absolute ruler who acts for the people's good. The noun is “benevolence”.
examples: The old man gave us a benevolent smile.
The charity was founded by a benevolent businessman.
Some describe him as a benevolent dictator.
The company is not a benevolent organization; it wants profit.
She is remembered as a benevolent teacher.

definition: Very confused and unable to understand what is happening.
usage: Patterns: bewildered by something; a bewildered look. The adjective “bewildering” describes something very confusing.
examples: The tourists looked bewildered by the subway map.
She was bewildered by his sudden change of mood.
He gave me a bewildered look.
Many voters are bewildered by the new rules.
Bewildered passengers waited for news of their delayed flight.

definition: To direct a large number of questions, messages, or information at someone; literally, to attack a place with bombs or shells.
usage: Pattern: bombard someone with something (questions/emails/adverts/information). The noun is “bombardment”.
examples: Reporters bombarded the minister with questions.
We are bombarded with advertising every day.
My inbox is bombarded with spam.
The city was bombarded for weeks during the war.
Children are bombarded with information online.

definition: A phrase, idea, or situation that has been used so often that it has become boring and lost its effect.
usage: Also written “cliche”. Collocations: an old/tired cliché; avoid clichés. The adjective “clichéd” describes unoriginal work. Teachers often advise avoiding clichés in essays.
examples: “Time flies” is a cliché, but it's true.
Try to avoid clichés in your writing.
The film is full of romantic clichés.
It's a cliché that money can't buy happiness.
His speech relied on tired clichés.

definition: Involved with others in an illegal or wrong activity.
usage: Pattern: complicit in something. Silence or inaction can make someone complicit. The noun is “complicity”.
examples: Several officials were complicit in the fraud.
By staying silent, we become complicit.
The company was accused of being complicit in human rights abuses.
He denied being complicit in the cover-up.
Bystanders who do nothing are partly complicit.

definition: To accept or allow behaviour that is morally wrong or offensive.
usage: It is usually negative: “We cannot condone violence.” It means to tolerate or approve, not to forgive.
examples: The school does not condone bullying of any kind.
I understand why he did it, but I can't condone it.
The government was accused of condoning police violence.
Silence can look like condoning bad behaviour.
No religion condones such cruelty.

definition: Done quickly and without much attention to detail.
usage: Collocations: a cursory glance/look/examination/inspection/reading. It is critical when care was needed.
examples: I only gave the report a cursory glance.
A cursory inspection missed serious problems.
Even a cursory reading shows the argument is weak.
The doctor gave him only a cursory examination.
The issue received only cursory attention in the meeting.

definition: To laugh at someone or something or say they are stupid or worthless.
usage: Patterns: deride someone/something as… It is formal. The noun is “derision” and the adjective “derisory” (ridiculously small: a derisory offer).
examples: Critics derided the plan as unrealistic.
His early paintings were derided by experts.
She was derided for her strong accent.
The proposal was derided as a publicity stunt.
Once derided, the idea is now widely accepted.

definition: To feel a very strong dislike and lack of respect for someone or something.
usage: It is stronger than “hate” in suggesting contempt. It is not usually used in continuous forms.
examples: She despises people who lie.
He despised his job but needed the money.
I despise cruelty to animals.
The dictator was despised by his people.
They despise each other but have to work together.

definition: Completely lacking something.
usage: Pattern: devoid of something (devoid of meaning/emotion/life/humour). It is formal and always followed by “of”.
examples: The film was completely devoid of humour.
His voice was devoid of emotion.
The landscape was devoid of trees.
The speech was devoid of any real content.
The room was cold and devoid of furniture.

definition: Skill in using your hands or body; also, skill in thinking or dealing with situations.
usage: Collocations: manual dexterity; with great dexterity; verbal/political dexterity. The adjective is “dexterous”.
examples: Surgeons need excellent manual dexterity.
She handled the difficult questions with great dexterity.
Video games may improve hand dexterity.
The pianist played with remarkable dexterity.
The job requires both physical and mental dexterity.

definition: A feeling that someone or something is not good enough to deserve respect or attention; as a verb, to regard with this feeling.
usage: Patterns: disdain for something; with disdain; disdain to do something (formal). The adjective “disdainful” describes a contemptuous attitude.
examples: She looked at the cheap wine with disdain.
He has open disdain for politicians.
Many artists disdain commercial success.
Her disdain for rules got her into trouble.
He spoke of his rivals with barely concealed disdain.

definition: To gradually disappear or make something disappear; also, to waste money or energy.
usage: Typical subjects: fog, heat, anger, tension, fears, energy. It is formal.
examples: The fog dissipated by mid-morning.
His anger slowly dissipated.
Tension in the room dissipated after the joke.
Heat dissipates quickly through metal.
He dissipated his fortune on gambling.

definition: Strongly believing that your opinions are right and refusing to consider other views.
usage: Collocations: a dogmatic approach/attitude/belief. It is critical. A “dogma” is a set of beliefs accepted without question.
examples: He's very dogmatic about how children should be raised.
A dogmatic approach to science slows progress.
Try not to be so dogmatic; listen to other opinions.
The party's dogmatic stance alienated moderate voters.
Good teachers avoid being dogmatic.

definition: Not active or growing now, but able to become active later.
usage: Collocations: a dormant volcano/virus/account/talent; lie/remain dormant. It is common in science and business.
examples: The volcano has been dormant for centuries.
Seeds can lie dormant in the soil for years.
The virus can remain dormant in the body.
Her dormant interest in music was revived.
Banks may close dormant accounts.

definition: Including a wide variety of styles, ideas, or sources.
usage: Collocations: eclectic taste/mix/collection/style. It is usually positive.
examples: She has eclectic taste in music, from jazz to K-pop.
The café has an eclectic mix of furniture.
The festival offers an eclectic programme of events.
His style is eclectic, combining old and new.
The library holds an eclectic collection of books.

definition: Believing that all people are equal and should have equal rights and opportunities.
usage: Collocations: an egalitarian society/principle/system/approach. The noun “egalitarianism” is used in political philosophy.
examples: Scandinavian countries are known for egalitarian values.
The company has an egalitarian culture with no private offices.
They aim to build a more egalitarian society.
Egalitarian principles underpin the education system.
Their marriage is egalitarian; they share all housework.

definition: Someone or something that is mysterious and difficult to understand.
usage: Collocations: remain an enigma; something of an enigma. The adjective “enigmatic” is common: an enigmatic smile.
examples: The artist remains an enigma even to her friends.
How the pyramids were built was long an enigma.
He's something of an enigma at the office.
The Mona Lisa is famous for her enigmatic smile.
The cause of the illness is still an enigma.

definition: Lasting for only a very short time.
usage: Collocations: ephemeral fame/beauty/pleasure/trends. It is literary; “short-lived” is more common.
examples: Fame on social media is often ephemeral.
Fashion trends are increasingly ephemeral.
The beauty of cherry blossoms is ephemeral.
Instagram stories are ephemeral, disappearing after a day.
Their happiness proved ephemeral.

definition: A perfect or typical example of a particular quality or type.
usage: Pattern: the epitome of something (elegance/cool/success/kindness). Note the pronunciation: four syllables, ending in /mi/. The verb “epitomize” means to be a perfect example.
examples: She is the epitome of elegance.
The hotel is the epitome of luxury.
He was the epitome of a gentleman.
This dish is the epitome of Vietnamese street food.
The building epitomizes modern Japanese design.

definition: Full of energy, excitement, and cheerfulness.
usage: Collocations: an exuberant personality/crowd/celebration/style. The noun is “exuberance” (youthful exuberance).
examples: The exuberant crowd danced in the streets.
She has an exuberant personality.
The children were exuberant on the last day of school.
The painting is full of exuberant colour.
His exuberant celebration earned him a yellow card.

definition: Having or showing very strong and sincere feelings or beliefs.
usage: Collocations: a fervent supporter/believer/hope/prayer/admirer. The adverb “fervently” is common: “fervently hope”.
examples: She is a fervent supporter of animal rights.
It is my fervent hope that peace will return.
He was a fervent believer in free education.
The team has a fervent fan base.
I fervently hope you're right.

definition: A complete failure, especially one that is embarrassing or ridiculous.
usage: Collocations: a complete/total fiasco; turn into/end in a fiasco. Plural: fiascos. It is informal to neutral.
examples: The product launch was a complete fiasco.
The party ended in a fiasco when the police arrived.
The new ticketing system turned into a fiasco.
After last year's fiasco, they hired professional organizers.
The election was a fiasco for the ruling party.

definition: Very obvious and shocking, especially when breaking a rule or law.
usage: Collocations: a flagrant violation/breach/disregard/abuse. It is similar to “blatant” but more formal.
examples: The attack was a flagrant violation of international law.
The company showed flagrant disregard for safety.
It was a flagrant abuse of power.
The player was sent off for a flagrant foul.
Such flagrant cheating cannot be ignored.

definition: To shock or excite someone into taking action.
usage: Patterns: galvanize someone into action; galvanize support/opinion. British spelling also “galvanise”. Technically, galvanized steel is coated with zinc.
examples: The disaster galvanized the community into action.
Her speech galvanized support for the campaign.
The defeat galvanized the team.
Young activists have galvanized public opinion on climate change.
The fence is made of galvanized steel.

definition: Enjoying the company of other people; sociable. Of animals, living in groups.
usage: Collocations: a gregarious person/nature/personality. Opposite: introverted, solitary.
examples: She's gregarious and makes friends easily.
His gregarious nature makes him a great host.
Sheep are gregarious animals.
Gregarious people often enjoy jobs with lots of social contact.
Despite being gregarious, he values time alone.

definition: Consisting of parts or people that are very different from each other.
usage: Collocations: a heterogeneous group/population/sample/mixture. It is formal and common in research. Opposite: homogeneous.
examples: The class is heterogeneous, with students of very different levels.
Cities have increasingly heterogeneous populations.
The sample was too heterogeneous to draw clear conclusions.
The party is a heterogeneous coalition of interests.
Teaching heterogeneous groups requires flexibility.

definition: Consisting of parts or people that are similar or of the same kind.
usage: Collocations: a homogeneous group/society/population/mixture. Some writers also use “homogenous”. Opposite: heterogeneous.
examples: Japan is often described as a relatively homogeneous society.
Mix the ingredients until the mixture is homogeneous.
The study's participants were a homogeneous group of students.
Globalization may make cultures more homogeneous.
The team is too homogeneous to generate new ideas.

definition: Peculiar to a particular person; unusual and individual.
usage: Collocations: an idiosyncratic style/approach/habit/taste. The noun “idiosyncrasy” means an unusual habit or feature.
examples: The writer has a highly idiosyncratic style.
His idiosyncratic teaching methods are popular with students.
Everyone has idiosyncratic habits.
The museum reflects the founder's idiosyncratic tastes.
Her idiosyncratic way of dressing makes her stand out.

definition: Perfect, with no mistakes or faults.
usage: Collocations: impeccable manners/taste/English/timing/record/service. The adverb “impeccably” is common: “impeccably dressed”.
examples: She speaks impeccable English.
The hotel's service was impeccable.
He has an impeccable safety record.
The comedian's timing is impeccable.
He's always impeccably dressed.

definition: Very poor; also, made weaker or lacking in quality.
usage: Collocations: impoverished families/communities/areas; an impoverished vocabulary/culture. It is formal; “poor” is the everyday word.
examples: The charity helps impoverished families.
Many people in the impoverished region lack clean water.
War left the country impoverished.
Without arts education, children's lives are impoverished.
The soil was impoverished by years of overuse.

definition: Strange or out of place because it does not match its surroundings.
usage: Collocations: an incongruous mix/sight/combination. It is formal and often describes something mildly absurd.
examples: A modern glass building looks incongruous in the old town.
The cheerful music was incongruous with the sad scene.
It was an incongruous sight: a cow in the city centre.
His formal suit seemed incongruous at the beach party.
The film mixes horror and comedy in an incongruous way.

definition: Firmly fixed and difficult to change or remove.
usage: Collocations: deeply ingrained habits/attitudes/beliefs/prejudices; ingrained dirt. Often used with “deeply”.
examples: These attitudes are deeply ingrained in our culture.
Bad habits can become ingrained.
Ingrained prejudices are hard to change.
Respect for elders is ingrained in Vietnamese society.
The carpet was full of ingrained dirt.

definition: Always wanting more and never satisfied.
